        "text_sha256": "6fbaf67674d4e4f6e2cdb830663f2349a150fb69b239a972d0ba553f2ae14289",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "The choice of similarity function is also important. In this work, we use cosine similarity, a widely\nadopted metric for measuring vector similarity in models that process vision and language. For\ninstance, CLIP also employs cosine similarity to assess the similarity between text and image\nfeatures. Although it might not be the optimal choice, we believe that cosine similarity is a general,\nrepresentative, and valid choice for facilitating fast retrieval tasks.\nD.4\nThe Quality of Retrieval\nWe quantify the quality of our retrieval method as follows: We examine the retrieval subgraph, and if\nthe label is contained within it, we consider it a successful retrieval. We calculate the retrieval success\nrate of our method and the retrieval method proposed in KAPING [1] on the WebQSP dataset.\nTable 11: The quality of retrieval methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nMethod\nRetrieval Accuracy\nKAPING [1] (top-k triple retrieval)\n60.81\nG-Retriever\n70.49\nAs shown in Table 11, these results validate the effectiveness of our retrieval method. In contrast to\nthe triple-based retrieval in KAPING, which relies on the similarity between triples and the query,\nour PCST-based subgraph retrieval is more accurate as it takes the graph structure into account. By\ndesign, it retrieves connected subgraphs, capturing not just nodes or edges with high relevance scores,\nbut also those that act as \"bridges\" connecting other highly relevant nodes and edges.\n18\n\nE\nDiscussion on the Complexity\nE.1\nThe integration of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "7c357b448e5680712a09e43acea7708d22e67cc997b09b517737f7b0694e07e6",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "IRCoT + HippoRAG (Contriever)\n43.9\n56.6\n75.3\n93.4\n65.8\n82.3\n61.7\n77.4\nIRCoT + HippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n45.3\n57.6\n75.8\n93.9\n67.0\n83.0\n62.7\n78.2\n3.4\nImplementation Details\nBy default, we use GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 [55] with temperature of 0 as our LLM L and Contriever\n[35] or ColBERTv2 [70] as our retriever M. We use 100 examples from MuSiQue’s training data\nto tune HippoRAG’s two hyperparameters: the synonymy threshold τ at 0.8 and the PPR damping\nfactor at 0.5, which determines the probability that PPR will restart a random walk from the query\nnodes instead of continuing to explore the graph. Generally, we find that HippoRAG’s performance\nis rather robust to its hyperparameters. More implementation details can be found in Appendix H.\n4\n"

        "text_sha256": "2fb4210cc632b644a2704ddebc576b1d61565aa93c41eee447907c70b2cb6fd7",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "Although offline indexing time and costs are higher for HippoRAG than IRCoT—around 10 times\nslower and $15 more expensive for every 10,000 passages 7, these costs can be dramatically reduced\nby leveraging open source LLMs. As shown in our ablation study in Table 5 Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct\n[1] performs similarly to GPT-3.5 Turbo even though it can be deployed locally using vLLM [40]\nand 4 H100 GPUs to index 10,000 documents in around 4 hours, as seen in Table 18. Additionally,\nsince these costs could be even further reduced by locally deploying this model, the barriers for using\nHippoRAG at scale could be well within the computational budget of many organizations. Finally,\nwe note that even if LLM generation cost drops, the online retrieval efficiency gains discussed above\nremain intact given that the number of tokens required for IRCoT vs. HippoRAG stay constant and\nLLM use is likely to also remain the system’s main computational bottleneck.\nTable 18: Average cost and latency measurements for offline indexing using GPT-3.5 Turbo and\nlocally deployed Llama-3.1 (8B and 70B) using vLLM on 10,000 passages.\nModel\nMetric\nColBERTv2\nIRCoT\nHippoRAG\nGPT-3.5 Turbo-1106 (Main Results)\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n0\n15\nTime (minutes)\n7\n7\n60\nGPT-3.5 Turbo-0125\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n0\n8\nTime (minutes)\n7\n7\n60\nLlama-3.1-8B-Instruct\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n0\n0\nTime (minutes)\n7\n7\n120\nLlama-3.1-70B-Instruct\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n0\n0\nTime (minutes)\n7\n7\n250\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "81899faeebab6f6f4c3f4d9b271d5d9426167a1c12f571c4faec7b5fe4b510c3",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "6We use a single thread to query the OpenAI API for online retrieval in both IRCoT and HippoRAG. Since\nIRCoT is an iterative process and each of the iterations must be done sequentially, these speed comparisons are\nappropriate.\n7To speed up indexing, we use 10 threads querying gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 through the OpenAI API in parallel.\nAt the time of writing, the cost of the API is $1 for a million input tokens and $2 for a million output tokens.\n28\n\nH\nImplementation Details & Compute Requirements\nApart from the details included in §3.4, we use implementations based on PyTorch [59] and Hug-\ngingFace [86] for both Contriever [35] and ColBERTv2 [70]. We use the python-igraph [13]\nimplementation of the PPR algorithm. For BM25, we employ Elastic Search [24]. For multi-step\nretrieval, we use the same prompt implementation as IRCoT [78] and retrieve the top-10 passages at\neach step. We set the maximum number of reasoning steps to 2 for HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand 4 for MuSiQue due to their maximum reasoning chain length. We combine IRCoT with different\nretrievers by replacing its base retriever BM25 with each retrieval method, including HippoRAG,\nnoted as “IRCoT + HippoRAG” below.8 For the QA reader, we use top-5 retrieved passages as the\ncontext and 1-shot QA demonstration with CoT prompting strategy [78].\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "194de2ee4d7893097517b36bb7f0c796fc9a3c3074b86643fdc29c5af5c50461",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "After the query nodes Rq are found, we run the PPR algorithm over the hippocampal index, i.e., a\nKG with |N| nodes and |E| + |E′| edges (triple-based and synonymy-based), using a personalized\nprobability distribution #»n defined over N, in which each query node has equal probability and all\nother nodes have a probability of zero. This allows probability mass to be distributed to nodes that are\nprimarily in the (joint) neighborhood of the query nodes, such as Professor Thomas, and contribute to\neventual retrieval. After running the PPR algorithm, we obtain an updated probability distribution\n#»\nn′ over N. Finally, in order to obtain passage scores, we multiply #»\nn′ with the previously defined P\nmatrix to obtain #»p , a ranking score for each passage, which we use for retrieval.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "6fd99e0edc4b65a8e5213842eddd8adaea5115db099f0b9342e4b18cb94d16ae",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "OpenIE Alternatives. To determine if using a closed model like GPT-3.5 is essential to retain our\nperformance improvements, we replace it with an end-to-end OpenIE model REBEL [34] as well\nas the 8B and 70B instruction-tuned versions of Llama-3.1, a class of strong open-weight LLMs\n[1]. As shown in Table 5 row 2, building our KG using REBEL results in large performance drops,\nunderscoring the importance of LLM flexibility. Specifically, GPT-3.5 produces twice as many triples\nas REBEL, indicating its bias against producing triples with general concepts and leaving many\nuseful associations behind.\nIn terms of open-weight LLMs, Table 5 (rows 3-4) shows that the performance of Llama-3.1-8B is\ncompetitive with GPT-3.5 in all datasets except for 2Wiki, where performance drops substantially.\nNevertheless, the stronger 70B counterpart outperforms GPT-3.5 in two out of three datasets and is still\ncompetitive in 2Wiki. The strong performance of Llama-3.1-70B and the comparable performance of\neven the 8B model is encouraging since it offers a cheaper alternative for indexing over large corpora.\nThe graph statistics for these OpenIE alternatives can be found in Appendix C.\nTo understand the relationship between OpenIE and retrieval performance more deeply, we extract\n239 gold triples from 20 examples from the MuSiQue training set. We then perform a small-scale\nintrinsic evaluation using the CaRB [6] framework for OpenIE. We find that both Llama-3.1-Instruct\n"

        "text": "A.7.4\nRETRIEVAL COSTS\nWe present the retrieval time and number of retrieved reasoning paths in Figure 4. From results,\nwe can see that the retrieval time increases with the number of top-K relation paths. Therefore, we\nshould select a proper K to balance the retrieval time and the number of retrieved reasoning paths.\nIn experiments, we set K = 3.\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "One of HippoRAG’s main advantages against iterative retrieval methods is the dramatic online\nretrieval efficiency gains brought on by its single-step multi-hop retrieval ability in terms of both\ncost and time. Specifically, as seen in Table 17, retrieval costs for IRCoT are 10 to 30 times higher\nthan HippoRAG since it only requires extracting relevant named entities from the query instead of\nprocessing all of the retrieved documents. In systems with extremely high usage, a cost difference of\nan order of magnitude such as this one could be extremely important. The difference with IRCoT in\nterms of latency is also substantial, although more challenging to measure exactly. Also as seen in\nTable 17, HippoRAG can be 6 to 13 times faster than IRCoT, depending on the number of retrieval\nrounds that need to be executed (2-4 in our experiments).6\nTable 17: Average cost and efficiency measurements for online retrieval using GPT-3.5 Turbo on\n1,000 queries.\nColBERTv2\nIRCoT\nHippoRAG\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n1-3\n0.1\nTime (minutes)\n1\n20-40\n3\n"

        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 659,
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly.         "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 596,
        "text": "Enhancing Scalability and Efficiency in Graph LLMs. Recent research endeavors have explored\ntranslating graphs into natural language, such as by flattening nodes and edges into a text sequence,\nenabling their processing by LLMs for graph-based tasks [56, 6]. However, this method faces critical\nscalability issues.         "score": 8.029783930396661e-05,

        "start_char": 298,
        "end_char": 935,
        "text": "lability issues. G-Retriever overcomes these issues with its RAG component, which allows for\neffective scaling to larger graphs by selectively retrieving only relevant parts of the graph.\nTailoring the RAG Approach to Graphs.     "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567": [

        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 645,
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.00016603845870122313,
        "pair_tokens": 198
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567",
        "start_char": 322,
        "end_char": 975,
        "text": "rge language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\n",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.04569203406572342,
        "pair_tokens": 198

        "start_char": 648,
        "end_char": 1304,
        "text": "rld textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask ",
        "document_tokens": 160,

        "end_char": 1542,
        "text": "he first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem.         "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 710,
        "text": "One of HippoRAG’s main advantages against iterative retrieval methods is the dramatic online\nretrieval efficiency gains brought on by its single-step multi-hop retrieval ability in terms of both\ncost and time. The difference with IRCoT in\nterms of latency is also substantial, although more challenging to measure exactly. Also as seen in\nTable 17, Hippo",

        "text": "amed entities from the query instead of\nprocessing all of the retrieved documents. The difference with IRCoT in\nterms of latency is also substantial, although more challenging to measure exactly.         "text": "Tackling Hallucination in Graph LLMs. LLMs are prone to hallucination, a phenomenon where the\ngenerated content is factually inaccurate or nonsensical [12].         "text": "-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31].         "text": "The Need for a Comprehensive GraphQA Benchmark. Despite extensive research in QA, a com-\nprehensive benchmark specifically tailored for the graph modality is lacking. In contrast to existing\nbenchmarks that focus on basic graph-based reasoning tasks such as node degree, edge existence, and\nshortest path [6, 44], our benchmark addresses complex and real-world graph applications including\ncommon sense reasoning, scene understanding, and knowledge graph reasoning (refer to Figure ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.00020988310279790312,

        "start_char": 340,
        "end_char": 996,
        "text": "aph modality is lacking.         "text": "The findings on MetaQA are presented in Table 2.\nThe performance of KG-GPT is impressive, scoring\n96.3%, 94.4%, and 94.0% on 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-\nhop tasks respectively. The qualitative\nresults including the graphs retrieved by KG-GPT\nare in Appendix E.2.\n4.3\nError Analysis\n"

        "text_sha256": "d0a1cfcc148248fe6fe6ff3aa310a7a548ac4cc0c467a45281828705a5ce8fa2",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "For evaluation on FACTKG, we use the same base-\nlines as in Kim et al. (2023). These baselines are\ndivided into two distinct categories: Claim Only\nand With Evidence. In the Claim Only setting, the\nmodels are provided only with the claim as their\ninput and predict the label. For this setting, in ad-\ndition to the existing baselines, we implement a\n12-shot ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2023b) baseline. In\nthe With Evidence scenario, models consist of an\nevidence graph retriever and a claim verification\nmodel. We employ the KG version of GEAR (Zhou\net al., 2019) as a fully supervised model.\nIn our exploration of MetaQA, we use a selection\nof prototypical baselines well-known in the field\nof KGQA. These include models such as KV-Mem\n(Xu et al., 2019), GraftNet (Sun et al., 2018), Em-\nbedKGQA (Saxena et al., 2020), NSM (He et al.,\n2021), and UniKGQA (Jiang et al., 2022), which\noperate in a fully supervised fashion. Additionally,\nwe implement a 12-shot ChatGPT baseline.\n4\nResults & Analysis\n4.1\nFACTKG\nWe evaluated the models’ prediction capability for\nlabels (i.e. Supported or Refuted) and presented\nthe accuracy score in Table 1. As a result, KG-GPT\noutperforms Claim Only models BERT, BlueBERT,\nand Flan-T5 with performance enhancements of\n7.48%, 12.75%, and 9.98% absolute, respectively.\nIt also outperforms 12-shot ChatGPT by 4.20%.\nThese figures emphasize the effectiveness of our\nframework in extracting the necessary evidence for\nclaim verification, highlighting the positive impact\n\nInput Type\nTraining\nStrategy\nMethods\nAccuracy\nClaim Only\n"

        "text_sha256": "e1ec04d6ff7d423c0819001e42e2b8c624152f04c33383b89dc5499e71a50b05",
        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining structured and\nunstructured data management in the LLMs’ con-\ntext.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "c716d8b21c66e4648be49e2f4ee19f778ee1bcb1e7cad440894c67e0aa095b87",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our framework on two tasks that re-\nquire KG grounding: fact-verification and question-\nanswering. A detailed description of experimental\nsettings can be found in Appendix C.\n3.1\nDataset\n3.1.1\nFACTKG\nFACTKG (Kim et al., 2023) serves as a practical\nand challenging dataset meticulously constructed\nfor the purpose of fact verification, employing a\nknowledge graph for validation purposes. It encom-\npasses 108K claims that can be verified via DBpe-\ndia (Lehmann et al., 2015), which is one of the\navailable comprehensive knowledge graphs. These\nclaims are categorized as either Supported or Re-\nfuted. FACTKG embodies five diverse types of\nreasoning that represent the intrinsic characteris-\ntics of the KG: One-hop, Conjunction, Existence,\nMulti-hop, and Negation. To further enhance its\npractical use, FACTKG integrates claims in both\ncolloquial and written styles. Examples of claims\nfrom FACTKG can be found in Appendix D.\n3.1.2\nMetaQA\nMetaQA (Zhang et al., 2018) is a carefully curated\ndataset intended to facilitate the study of question-\nanswering that leverages KG-based approaches in\nthe field of movies. The dataset encompasses over\n400K questions, including instances of 1-hop, 2-\nhop, and 3-hop reasoning. Additionally, it covers a\ndiverse range of question styles. Examples of ques-\ntions from MetaQA can be found in Appendix D.\n3.2\nBaselines\n"

        "text_sha256": "93f2bbcd4f2e73d22123a0b360c4293fdaea9ddbdb4e4a14f998b2eb37755844",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "3b3bc1c7333f21c87a4f02d6288ab2af143036abdf4856f95fab0852c594d454",
        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "Experiment\nWe conduct experiments on three complex rea-\nsoning tasks over structured data, i.e., KGQA,\nTableQA, and DB based text-to-SQL.\n5.1\nDatasets\nFor KG based QA (KGQA), we adopt two\nbenchmark datasets, i.e., WebQuestionsSP (We-\nbQSP) (Yih et al., 2016) and MetaQA (Zhang et al.,\n2018) for evaluation. The answer entities in We-\nbQSP require up to 2-hop reasoning on the Free-\nbase KG. In contrast, MetaQA contains questions\nin the movie domain, whose answer entities are up\nto 3 hops away from the topic entities on a movie\nKG (based on OMDb). According to the num-\nber of hops, it is split into three sub-datasets, i.e.,\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop.\nFor Table based QA (TableQA), we adopt\nthree widely-used datasets, weakly-supervised Wik-\niSQL (WikiSQL) (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTable-\nQuestions (WTQ) (Pasupat and Liang, 2015), and\nTabFact (Chen et al., 2020). The first two are typ-\nical table-based question answering datasets, and\nthe third one is a multiple-choice dataset that con-\ncentrates on table fact verification. WikiSQL re-\nquires filtering and aggregating information over\nthe table content, and the WTQ demands more\nadvanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., sorting). Tab-\nFact needs to judge whether the provided statement\nagrees with the facts stored in a table.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "ffadad8a24b98afff5373c3d1a13f932f8b1ebfa0fc1da41a2a7f203f2283e40",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "62d2d6bc92494bd2583e0391cd268b756f954000661bdb5a9432e49168a291d3",
        "section": "Limitations",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "aac63ecd54869d7be7bd79a81cd71115deb4c53bd48bfda155d0cf47f886706e",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "KG-based Question Answering (KGQA).\nThis\ntask aims to find the answer entities for the question\nbased on the KG. Following existing work (Sun\net al., 2018), we denote the mentioned entity in\nthe given question q as the topic entity eT , and\nassume it has been linked to some specific en-\ntity on the KG through existing linking tools (e.g.,\nGoogle Knowledge Graph Search API) or mod-\nels (e.g., ELQ (Li et al., 2020)). Starting from eT ,\nwe perform the invoking-linearization-generation\nprocedure two times using the two interfaces in\nKG sequentially. First, we invoke the interface\nExtract_Neighbor_Relation(eT ) to extract the can-\ndidate one-hop relations, linearize them to com-\npose the input prompt, and then leverage the LLM\nto select the useful relations {r} according to the\nquestion. Then, based on {r}, we invoke the Ex-\ntract_Triples (eT , {r}) interface to collect the rel-\nevant triples for the head entity eT and relation in\n{r}, then linearize this information, and finally em-\nploy the LLM to select the most relevant triples,\nwhose tail entities will be considered as the final\nanswer. Besides, we can also consider the multi-\nhop KGQA task (Lan et al., 2021), where after\nselecting the triples of the current hop, the LLM\nshould assess whether the current information is\nsufficient to answer the question. Then, LLMs will\nmake according actions based on the assessment,\ni.e., stopping the iterations for producing the an-\nswer or continuing the iterations on next-hop tail\nentities from selected triples.\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "that CLQA-Wiki is a very challenging dataset, but\nLPKG(Llama3) still outperforms the baseline meth-\nods. At the same time, compared to ICLPKG(GPT-\n3.5), LPKG(Llama3) has an average improvement\nof over 20%, highlighting the importance of using\nKG-sourced planning data.\nIn addition, we conduct more fine-grained exper-\niments based on the type of questions, and the ex-\nperimental results are shown in Figure 4. We found\nthat LPKG(Llama3) performs more prominently\non some complex questions, such as the 3p, 2i, and\n2u questions, demonstrating the advantages of our\nframework in dealing with complex logic questions.\nAt the same time, we also found that direct retrieval\nperforms well on some types of questions, such as\n3i and compare questions. This may be due to the\nfact that in the process of verbalizing these ques-\ntions, the assembly of sub-questions into complex\nquestions is relatively straightforward, allowing an-\nswers to each sub-questions to be obtained directly\nthrough the retrieval of complex questions or the\nknowledge of the LLM itself.\nCase Study\nTo more intuitively demonstrate the\neffectiveness of KG-source planning data, we con-\nduct a case study on CLQA-Wiki, detailed in Fig-\nure 5 in Appendix A. When planning a 2i question\n“What sport is associated with John Madden and\nBen Johnson?”, GPT-3.5 generates some meaning-\nless sub-questions and incorrectly defines the ques-\ntion type, which will definitely lead to incorrect\nanswers. But LPKG(Llama3) could identify it as a\n2i question and provide the correct sub-questions\nand planning steps, thereby helping to obtain the\ncorrect answer during final parsing and execution.\n6\n"
      }

        "section": "Supplementary",
        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. However, on MuSiQue, KNN-MDR achieves the\nworst trade-off between Precision and SF-EM compared\nwith KNN-ST and TF-IDF. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality. Note that\nalthough here KNN-ST leads to a better KG than KNN-\nMDR, it does not mean the KNN baseline in Table 1 should\nperform better than MDR because the baseline name only\nrefers to the retrieval method while the name in this figure\nrefers to the KG construction method.\n"

        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "Main Results (RQ1,RQ2)\nTable 2 shows results\non conventional complex QA datasets. Since the\nQA LLM remains unchanged in our framework, we\nuse “LPKG(Llama3)” and “LPKG(CodeQwen)” to\nrepresent LPKG frameworks using different plan-\nning LLMs, respectively. They are fine-tuned on\nLlama3-8B-Instruct and CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat\nwith KG-sourced planning data. It can be found\nthat our framework outperforms the baseline meth-\nods on the majority of datasets. Particularly, com-\npared to ReAct and Self-Ask, our approach shows\nsignificant improvement. It is worth noting that\nboth ReAct and Self-Ask iterative planning and\nRAG in their workflows, whereas our approach de-\ncouples planning and RAG into two separate mod-\nels. This allows each model to focus more inten-\nsively on its individual task. Moreover, we specifi-\ncally enhance the planning part by fine-tuning Mp\nwith planning data sourced from KG.         "text_sha256": "a254e8856461cfa011d06564c6d0fe2a337b5b019845bcdcb7fad7506d896e08",
        "section": "B.1 FACTKG",
        "text": "B.1\nFACTKG\nIn FACTKG, we develop a new KG called Type-\nDBpedia. This graph comprises types found in DB-\npedia and connects them through relations, thereby\nenhancing the usability of KG content. We describe\nthe detailed process of incorporating Ri using DB-\npedia and TypeDBpedia in Algorithm 1.\nWe denote the entities as E1 and E2 because the\nsub-sentence always includes two entities in FAC-\nTKG. Relations (e, DBpedia) represents the set\nof relations connected to e in DBpedia. Similarly,\nRelations (T, TypeDBpedia) represents the set of\nrelations connected to T in TypeDBpedia.\nAlgorithm 1: Extract Relation Candidates\nInput: Entity Set E = {E1, E2},\nDBpedia, TypeDBpedia\nOutput: Relation Candidates Ri\nInitialization: T = ∅, RT = ∅, RE = ∅,\nRi = ∅\nfor each entity e in E do\nif isType (e) then\nT ←T ∪{e}\nend\nelse\nif isEmpty (RE) then\nRE ←Relations (e, DBpedia)\nend\nelse\nRE ←RE ∩Relations (e,\nDBpedia)\nend\nend\nend\nif not isEmpty (T) then\nRT ←Relations (T, TypeDBpedia)\nRi ←RE ∩RT\nend\nelse\nRi ←RE\nend\nB.2\nMetaQA\nFor the n-hop task in MetaQA, Ri is constructed\nfrom the relations within n-hops from the seed\nentity.\nC\nExperimental Settings\nWe utilize ChatGPT2 (OpenAI, 2023b) across all\n"
      }

    "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 684,
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n",
        "document_tokens": 154,
        "score": 0.3551037311553955,
        "pair_tokens": 199
      }
    ],
    "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 607,
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, resp",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.20641373097896576,
        "pair_tokens": 205

        "end_char": 918,
        "text": " address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the ",

        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 587,
        "text": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining stru",

        "pair_tokens": 205

    "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 591,
        "text": "KG-based Question Answering (KGQA).\nThis\ntask aims to find the answer entities for the question\nbased on the KG. Following existing work (Sun\net al., 2018), we denote the mentioned entity in\nthe given question q as the topic entity eT , and\nassume it has been linked to some specific en-\ntity on the KG through existing linking tools (e.g.,\nGoogle Knowledge Graph Search API) or mod-\nels (e.g., ELQ (Li et al., 2020)). Starting from eT ,\nwe perform the invoking-linearization-generation\nprocedure two times using the two interfaces in\nKG sequentially. First, we invoke the interface\nExtract_",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.008847354911267757,
        "pair_tokens": 205
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1",
        "start_char": 295,
        "end_char": 850,
        "text": " the KG through existing linking tools (e.g.,\nGoogle Knowledge Graph Search API) or mod-\nels (e.g., ELQ (Li et al., 2020)). Starting from eT ,\nwe perform the invoking-linearization-generation\nprocedure two times using the two interfaces in\nKG sequentially. First, we invoke the interface\nExtract_Neighbor_Relation(eT ) to extract the can-\ndidate one-hop relations, linearize them to com-\npose the input prompt, and then leverage the LLM\nto select the useful relations {r} according to the\nquestion. Then, based on {r}, we invoke the Ex-\ntract_Triples (eT ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.01750955730676651,
        "pair_tokens": 205
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1",
        "start_char": 572,
        "end_char": 1159,
        "text": " interface\nExtract_Neighbor_Relation(eT ) to extract the can-\ndidate one-hop relations, linearize them to com-\npose the input prompt, and then leverage the LLM\nto select the useful relations {r} according to the\nquestion. Then, based on {r}, we invoke the Ex-\ntract_Triples (eT , {r}) interface to collect the rel-\nevant triples for the head entity eT and relation in\n{r}, then linearize this information, and finally em-\nploy the LLM to select the most relevant triples,\nwhose tail entities will be considered as the final\nanswer. Besides, we can also consider the multi-\nhop KGQA task ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.09041372686624527,
        "pair_tokens": 205
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1",
        "start_char": 865,
        "end_char": 1494,
        "text": "e to collect the rel-\nevant triples for the head entity eT and relation in\n{r}, then linearize this information, and finally em-\nploy the LLM to select the most relevant triples,\nwhose tail entities will be considered as the final\nanswer. Besides, we can also consider the multi-\nhop KGQA task (Lan et al., 2021), where after\nselecting the triples of the current hop, the LLM\nshould assess whether the current information is\nsufficient to answer the question. Then, LLMs will\nmake according actions based on the assessment,\ni.e., stopping the iterations for producing the an-\nswer or continuing the iterations on next-hop tail\nen",

        "score": 0.11920291930437088,

        "start_char": 1179,
        "end_char": 1524,
        "text": "where after\nselecting the triples of the current hop, the LLM\nshould assess whether the current information is\nsufficient to answer the question. Then, LLMs will\nmake according actions based on the assessment,\ni.e., stopping the iterations for producing the an-\nswer or continuing the iterations on next-hop tail\nentities from selected triples.\n",

        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "In both FACTKG and MetaQA, there are no cor-\nresponding ground truth graphs containing seed\nentities. This absence makes a quantitative step-by-\nstep analysis challenging. Therefore, we carried\nout an error analysis, extracting 100 incorrect sam-\nples from each dataset: FACTKG, MetaQA-1hop,\nMetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop. Table 3 shows\nthe number of errors observed at each step. No-\ntably, errors during the graph retrieval phase are\nthe fewest among the three steps. This suggests\nthat once sentences are correctly segmented, iden-\ntifying relations within them becomes relatively\neasy. Furthermore, a comparative analysis between\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop\nindicates that as the number of hops increases, so\ndoes the diversity of the questions. This heightened\ndiversity in turn escalates the errors in Sentence\nSegmentation.\n4.4\nAblation Study\n4.4.1\nNumber of In-context Examples\nThe results for the 12-shot, 8-shot, and 4-shot\nfrom the FACTKG and MetaQA datasets are re-\nported in Table 1 and Table 2, respectively.         "text_sha256": "d0a1cfcc148248fe6fe6ff3aa310a7a548ac4cc0c467a45281828705a5ce8fa2",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "For evaluation on FACTKG, we use the same base-\nlines as in Kim et al. (2023). These baselines are\ndivided into two distinct categories: Claim Only\nand With Evidence. In the Claim Only setting, the\nmodels are provided only with the claim as their\ninput and predict the label. For this setting, in ad-\ndition to the existing baselines, we implement a\n12-shot ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2023b) baseline. In\nthe With Evidence scenario, models consist of an\nevidence graph retriever and a claim verification\nmodel. We employ the KG version of GEAR (Zhou\net al., 2019) as a fully supervised model.\nIn our exploration of MetaQA, we use a selection\nof prototypical baselines well-known in the field\nof KGQA. These include models such as KV-Mem\n(Xu et al., 2019), GraftNet (Sun et al., 2018), Em-\nbedKGQA (Saxena et al., 2020), NSM (He et al.,\n2021), and UniKGQA (Jiang et al., 2022), which\noperate in a fully supervised fashion. Additionally,\nwe implement a 12-shot ChatGPT baseline.\n4\nResults & Analysis\n4.1\nFACTKG\nWe evaluated the models’ prediction capability for\nlabels (i.e. Supported or Refuted) and presented\nthe accuracy score in Table 1. As a result, KG-GPT\noutperforms Claim Only models BERT, BlueBERT,\nand Flan-T5 with performance enhancements of\n7.48%, 12.75%, and 9.98% absolute, respectively.\nIt also outperforms 12-shot ChatGPT by 4.20%.\nThese figures emphasize the effectiveness of our\nframework in extracting the necessary evidence for\nclaim verification, highlighting the positive impact\n\nInput Type\nTraining\nStrategy\nMethods\nAccuracy\nClaim Only\n"

        "text_sha256": "93f2bbcd4f2e73d22123a0b360c4293fdaea9ddbdb4e4a14f998b2eb37755844",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n"
      }

        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our framework on two tasks that re-\nquire KG grounding: fact-verification and question-\nanswering. A detailed description of experimental\nsettings can be found in Appendix C.\n3.1\nDataset\n3.1.1\nFACTKG\nFACTKG (Kim et al., 2023) serves as a practical\nand challenging dataset meticulously constructed\nfor the purpose of fact verification, employing a\nknowledge graph for validation purposes. It encom-\npasses 108K claims that can be verified via DBpe-\ndia (Lehmann et al., 2015), which is one of the\navailable comprehensive knowledge graphs. These\nclaims are categorized as either Supported or Re-\nfuted. FACTKG embodies five diverse types of\nreasoning that represent the intrinsic characteris-\ntics of the KG: One-hop, Conjunction, Existence,\nMulti-hop, and Negation. To further enhance its\npractical use, FACTKG integrates claims in both\ncolloquial and written styles. Examples of claims\nfrom FACTKG can be found in Appendix D.\n3.1.2\nMetaQA\nMetaQA (Zhang et al., 2018) is a carefully curated\ndataset intended to facilitate the study of question-\nanswering that leverages KG-based approaches in\nthe field of movies. The dataset encompasses over\n400K questions, including instances of 1-hop, 2-\nhop, and 3-hop reasoning. Additionally, it covers a\ndiverse range of question styles. Examples of ques-\ntions from MetaQA can be found in Appendix D.\n3.2\nBaselines\n"

        "text_sha256": "e1ec04d6ff7d423c0819001e42e2b8c624152f04c33383b89dc5499e71a50b05",
        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining structured and\nunstructured data management in the LLMs’ con-\ntext.\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "B.1 FACTKG",
        "text": "B.1\nFACTKG\nIn FACTKG, we develop a new KG called Type-\nDBpedia. This graph comprises types found in DB-\npedia and connects them through relations, thereby\nenhancing the usability of KG content. We describe\nthe detailed process of incorporating Ri using DB-\npedia and TypeDBpedia in Algorithm 1.\nWe denote the entities as E1 and E2 because the\nsub-sentence always includes two entities in FAC-\nTKG. Relations (e, DBpedia) represents the set\nof relations connected to e in DBpedia. Similarly,\nRelations (T, TypeDBpedia) represents the set of\nrelations connected to T in TypeDBpedia.\nAlgorithm 1: Extract Relation Candidates\nInput: Entity Set E = {E1, E2},\nDBpedia, TypeDBpedia\nOutput: Relation Candidates Ri\nInitialization: T = ∅, RT = ∅, RE = ∅,\nRi = ∅\nfor each entity e in E do\nif isType (e) then\nT ←T ∪{e}\nend\nelse\nif isEmpty (RE) then\nRE ←Relations (e, DBpedia)\nend\nelse\nRE ←RE ∩Relations (e,\nDBpedia)\nend\nend\nend\nif not isEmpty (T) then\nRT ←Relations (T, TypeDBpedia)\nRi ←RE ∩RT\nend\nelse\nRi ←RE\nend\nB.2\nMetaQA\nFor the n-hop task in MetaQA, Ri is constructed\nfrom the relations within n-hops from the seed\nentity.\nC\nExperimental Settings\nWe utilize ChatGPT2 (OpenAI, 2023b) across all\n"

        "text_sha256": "3b3bc1c7333f21c87a4f02d6288ab2af143036abdf4856f95fab0852c594d454",
        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "Experiment\nWe conduct experiments on three complex rea-\nsoning tasks over structured data, i.e., KGQA,\nTableQA, and DB based text-to-SQL.\n5.1\nDatasets\nFor KG based QA (KGQA), we adopt two\nbenchmark datasets, i.e., WebQuestionsSP (We-\nbQSP) (Yih et al., 2016) and MetaQA (Zhang et al.,\n2018) for evaluation. The answer entities in We-\nbQSP require up to 2-hop reasoning on the Free-\nbase KG. In contrast, MetaQA contains questions\nin the movie domain, whose answer entities are up\nto 3 hops away from the topic entities on a movie\nKG (based on OMDb). According to the num-\nber of hops, it is split into three sub-datasets, i.e.,\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop.\nFor Table based QA (TableQA), we adopt\nthree widely-used datasets, weakly-supervised Wik-\niSQL (WikiSQL) (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTable-\nQuestions (WTQ) (Pasupat and Liang, 2015), and\nTabFact (Chen et al., 2020). The first two are typ-\nical table-based question answering datasets, and\nthe third one is a multiple-choice dataset that con-\ncentrates on table fact verification. WikiSQL re-\nquires filtering and aggregating information over\nthe table content, and the WTQ demands more\nadvanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., sorting). Tab-\nFact needs to judge whether the provided statement\nagrees with the facts stored in a table.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "ffadad8a24b98afff5373c3d1a13f932f8b1ebfa0fc1da41a2a7f203f2283e40",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "62d2d6bc92494bd2583e0391cd268b756f954000661bdb5a9432e49168a291d3",
        "section": "Limitations",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "aac63ecd54869d7be7bd79a81cd71115deb4c53bd48bfda155d0cf47f886706e",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "KG-based Question Answering (KGQA).\nThis\ntask aims to find the answer entities for the question\nbased on the KG. Following existing work (Sun\net al., 2018), we denote the mentioned entity in\nthe given question q as the topic entity eT , and\nassume it has been linked to some specific en-\ntity on the KG through existing linking tools (e.g.,\nGoogle Knowledge Graph Search API) or mod-\nels (e.g., ELQ (Li et al., 2020)). Starting from eT ,\nwe perform the invoking-linearization-generation\nprocedure two times using the two interfaces in\nKG sequentially. First, we invoke the interface\nExtract_Neighbor_Relation(eT ) to extract the can-\ndidate one-hop relations, linearize them to com-\npose the input prompt, and then leverage the LLM\nto select the useful relations {r} according to the\nquestion. Then, based on {r}, we invoke the Ex-\ntract_Triples (eT , {r}) interface to collect the rel-\nevant triples for the head entity eT and relation in\n{r}, then linearize this information, and finally em-\nploy the LLM to select the most relevant triples,\nwhose tail entities will be considered as the final\nanswer. Besides, we can also consider the multi-\nhop KGQA task (Lan et al., 2021), where after\nselecting the triples of the current hop, the LLM\nshould assess whether the current information is\nsufficient to answer the question. Then, LLMs will\nmake according actions based on the assessment,\ni.e., stopping the iterations for producing the an-\nswer or continuing the iterations on next-hop tail\nentities from selected triples.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "ffc9f975f2b7353123b586effa1bd8d3b9c4f9b7f2fbb883fbaf6af993ed8df7",
        "section": "Supplementary",
        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. However, on MuSiQue, KNN-MDR achieves the\nworst trade-off between Precision and SF-EM compared\nwith KNN-ST and TF-IDF. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality. Note that\nalthough here KNN-ST leads to a better KG than KNN-\nMDR, it does not mean the KNN baseline in Table 1 should\nperform better than MDR because the baseline name only\nrefers to the retrieval method while the name in this figure\nrefers to the KG construction method.\n"

        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "Main Results (RQ1,RQ2)\nTable 2 shows results\non conventional complex QA datasets. Since the\nQA LLM remains unchanged in our framework, we\nuse “LPKG(Llama3)” and “LPKG(CodeQwen)” to\nrepresent LPKG frameworks using different plan-\nning LLMs, respectively. They are fine-tuned on\nLlama3-8B-Instruct and CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat\nwith KG-sourced planning data. It can be found\nthat our framework outperforms the baseline meth-\nods on the majority of datasets. Particularly, com-\npared to ReAct and Self-Ask, our approach shows\nsignificant improvement. It is worth noting that\nboth ReAct and Self-Ask iterative planning and\nRAG in their workflows, whereas our approach de-\ncouples planning and RAG into two separate mod-\nels. This allows each model to focus more inten-\nsively on its individual task. Moreover, we specifi-\ncally enhance the planning part by fine-tuning Mp\nwith planning data sourced from KG. These two\nchanges have brought significant improvements to\n1https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-3-5-turbo\n\nPlanning\nRAG\nHotPotQA\n2WikiMQA\nBamboogle\nMuSiQue\nDirect\n%\n%\n0.268\n0.284\n0.128\n0.090\nCoT\n\"\n%\n0.288\n0.286\n0.280\n0.090\nDirect RAG\n%\n\"\n0.292\n0.230\n0.080\n0.088\nReAct\n\"\n\"\n0.211\n0.216\n0.168\n0.060\nSelf-Ask\n\"\n\"\n0.176\n0.194\n0.136\n0.116\nICLPKG(GPT-3.5)\n\"\n\"\n0.352\n0.344\n0.296\n0.254\nLPKG(CodeQwen)\n\"\n\"\n0.338\n0.356\n0.280\n0.266\nLPKG(Llama3)\n\"\n\"\n0.376\n0.372\n0.304\n0.296\n"

        "section": "Experiment",
        "text": "that CLQA-Wiki is a very challenging dataset, but\nLPKG(Llama3) still outperforms the baseline meth-\nods. At the same time, compared to ICLPKG(GPT-\n3.5), LPKG(Llama3) has an average improvement\nof over 20%, highlighting the importance of using\nKG-sourced planning data.\nIn addition, we conduct more fine-grained exper-\niments based on the type of questions, and the ex-\nperimental results are shown in Figure 4. We found\nthat LPKG(Llama3) performs more prominently\non some complex questions, such as the 3p, 2i, and\n2u questions, demonstrating the advantages of our\nframework in dealing with complex logic questions.\nAt the same time, we also found that direct retrieval\nperforms well on some types of questions, such as\n3i and compare questions. This may be due to the\nfact that in the process of verbalizing these ques-\ntions, the assembly of sub-questions into complex\nquestions is relatively straightforward, allowing an-\nswers to each sub-questions to be obtained directly\nthrough the retrieval of complex questions or the\nknowledge of the LLM itself.\nCase Study\nTo more intuitively demonstrate the\neffectiveness of KG-source planning data, we con-\nduct a case study on CLQA-Wiki, detailed in Fig-\nure 5 in Appendix A. When planning a 2i question\n“What sport is associated with John Madden and\nBen Johnson?”, GPT-3.5 generates some meaning-\nless sub-questions and incorrectly defines the ques-\ntion type, which will definitely lead to incorrect\nanswers. But LPKG(Llama3) could identify it as a\n2i question and provide the correct sub-questions\nand planning steps, thereby helping to obtain the\ncorrect answer during final parsing and execution.\n6\n"

        "chunk_id": "chunk_3aa0cdece98e31f453ae4c5546e718b8",
        "text": "For evaluation on FACTKG, we use the same base-\nlines as in Kim et al. (2023). These baselines are\ndivided into two distinct categories: Claim Only\nand With Evidence. In the Claim Only setting, the\nmodels are provided only with the claim as their\ninput and predict the label. For this setting, in ad-\ndition to the existing baselines, we implement a\n12-shot ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2023b) baseline. In\nthe With Evidence scenario, models consist of an\nevidence graph retriever and a claim verification\nmodel. We employ the KG version of GEAR (Zhou\net al., 2019) as a fully supervised model.\nIn our exploration of MetaQA, we use a selection\nof prototypical baselines well-known in the field\nof KGQA. Additionally,\nwe implement a 12-shot ChatGPT baseline.\n4\nResults & Analysis\n4.1\nFACTKG\nWe evaluated the models’ prediction capability for\nlabels (i.e. Supported or Refuted) and presented\nthe accuracy score in Table 1.     "chunk_cb0cb02a1cffcc44146c10998e6d6034": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_cb0cb02a1cffcc44146c10998e6d6034",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our framework on two tasks that re-\nquire KG grounding: fact-verification and question-\nanswering. A detailed description of experimental\nsettings can be found in Appendix C.\n3.1\nDataset\n3.1.1\nFACTKG\nFACTKG (Kim et al., 2023) serves as a practical\nand challenging dataset meticulously constructed\nfor the purpose of fact verification, employing a\nknowledge graph for validation purposes. It encom-\npasses 108K claims that can be verified via DBpe-\ndia (Lehmann et al., 2015), which is one of the\navailable comprehensive knowledge graphs. These\nclaims are categorized as either Supported or Re-\nfuted. FACTKG embodies five diverse types of\nreasoning that represent the intrinsic characteris-\ntics of the KG: One-hop, Conjunction, Existence,\nMulti-hop, and Negation. To further enhance its\npractical use, FACTKG integrates claims in both\ncolloquial and written styles. Examples of claims\nfrom FACTKG can be found in Appendix D.\n3.1.2\nMetaQA\nMetaQA (Zhang et al., 2018) is a carefully curated\ndataset intended to facilitate the study of question-\nanswering that leverages KG-based approaches in\nthe field of movies. The dataset encompasses over\n400K questions, including instances of 1-hop, 2-\nhop, and 3-hop reasoning. Additionally, it covers a\ndiverse range of question styles. Examples of ques-\ntions from MetaQA can be found in Appendix D.\n3.2\nBaselines\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1379,
        "score": 0.7037531137466431,

    "chunk_a4963bc9a949cc8fa87d1c46b7c95760": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_a4963bc9a949cc8fa87d1c46b7c95760",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n",

        "chunk_id": "chunk_710cdd68fb6c3e90f213f8f4e175614e",
        "text": "B.1\nFACTKG\nIn FACTKG, we develop a new KG called Type-\nDBpedia. This graph comprises types found in DB-\npedia and connects them through relations, thereby\nenhancing the usability of KG content. We describe\nthe detailed process of incorporating Ri using DB-\npedia and TypeDBpedia in Algorithm 1.\nWe denote the entities as E1 and E2 because the\nsub-sentence always includes two entities in FAC-\nTKG. Relations (e, DBpedia) represents the set\nof relations connected to e in DBpedia. Similarly,\nRelations (T, TypeDBpedia) represents the set of\nrelations connected to T in TypeDBpedia.\nAlgorithm 1: Extract Relation Candidates\nInput: Entity Set E = {E1, E2},\nDBpedia, TypeDBpedia\nOutput: Relation Candidates Ri\nInitialization: T = ∅, RT = ∅, RE = ∅,\nRi = ∅\nfor each entity e in E do\nif isType (e) then\nT ←T ∪{e}\nend\nelse\nif isEmpty (RE) then\nRE ←Relations (e, DBpedia)\nend\nelse\nRE ←RE ∩Relations (e,\nDBpedia)\nend\nend\nend\nif not isEmpty (T) then\nRT ←Relations (T, TypeDBpedia)\nRi ←RE ∩RT\nend\nelse\nRi ←RE\nend\nB.2\nMetaQA\nFor the n-hop task in MetaQA, Ri is constructed\nfrom the relations within n-hops from the seed\nentity.\nC\nExperimental Settings\nWe utilize ChatGPT2 (OpenAI, 2023b) across all\n",

    "chunk_5a1fd5f3826cd78a6219d6bddfaa91da": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_5a1fd5f3826cd78a6219d6bddfaa91da",
        "text": "Experiment\nWe conduct experiments on three complex rea-\nsoning tasks over structured data, i.e., KGQA,\nTableQA, and DB based text-to-SQL.\n5.1\nDatasets\nFor KG based QA (KGQA), we adopt two\nbenchmark datasets, i.e., WebQuestionsSP (We-\nbQSP) (Yih et al., 2016) and MetaQA (Zhang et al.,\n2018) for evaluation. The answer entities in We-\nbQSP require up to 2-hop reasoning on the Free-\nbase KG. In contrast, MetaQA contains questions\nin the movie domain, whose answer entities are up\nto 3 hops away from the topic entities on a movie\nKG (based on OMDb). According to the num-\nber of hops, it is split into three sub-datasets, i.e.,\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop.\nFor Table based QA (TableQA), we adopt\nthree widely-used datasets, weakly-supervised Wik-\niSQL (WikiSQL) (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTable-\nQuestions (WTQ) (Pasupat and Liang, 2015), and\nTabFact (Chen et al., 2020). The first two are typ-\nical table-based question answering datasets, and\nthe third one is a multiple-choice dataset that con-\ncentrates on table fact verification. WikiSQL re-\nquires filtering and aggregating information over\nthe table content, and the WTQ demands more\nadvanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., sorting). Tab-\nFact needs to judge whether the provided statement\nagrees with the facts stored in a table.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1301,
        "score": 0.5783290863037109,
        "pair_tokens": 430
      }
    ],
    "chunk_d9eb528a051dc54a057f53f0af7fe0e6": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_d9eb528a051dc54a057f53f0af7fe0e6",
        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality.         "chunk_id": "chunk_7d8a9ac9d054b8b2a730410c6aafbaec",
        "text": "that CLQA-Wiki is a very challenging dataset, but\nLPKG(Llama3) still outperforms the baseline meth-\nods. At the same time, compared to ICLPKG(GPT-\n3.5), LPKG(Llama3) has an average improvement\nof over 20%, highlighting the importance of using\nKG-sourced planning data.\nIn addition, we conduct more fine-grained exper-\niments based on the type of questions, and the ex-\nperimental results are shown in Figure 4. We found\nthat LPKG(Llama3) performs more prominently\non some complex questions, such as the 3p, 2i, and\n2u questions, demonstrating the advantages of our\nframework in dealing with complex logic questions.\nAt the same time, we also found that direct retrieval\nperforms well on some types of questions, such as\n3i and compare questions. This may be due to the\nfact that in the process of verbalizing these ques-\ntions, the assembly of sub-questions into complex\nquestions is relatively straightforward, allowing an-\nswers to each sub-questions to be obtained directly\nthrough the retrieval of complex questions or the\nknowledge of the LLM itself.\nCase Study\nTo more intuitively demonstrate the\neffectiveness of KG-source planning data, we con-\nduct a case study on CLQA-Wiki, detailed in Fig-\nure 5 in Appendix A. When planning a 2i question\n“What sport is associated with John Madden and\nBen Johnson?”, GPT-3.5 generates some meaning-\nless sub-questions and incorrectly defines the ques-\ntion type, which will definitely lead to incorrect\nanswers. But LPKG(Llama3) could identify it as a\n2i question and provide the correct sub-questions\nand planning steps, thereby helping to obtain the\ncorrect answer during final parsing and execution.\n6\n",

    "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 684,
        "score": 0.3551037311553955,
        "pair_tokens": 199
      }
    ],
    "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 936,
        "score": 0.5746335387229919,
        "pair_tokens": 287
      }
    ],
    "chunk_45c598ca774c47ab2be0c3b734efd4de": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_45c598ca774c47ab2be0c3b734efd4de",
        "text": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining structured and\nunstructured data management in the LLMs’ con-\ntext.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 651,
        "score": 0.6241790056228638,
        "pair_tokens": 222
      }
    ],

They are fine-tuned on\nLlama3-8B-Instruct and CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat\nwith KG-sourced planning data. It can be found\nthat our framework outperforms the baseline meth-\nods on the majority of datasets. This allows each model to focus more inten-\nsively on its individual task. Moreover, we specifi-\ncally enhance the planning part by fine-tuning Mp\nwith planning data sourced from KG.     "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_55f3e1163ab88d1a50c645afccb9afe1",
        "text": "KG-based Question Answering (KGQA).\nThis\ntask aims to find the answer entities for the question\nbased on the KG. Following existing work (Sun\net al., 2018), we denote the mentioned entity in\nthe given question q as the topic entity eT , and\nassume it has been linked to some specific en-\ntity on the KG through existing linking tools (e.g.,\nGoogle Knowledge Graph Search API) or mod-\nels (e.g., ELQ (Li et al., 2020)). Starting from eT ,\nwe perform the invoking-linearization-generation\nprocedure two times using the two interfaces in\nKG sequentially. First, we invoke the interface\nExtract_Neighbor_Relation(eT ) to extract the can-\ndidate one-hop relations, linearize them to com-\npose the input prompt, and then leverage the LLM\nto select the useful relations {r} according to the\nquestion. Then, based on {r}, we invoke the Ex-\ntract_Triples (eT , {r}) interface to collect the rel-\nevant triples for the head entity eT and relation in\n{r}, then linearize this information, and finally em-\nploy the LLM to select the most relevant triples,\nwhose tail entities will be considered as the final\nanswer. Besides, we can also consider the multi-\nhop KGQA task (Lan et al., 2021), where after\nselecting the triples of the current hop, the LLM\nshould assess whether the current information is\nsufficient to answer the question. Then, LLMs will\nmake according actions based on the assessment,\ni.e., stopping the iterations for producing the an-\nswer or continuing the iterations on next-hop tail\nentities from selected triples.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1524,
        "score": 0.2018132209777832,
        "pair_tokens": 452
      }
    ],

      "text": "cost(S) = |ES| × Ce,\n(8)\nand Ce denotes a predefined cost per edge, which is adjustable to control the subgraph size.\nThe original PCST algorithm is designed for node prizes only. However, given the significance of\nedge semantics in certain scenarios, we adapt the algorithm to accommodate edge prizes as follows:\nConsider an edge e with a cost Ce and a prize Pe. If Ce > Pe, it can be treated as a reduced edge cost\nof Ce −Pe. However, if Pe > Ce, negative edge costs are not allowed in the original algorithm. Our\nsolution involves replacing edge e with a ‘virtual node’ ve, connected to both endpoints of e. This\nvirtual node is assigned a prize of Pe −Ce, and the cost of the two new edges leading to the virtual\nnode is set to zero. This modification effectively mirrors the original problem, as including edge e\nin the original graph is analogous to including the virtual node in the modified graph. Finally, we\noptimize the PCST problem using a near-linear time approach [9].\n5.4\nAnswer Generation\nGraph Encoder. Let S∗= (V ∗, E∗) represent the retrieved subgraph. We use a graph encoder to\nmodel the structure of this graph, specifically using a standard Graph Attention Network (GAT) [43].\nOur approach for encoding the retrieved subgraph is defined as follows:\nhg = POOL(GNNϕ1(S∗)) ∈Rdg,\n(9)\nHere, POOL denotes the mean pooling operation, and dg is the dimension of the graph encoder.\nProjection Layer.       "quote": "Method\nExplaGraphs\nSceneGraphs\nWebQSP\nInference-only\nZero-shot\n0.5650\n0.3974\n41.06\nZero-CoT [18]\n0.5704\n0.5260\n51.30\nCoT-BAG [44]\n0.5794\n0.5680\n39.60\nKAPING [1]\n0.6227\n0.4375\n52.64\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt tuning\n0.5763 ± 0.0243\n0.6341 ± 0.0024\n48.34 ± 0.64\nGraphToken [31]\n0.8508 ± 0.0551\n0.4903 ± 0.0105\n57.05 ± 0.74\nG-Retriever\n0.8516 ± 0.0092\n0.8131 ± 0.0162\n70.49 ± 1.21\n∆Prompt tuning\n↑47.77%\n↑28.23%\n↑45.81%\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n0.8538 ± 0.0353\n0.7862 ± 0.0031\n66.03 ± 0.47\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n0.8705 ± 0.0329\n0.8683 ± 0.0072\n73.79 ± 0.70\n∆LoRA\n↑1.95%\n↑11.74%\n↑10.44%\nTable 3 demonstrates the effectiveness of our method across three datasets in various configurations.\nIn the inference-only setting, G-Retriever surpasses all baselines. Notably, LLM can perform even\nbetter when no graph knowledge is provided (i.e., question only), which might be attributed to the\ncomplexity and potential noise in the knowledge. For frozen LLM with prompt tuning, G-Retriever\noutperforms traditional prompt tuning and GraphToken [31], a graph prompt tuning-based method,\nwith average performance increases of 40.6% and 30.8% respectively.       "quote": "• KG retrieval + GPT-3.5 We compare with exist-\ning KG retrieval methods (Jia et al., 2021; Sun\net al., 2023), which aim to find the shortest KG\npath between every pair of question entities. The\nfinal prompt is then retrieved from KG to guide\nGPT-3.5 model to answer questions. For fair\ncomparisons, we use the same preliminary pro-\ncess as our method to recognize the entities in\nquestion query. The key differences between\nMindMap and these are that they do not think\non multiple evidence KG sub-graphs with multi-\nthought in LLM, and without backtracking evi-\ndence sources.\n• Tree-of-thought (TOT) We compare TOT as a\ntypical Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022b) base-\nline with MindMap. TOT is a method that uses\na tree structure to solve complex problems(Yao\net al., 2023a). By extending one inference path\ninto multiple inference paths, the model can syn-\nthesize the results of multiple inference paths to\nobtain the final conclusion.\nD\nPrompt Engine\n• The instructions of MindMap components.\nTable 9 shows the instruction of Step I: en-\ntity recognition, which aims to identify and\nlabel medical entities in the user query. Table\n10 shows the templates of Step II (Evidence\nGraph Aggregation), which generates natural\nlanguage sentences from the evidence graph\nnodes and edges.\n• The instructions of baseline methods: Table\n11 shows the prompt template of two docu-\nment retrieval methods (BM25 Retrieval and\nEmbedding Retrieval). The input is the ques-\ntion and the most related document context.\n",

      "quote": "In Figure 4(c) (Appendix F), when faced with a\nquestion where GPT-3.5 is accurate but KG Re-\ntriever errs, MindMap achieves an accuracy rate\nof 55%. We attribute the low accuracy of the KG\nRetriever to its inability to retrieve the necessary\nknowledge for problem-solving. MindMap effec-\ntively addresses such instances by leveraging the\nLLM inherent knowledge, identifying pertinent ex-\nternal explicit knowledge, and seamlessly integrat-\ning it into a unified graph structure.\n4.6.2\nHow robust is MindMap to unmatched\nfact queries?\nThe question in Figure 6 (Appendix F) contains\nmisleading symptom facts, such as ‘jaundice in my\neyes’ leading baseline models to retrieve irrelevant\nknowledge linked to ‘eye’. This results in failure\nto identify the correct disease, with recommended\ndrugs and tests unrelated to liver disease. In con-\ntrast, our model MindMap accurately identifies\ncirrhosis’ and recommends the relevant ‘blood test’\nshowcasing its robustness.\n4.6.3\nHow does MindMap aggregate evidence\ngraphs considering entity semantics?\n",

        "section": "References",
        "text": "• KG retrieval + GPT-3.5 We compare with exist-\ning KG retrieval methods (Jia et al., 2021; Sun\net al., 2023), which aim to find the shortest KG\npath between every pair of question entities. The\nfinal prompt is then retrieved from KG to guide\nGPT-3.5 model to answer questions. For fair\ncomparisons, we use the same preliminary pro-\ncess as our method to recognize the entities in\nquestion query. The key differences between\nMindMap and these are that they do not think\non multiple evidence KG sub-graphs with multi-\nthought in LLM, and without backtracking evi-\ndence sources.\n• Tree-of-thought (TOT) We compare TOT as a\ntypical Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022b) base-\nline with MindMap. TOT is a method that uses\na tree structure to solve complex problems(Yao\net al., 2023a). By extending one inference path\ninto multiple inference paths, the model can syn-\nthesize the results of multiple inference paths to\nobtain the final conclusion.\nD\nPrompt Engine\n• The instructions of MindMap components.\nTable 9 shows the instruction of Step I: en-\ntity recognition, which aims to identify and\nlabel medical entities in the user query. Table\n10 shows the templates of Step II (Evidence\nGraph Aggregation), which generates natural\nlanguage sentences from the evidence graph\nnodes and edges.\n• The instructions of baseline methods: Table\n11 shows the prompt template of two docu-\nment retrieval methods (BM25 Retrieval and\nEmbedding Retrieval). The input is the ques-\ntion and the most related document context.\n"
