However,\nMindMap enables LLM to synergistically infer\nfrom both the retrieved evidence graphs and its\nown knowledge. We attribute this ability to three\naspects: (1) Language Understanding, as LLM can\ncomprehend and extract the knowledge from Gm\nand the query in natural language, (2) Knowledge\nReasoning, as LLM can perform entity disambigua-\ntion and produce the final answer based on the\nmind map constructed from Gm, and (3) Knowl-\nedge Enhancement, as LLM can leverage its im-\nplicit knowledge to expand, connect, and improve\nthe information relevant to the query. This ability\nis especially valuable when the external knowledge\ninput is inaccurate.\n4\n"

        "section": "Method",
        "text": "Figure 4 in Appendix F illustrates MindMap’s per-\nformance on diverse question types.\nFor drug-\nrelated questions (a) and (d), which demand in-\ndepth knowledge, MindMap outperforms other\nmethods.\nDisease-related questions (b) and (f)\nshow comparable results between retrieval methods\nand MindMap, indicating that incorporating exter-\nnal knowledge mitigates errors in language model\noutputs. Notably, for general knowledge questions\n(c), LLMs like GPT-3.5 perform better, while re-\ntrieval methods lag. This suggests that retrieval\nmethods may overlook the knowledge embedded\nin LLMs. Conversely, MindMap performs as well\nas GPT-3.5 in handling general knowledge ques-\ntions, highlighting its effectiveness in synergizing\nLLM and KG knowledge for adaptable inference\nacross datasets with varying KG fact accuracies.\n5\n"

        "text_sha256": "3bd40790bb9dff09d1b1437625139441c9ae55d33b6946da3cafd3c30a15cda2",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our method for a suite of question &\nanswering tasks that require sophisticated reason-\ning and domain knowledge and compare it with\nretrieval-based baselines.\n4.1\nExperimental Setup\nWe evaluate the utilization of external knowl-\nedge graphs by MindMap in complex question-\nanswering tasks across three medical Q&A\ndatasets:\nGenMedGPT-5k, CMCQA, and Ex-\nplainCPE. These datasets cover patient-doctor\ndialogues, multi-round clinical dialogues, and\nmultiple-choice questions from the Chinese Na-\ntional Licensed Pharmacist Examination, respec-\ntively. To support KG-enhanced methods, we con-\nstruct two knowledge graphs (EMCKG and CM-\nCKG) containing entities and relationships related\nto medical concepts. The ExplainCPE dataset uti-\nlizes CMCKG with knowledge mismatches to as-\nsess the impact of incorrect retrieval knowledge\non model performance. We compare MindMap’s\nability to integrate implicit and explicit knowledge\nwith various baselines, including vanilla GPT-3.5\nand GPT-4, as well as the tree-of-thought method\n(TOT) (Yao et al., 2023a), which uses a tree struc-\nture for reasoning. Additionally, we consider three\nretrieval-augmented baselines: BM25 retriever,\nText Embedding retriever, and KG retriever, see\ninstruction details in Appendix D. These base-\nlines leverage different methods and sources for\nevidence retrieval, with gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 as the\nbackbone for all retrieval-based methods. Detailed\ndescriptions of these baselines are provided in Ap-\npendix C.\n4.2\nMedical Question Answering\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "90ca4f68b057c367329013735770680c3cb229ca8407ea6f02fe863718b0e2e4",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "be177440a5c4c624cab1e1c136c414c0e78ce6f931f17d787387a8590bbd2866",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "MindMap still outshines all retrieval-based meth-\nods, including KG Retriever. This suggests previ-\nous retrieval-based approaches might overly rely\non retrieved external knowledge, compromising\nthe language model’s (LLM) ability to grasp intri-\ncate logic and dialogue nuances using its implicit\nknowledge. Conversely, MindMap leverages both\nexternal and implicit knowledge in graph reasoning,\nyielding more accurate answers.\n4.4\nGenerate with Mismatch Knowledge from\nKG\nIn addressing the robustness of MindMap concern-\ning the factual correctness of KG, we leverage\nthe identical KG dataset employed in the second\ndataset - ExplainPE. Consequently, the knowledge\nretrieved may tend to be redundant or devoid of\naccurate information. This aspect is particularly\ncrucial since it mirrors a common scenario in pro-\nduction, where LLM often needs to generate an-\nswers by amalgamating both its implicit knowledge\nand the knowledge retrieved from external sources.\n4.4.1\nEvaluation Metrics\nWe evaluate all methods based on the accuracy of\nthe generated choice and the quality of the expla-\nnations. For assessing explanation quality, we use\nBERTScore and GPT-4 ranking. We specifically\ninstruct the GPT-4 rater to prioritize the correctness\nof the explanation over its helpfulness or integrity.\n4.4.2\nResults\n"

        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets. These results\nunderscore the significant reduction in hallucinations with G-Retriever, particularly in the challenging\ntask of accurately citing both nodes and edges in graph-based contexts.\nG\nDemonstrations\nWe demonstrate the interaction capabilities of G-Retriever with creative questions on different\ndatasets: ExplaGraphs, SceneGraphs, and WebQSP. These examples are showcased in Tables 13,\n14, and 15, respectively.         "text_sha256": "f09d745f6be393fbeefac283ef11e5fa373bec170414a1eae9ebda9970ce0697",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nLarge language models (LLMs) have achieved\nremarkable performance in natural language\nunderstanding and generation tasks. However,\nthey often suffer from limitations such as diffi-\nculty in incorporating new knowledge, gener-\nating hallucinations, and explaining their rea-\nsoning process. To address these challenges,\nwe propose a novel prompting pipeline, named\nMindMap, that leverages knowledge graphs\n(KGs) to enhance LLMs’ inference and trans-\nparency. Our method enables LLMs to com-\nprehend KG inputs and infer with a combina-\ntion of implicit and external knowledge. More-\nover, our method elicits the mind map of LLMs,\nwhich reveals their reasoning pathways based\non the ontology of knowledge. We evaluate our\nmethod on diverse question & answering tasks,\nespecially in medical domains, and show sig-\nnificant improvements over baselines. We also\nintroduce a new hallucination evaluation bench-\nmark and analyze the effects of different com-\nponents of our method. Our results demonstrate\nthe effectiveness and robustness of our method\nin merging knowledge from LLMs and KGs for\ncombined inference. To reproduce our results\nand extend the framework further, we make our\ncodebase available at https://github.com/wyl-\nwilling/MindMap.\n1\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "301d2001db65c52b87a43c9698e090e5d0df9e1e6213ed8b8ca7533a49e5bfb7",
        "section": "Method",
        "text": "In Figure 7 of Appendix F, nodes like ‘vaginitis’\nand ‘atrophic vaginitis’ are present in different\nevidence sub-graphs but share a semantic iden-\ntity. MindMap allows LLMs to disambiguate and\nmerge these diverse evidence graphs for more ef-\nfective reasoning. The resulting mind maps also\nmap entities back to the input evidence graphs. Ad-\nditionally, Figure 7 illustrates the GPT-4 rater’s\npreference for total factual correctness and disease\ndiagnosis factual correctness across methods. No-\ntably, MindMap is highlighted for providing more\nspecific disease diagnosis results compared to the\nbaseline, which offers vague mentions and lacks\ntreatment options. In terms of disease diagnosis\nfactual correctness, the GPT-4 rater observes that\nMindMap aligns better with the ground truth.\n4.6.4\nHow does MindMap visualize the\ninference process and evidence sources?\nFigure 8 in Appendix F presents a comprehensive\nresponse to a CMCQA question. It includes a sum-\nmary, an inference process, and a mind map. The\nsummary extracts the accurate result from the mind\nmap, while the inference process displays multiple\nreasoning chains from the entities on the evidence\ngraph Gm. The mind map combines all the infer-\nence chains into a reasoning graph, providing an in-\ntuitive understanding of knowledge connections in\neach step and the sources of evidence sub-graphs.\n4.6.5\nHow does MindMap leverage LLM\nknowledge for various tasks?\n"
      }

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Figure 2: A conceptual demonstration of evidence query sub-graphs, merged reasoning sub-graphs, and mind map.\nThe entity inputs Vq is identified from the input. Lines and circles of the same color indicate that they correspond.\nThe red dashed lines in the MindMap box illustrate the augmentation operation based on the knowledge of LLM.\nknowledge bases, knowledge graphs (KG) are es-\ntablished by the triples of entities and relations, i.e.,\n{head, relation, tail}. They can provide ex-\nplicit knowledge representation and interpretable\nreasoning paths. Besides, KGs are amenable to con-\ntinual modifications to debug the existing knowl-\nedge or add new knowledge. Due to their flexibility,\npreciseness, and interpretability, KGs emerged as a\npromising complement to the drawbacks of LLMs\n(Pan et al., 2023). For instance, KG triples were\nadded to the training of LLMs (Zhang et al., 2019b)\nor KG encoders were entangled with LLM layers\nfor joint inference and optimization on graph and\ntext data (Zhang et al., 2022). By contrast, our work\npivots on the synergistic inference of KGs and fixed\nLLMs, which is applicable to powerful pre-trained\nLLMs, such as commercial LLM-as-service APIs.\nIn general, the prior arts in this venue can be cate-\ngorized into two genres:\n"

        "text_sha256": "ce3d7b113af7b849ddfe175491ce2cdc9295a83de33dbd6849c02e4a4dfc6338",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "The goal of this work is to build a plug-and-play\nprompting approach to elicit the graph-of-thoughts\nreasoning capability in LLMs. We call our method\nMindMap because it enables LLMs to comprehend\ngraphical inputs to build their own mind map that\nsupports evidence-grounded generation. A con-\nceptual demonstration of our framework is in Fig-\nure 2. Specifically, MindMap sparks the graph\nof thoughts of LLMs that (1) consolidates the re-\ntrieved facts from KGs and the implicit knowledge\nfrom LLMs, (2) discovers new patterns in input\nKGs, and (3) reasons over the mind map to yield\nfinal outputs. We conducted experiments on three\ndatasets to illustrate that MindMap outperforms\na series of prompting approaches by a large mar-\ngin. This work underscores how LLM can learn to\nconduct synergistic inference with KG. By integrat-\ning both implicit and explicit knowledge, LLMs\ncan achieve transparent and dependable inference,\nadapting to different levels of correctness in addi-\ntional KG information.\n2\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "3. LLM reasoning on the mind map: Last, we",
        "text": "To generate a mind map and find final results, we\nprovide LLMs with a prompt that has five compo-\nnents: a system instruction, a question, evidence\ngraphs Gm, a graph-of-thought instruction, and ex-\nemplars. The graph-of-thought instruction uses\nthe Langchain technique to guide LLMs to com-\nprehend and enhance the input, build their own\nmind map for reasoning, and index the knowledge\nsources of the mind map. The prompt template\nis detailed in Figure 3.         "text_sha256": "a0273f5461005636626a71d4e4d31b99ba6dbf6e6f2e9372ccb6b9a78f459b98",
        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nThis paper introduced knowledge graph (KG)\nprompting that 1) endows LLMs with the capabil-\nity of comprehending KG inputs and 2) facilitates\nLLMs inferring with a combined implicit knowl-\nedge and the retrieved external knowledge. We then\ninvestigate eliciting the mind map, where LLMs\nperform the reasoning and generate the answers\nwith rationales represented in graphs. Through\nextensive experiments on three question & answer-\ning datasets, we demonstrated that our approach,\nMindMap, achieves remarkable empirical gains\nover vanilla LLMs and retrieval-augmented genera-\ntion methods, and is robust to mismatched retrieval\nknowledge. We envision this work opens the door\nto fulfilling reliable and transparent LLM inference\nin production.\n"
      }

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. While existing works integrate LLMs and\nGNNs in various ways, they mostly focus on conventional graph tasks such as node, edge and graph\n1Our codes and datasets are available at: https://github.com/XiaoxinHe/G-Retriever\narXiv:2402.07630v3  [cs.LG]  27 May 2024\n\nNew Benchmark\nGraphQA\nNew Architecture\nG-Retriever\nTechniques\nRetrieval Augmented Generation\nGraph Prompt Tuning\nGraph Textualization\n"

        "text_sha256": "3714755ac8b668addb92b1cab1fd8d09829a000019a3635a68f283963e91d45d",
        "section": "Method",
        "text": "To evaluate hallucination, we instructed the models to answer graph-related questions, specifically\nidentifying supporting nodes or edges from the graph. We manually reviewed 100 responses from\nboth our method and the baseline (i.e., LLM with graph prompt tuning), verifying the existence\nof the nodes and edges referenced in the model’s output within the actual graph. Table 5 shows\nthat G-Retriever significantly reduces hallucinations by 54% compared to the baseline, as our graph\nretrieval ensures that the data is sourced directly from the actual graph, leading to less hallucination.\nSee Appendix F for details.\n6.5\nAblation Study\nIn this ablation study, we assess the individual impact of key components within our pipeline. As\nshown in Table 6, there are performance drops when any of these components are removed, with the\ngraph encoder and textualized graph showing declines of 22.51% and 19.19%, respectively. This\ndemonstrates their complementary effects in representing the graph in both textual and embedded\nformats. Additionally, the retrieval on graphs is also important to the overall performance. Further\ndetails are available in Appendix B.3. We also present additional studies on our framework: it is\nrobust to the choice of graph encoders (see Appendix B.4) and benefits from the increased scale of\nLLMs (see Appendix B.5).\nAdditionally, we include a detailed comparison with existing retrieval methods (see Appendix D), a\ndiscussion on the complexity (see Appendix E), and demonstrations on how to use G-Retriever to\n‘chat with your graph’ (see Appendix G).\n7\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "b19a2d053faea5a2dddcb08f15db46e39ca91c20626782da7eb4bd762a2963c5",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "b6ab2f5a2f84ccea28361c4a730a9200490821231bd0bd5594d92d3b2b0bd502",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with\nlarge language models (LLMs), particularly in med-\nical contexts, presents several potential challenges.\nOne significant concern is the risk of replicating\nany existing biases or errors in the knowledge\ngraphs. These graphs, often built from pre-existing\ndata sources, might contain outdated or partial in-\nformation, which could inadvertently influence the\nLLM’s outputs. Another issue lies in the integra-\ntion complexity between KGs and LLMs, which\ncould lead to unexpected errors or logical incon-\nsistencies, especially when addressing intricate or\nvague queries. This aspect is critically important\nin the medical field, where precision is paramount.\nMoreover, there’s a possibility that the LLMs might\nbecome excessively dependent on the KGs, which\ncould hinder their performance in scenarios where\nKGs are not accessible or are lacking in infor-\nmation. Additionally, the use of \"mind maps\" to\ntrace the LLMs’ reasoning paths, while innovative,\nraises questions about the models’ interpretability.\nIf these visual representations are complex or ob-\nscure, it may be difficult for users to understand\nhow conclusions were reached, potentially dimin-\nishing trust in these advanced systems. In summary,\nwhile the merger of KGs with LLMs is a promising\ndevelopment, it is crucial to address these poten-\ntial issues to ensure the responsible and efficacious\napplication of this technology.\n\n(b)\nReference\n(c)\nOutput \nMindMap\nGPT-3.5\n(a)\nQuestion\n"
      }

        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n"
      }

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "[Incorrect response with hallucinated nodes and edges]\nThe animal in the bushes is a deer.\nNodes:\n* Deer (node 1)\n* Bushes (node 2)\nEdges:\n* Deer →Bushes (edge 1)\n* Deer →Grass (edge 2)\n* Bushes →Grass (edge 3)\nG-Retriever (Ours)\n[Correct response with accurate node and edge references]\nBased on the information provided in the graph, the animal in the bushes is an elephant.\nThe nodes that support this answer are:\n* Node 1: The elephant is mentioned in the first line of the graph.\nThe edges that support this answer are:\n* The edge connects the elephant to the bushes, indicating that the elephant is in the bushes.\nTherefore, the answer to the question is: The animal in the bushes is an elephant.\noptimization problem, which takes the neighborhood information into account during retrieval. This\nalso allows the return of a subgraph most relevant to a query, thereby improving explainability.\nThe contributions of this paper are outlined as follows:\n• Pioneering the integration of Graph RAG. We present the first retrieval approach for\ngeneral textual graph tasks, which greatly enhances scalability and efficiency.\n• Enabling ‘Chat with Your Graph’. We develop a flexible question answering framework\nto handle complex and real-world textual graphs through a unified conversational interface.\n• Introducing A Novel GraphQA Benchmark. We introduce a diverse benchmark targeted\nat real-world graph question answering, filling a crucial research gap.\n• Empirical Findings. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of G-Retriever in\nmultiple domains and present the significant finding of hallucination in graph LLMs.\n2\n"

        "text_sha256": "c0453f83b6adf1f5d26a386b0e6c924b5f1ae30b67e4ce7c7739d3f2428d1ea0",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Tackling Hallucination in Graph LLMs. LLMs are prone to hallucination, a phenomenon where the\ngenerated content is factually inaccurate or nonsensical [12]. We validate the presence of this issue in\ngraph settings. In particular, we employ a baseline method that adapts MiniGPT-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31]. Our findings, shown in Table 1, indicate that hallucination, an important problem\nin text-based LLMs, is also prevalent in Graph LLMs. This may be attributed to the baseline’s\ninability to recall the entire graph structure from a single graph embedding, leading to the generation\nof incorrect nodes or edges during the QA task. In contrast, by employing RAG for direct information\nretrieval from the actual graph, our G-Retriever mitigates this issue, as substantiated by Table 1.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "17e686ca305ed342a6e4b876ac96da8f37e68e06319f70c04017865cd2c65d1a",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Enhancing Scalability and Efficiency in Graph LLMs. Recent research endeavors have explored\ntranslating graphs into natural language, such as by flattening nodes and edges into a text sequence,\nenabling their processing by LLMs for graph-based tasks [56, 6]. However, this method faces critical\nscalability issues. Converting a graph with thousands of nodes and edges into a text sequence results\nin an excessive number of tokens, surpassing the input capacity of many LLMs. An alternative of\ntruncating the graph text sequence to fit the LLM’s input token limit leads to loss of information and\nresponse quality. G-Retriever overcomes these issues with its RAG component, which allows for\neffective scaling to larger graphs by selectively retrieving only relevant parts of the graph.\nTailoring the RAG Approach to Graphs. Existing RAG methodologies are primarily designed\nfor simpler data types or knowledge graphs, where information is retrieved in a manner isolated\nfrom the graph structure [7, 1, 36, 16]. Hence, we introduce a new retrieval approach for general\ntextual graphs. Notably, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST)\n2\n\nTable 1: Observation and mitigation of hallucination in graph LLMs.\nUser\nelephants\ngrass\neating\nbushes\nin\nriver\non the side of\nstanding by\nelephant\nWhat kind of animal is in the bushes?\nAnswer the question and list the nodes or edges from the graph that support your answer.\nLLM w/ Graph Prompt Tuning\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "878dfab9da1f584983c6a8588286f2d607fcbca677d3130da85115644eb0d065",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "The Need for a Comprehensive GraphQA Benchmark. Question answering (QA) is a fundamen-\ntally important task in natural language processing, serving as a key benchmark for assessing LLMs\nand providing a unified interface for various capabilities. Despite extensive research in QA, a com-\nprehensive benchmark specifically tailored for the graph modality is lacking. In contrast to existing\nbenchmarks that focus on basic graph-based reasoning tasks such as node degree, edge existence, and\nshortest path [6, 44], our benchmark addresses complex and real-world graph applications including\ncommon sense reasoning, scene understanding, and knowledge graph reasoning (refer to Figure 2).\nThis is vital for measuring progress toward a model capable of answering a wide range of questions\nabout graphs from diverse applications.\nNew Architecture for GraphQA. To enable effective and efficient graph QA, even on large graphs,\nwe propose G-Retriever, a new framework combining the strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG\n(Figure 3). Next, we will discuss the motivation, strengths, and details of our model.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "5296e092b76168dc20a8da94b1042555c734b337134a82b9a13bc184fef87e8f",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "cost(S) = |ES| × Ce,\n(8)\nand Ce denotes a predefined cost per edge, which is adjustable to control the subgraph size.\nThe original PCST algorithm is designed for node prizes only. However, given the significance of\nedge semantics in certain scenarios, we adapt the algorithm to accommodate edge prizes as follows:\nConsider an edge e with a cost Ce and a prize Pe. If Ce > Pe, it can be treated as a reduced edge cost\nof Ce −Pe. However, if Pe > Ce, negative edge costs are not allowed in the original algorithm. Our\nsolution involves replacing edge e with a ‘virtual node’ ve, connected to both endpoints of e. This\nvirtual node is assigned a prize of Pe −Ce, and the cost of the two new edges leading to the virtual\nnode is set to zero. This modification effectively mirrors the original problem, as including edge e\nin the original graph is analogous to including the virtual node in the modified graph. Finally, we\noptimize the PCST problem using a near-linear time approach [9].\n5.4\nAnswer Generation\nGraph Encoder. Let S∗= (V ∗, E∗) represent the retrieved subgraph. We use a graph encoder to\nmodel the structure of this graph, specifically using a standard Graph Attention Network (GAT) [43].\nOur approach for encoding the retrieved subgraph is defined as follows:\nhg = POOL(GNNϕ1(S∗)) ∈Rdg,\n(9)\nHere, POOL denotes the mean pooling operation, and dg is the dimension of the graph encoder.\nProjection Layer. We incorporate a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to align the graph token with the\nvector space of the LLM:\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "The results demonstrate that our proposed method exhibits consistent robustness across different graph\nencoders. Notably, all three encoders – GCN, GAT, and GraphTransformer – demonstrate competitive\nand closely aligned performance on the WebQSP dataset, with Hit@1 scores of 70.70, 70.27, and\n70.49, respectively. However, the performance differentiation becomes more pronounced on the\nExplaGraphs dataset, where GraphTransformer exhibits a superior Hit@1 score of 0.8516, followed\nby GAT and GCN with scores of 0.8430 and 0.8394, respectively. This variation in performance\nacross the datasets highlights the importance of encoder selection based on the specific characteristics\nand requirements of the dataset.\nB.5\nThe Choice of LLM\nAs for the choice of LLM, we considered both Llama2-7b and Llama2-13b.         "text_sha256": "9ff8de731b4b958a056ef7c83d63573d8401a624d9dd02c6bbe1c9c5217ceb8d",
        "section": "unidentified",
        "text": "Abstract—Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and GPT4, are making new waves in the field of natural language\nprocessing and artificial intelligence, due to their emergent ability and generalizability. However, LLMs are black-box models, which\noften fall short of capturing and accessing factual knowledge. In contrast, Knowledge Graphs (KGs), Wikipedia and Huapu for example,\nare structured knowledge models that explicitly store rich factual knowledge. KGs can enhance LLMs by providing external knowledge\nfor inference and interpretability. Meanwhile, KGs are difficult to construct and evolve by nature, which challenges the existing methods\nin KGs to generate new facts and represent unseen knowledge. Therefore, it is complementary to unify LLMs and KGs together and\nsimultaneously leverage their advantages. In this article, we present a forward-looking roadmap for the unification of LLMs and KGs.\nOur roadmap consists of three general frameworks, namely, 1) KG-enhanced LLMs, which incorporate KGs during the pre-training and\ninference phases of LLMs, or for the purpose of enhancing understanding of the knowledge learned by LLMs; 2) LLM-augmented KGs,\nthat leverage LLMs for different KG tasks such as embedding, completion, construction, graph-to-text generation, and question\nanswering; and 3) Synergized LLMs + KGs, in which LLMs and KGs play equal roles and work in a mutually beneficial way to enhance\nboth LLMs and KGs for bidirectional reasoning driven by both data and knowledge. We review and summarize existing efforts within\nthese three frameworks in our roadmap and pinpoint their future research directions.\n"
      }
    },

        "chunk_id": "chunk_b8f804ce7bc81bbbf659aff60ac33d60",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1460,

    "chunk_000fb51c29790f99fdf023d7b338666c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_000fb51c29790f99fdf023d7b338666c",
        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets.         "text": "cost(S) = |ES| × Ce,\n(8)\nand Ce denotes a predefined cost per edge, which is adjustable to control the subgraph size.\nThe original PCST algorithm is designed for node prizes only. However, given the significance of\nedge semantics in certain scenarios, we adapt the algorithm to accommodate edge prizes as follows:\nConsider an edge e with a cost Ce and a prize Pe. If Ce > Pe, it can be treated as a reduced edge cost\nof Ce −Pe. However, if Pe > Ce, negative edge costs are not allowed in the original algorithm. Our\nsolution involves replacing edge e with a ‘virtual node’ ve, connected to both endpoints of e. This\nvirtual node is assigned a prize of Pe −Ce, and the cost of the two new edges leading to the virtual\nnode is set to zero. This modification effectively mirrors the original problem, as including edge e\nin the original graph is analogous to including the virtual node in the modified graph. Finally, we\noptimize the PCST problem using a near-linear time approach [9].\n5.4\nAnswer Generation\nGraph Encoder. Let S∗= (V ∗, E∗) represent the retrieved subgraph.     "chunk_2da94a87e97c2e0f30e8eec5659e202d": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_2da94a87e97c2e0f30e8eec5659e202d",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem.         "chunk_id": "chunk_8ef1b4863836f1f958a83a3660b9aae9",
        "text": "To generate a mind map and find final results, we\nprovide LLMs with a prompt that has five compo-\nnents: a system instruction, a question, evidence\ngraphs Gm, a graph-of-thought instruction, and ex-\nemplars. The prompt template\nis detailed in Figure 3. This variation in performance\nacross the datasets highlights the importance of encoder selection based on the specific characteristics\nand requirements of the dataset.\nB.5\nThe Choice of LLM\nAs for the choice of LLM, we considered both Llama2-7b and Llama2-13b.     "chunk_2f4809d54362f998c1c0710e915a721b": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_2f4809d54362f998c1c0710e915a721b",
        "text": "Abstract\nLarge language models (LLMs) have achieved\nremarkable performance in natural language\nunderstanding and generation tasks. However,\nthey often suffer from limitations such as diffi-\nculty in incorporating new knowledge, gener-\nating hallucinations, and explaining their rea-\nsoning process. To address these challenges,\nwe propose a novel prompting pipeline, named\nMindMap, that leverages knowledge graphs\n(KGs) to enhance LLMs’ inference and trans-\nparency. Our method enables LLMs to com-\nprehend KG inputs and infer with a combina-\ntion of implicit and external knowledge. More-\nover, our method elicits the mind map of LLMs,\nwhich reveals their reasoning pathways based\non the ontology of knowledge. We evaluate our\nmethod on diverse question & answering tasks,\nespecially in medical domains, and show sig-\nnificant improvements over baselines. We also\nintroduce a new hallucination evaluation bench-\nmark and analyze the effects of different com-\nponents of our method. Our results demonstrate\nthe effectiveness and robustness of our method\nin merging knowledge from LLMs and KGs for\ncombined inference. To reproduce our results\nand extend the framework further, we make our\ncodebase available at https://github.com/wyl-\nwilling/MindMap.\n1\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1253,
        "score": 0.3906501829624176,
        "pair_tokens": 345
      }
    ],
    "chunk_3230a7429a621a89f8fef1361c527b3a": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_3230a7429a621a89f8fef1361c527b3a",
        "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. While existing works integrate LLMs and\nGNNs in various ways, they mostly focus on conventional graph tasks such as node, edge and graph\n1Our codes and datasets are available at: https://github.com/XiaoxinHe/G-Retriever\narXiv:2402.07630v3  [cs.LG]  27 May 2024\n\nNew Benchmark\nGraphQA\nNew Architecture\nG-Retriever\nTechniques\nRetrieval Augmented Generation\nGraph Prompt Tuning\nGraph Textualization\n",

      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_675c20afd5f26d294c1e46627fdf87c2",
        "text": "To evaluate hallucination, we instructed the models to answer graph-related questions, specifically\nidentifying supporting nodes or edges from the graph. We manually reviewed 100 responses from\nboth our method and the baseline (i.e., LLM with graph prompt tuning), verifying the existence\nof the nodes and edges referenced in the model’s output within the actual graph. Table 5 shows\nthat G-Retriever significantly reduces hallucinations by 54% compared to the baseline, as our graph\nretrieval ensures that the data is sourced directly from the actual graph, leading to less hallucination.\nSee Appendix F for details.\n6.5\nAblation Study\nIn this ablation study, we assess the individual impact of key components within our pipeline. As\nshown in Table 6, there are performance drops when any of these components are removed, with the\ngraph encoder and textualized graph showing declines of 22.51% and 19.19%, respectively. This\ndemonstrates their complementary effects in representing the graph in both textual and embedded\nformats. Additionally, the retrieval on graphs is also important to the overall performance. Further\ndetails are available in Appendix B.3. We also present additional studies on our framework: it is\nrobust to the choice of graph encoders (see Appendix B.4) and benefits from the increased scale of\nLLMs (see Appendix B.5).\nAdditionally, we include a detailed comparison with existing retrieval methods (see Appendix D), a\ndiscussion on the complexity (see Appendix E), and demonstrations on how to use G-Retriever to\n‘chat with your graph’ (see Appendix G).\n7\n",

    "chunk_959c988b96d931d1ebc6098683c56d6b": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_959c988b96d931d1ebc6098683c56d6b",
        "text": "Conclusion\nThis paper introduced knowledge graph (KG)\nprompting that 1) endows LLMs with the capabil-\nity of comprehending KG inputs and 2) facilitates\nLLMs inferring with a combined implicit knowl-\nedge and the retrieved external knowledge. We then\ninvestigate eliciting the mind map, where LLMs\nperform the reasoning and generate the answers\nwith rationales represented in graphs. Through\nextensive experiments on three question & answer-\ning datasets, we demonstrated that our approach,\nMindMap, achieves remarkable empirical gains\nover vanilla LLMs and retrieval-augmented genera-\ntion methods, and is robust to mismatched retrieval\nknowledge. We envision this work opens the door\nto fulfilling reliable and transparent LLM inference\nin production.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 753,
        "score": 0.3293917179107666,
        "pair_tokens": 233
      }

    "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3",
        "text": "Tackling Hallucination in Graph LLMs. LLMs are prone to hallucination, a phenomenon where the\ngenerated content is factually inaccurate or nonsensical [12]. We validate the presence of this issue in\ngraph settings. In particular, we employ a baseline method that adapts MiniGPT-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31]. Our findings, shown in Table 1, indicate that hallucination, an important problem\nin text-based LLMs, is also prevalent in Graph LLMs. This may be attributed to the baseline’s\ninability to recall the entire graph structure from a single graph embedding, leading to the generation\nof incorrect nodes or edges during the QA task. In contrast, by employing RAG for direct information\nretrieval from the actual graph, our G-Retriever mitigates this issue, as substantiated by Table 1.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 892,
        "score": 0.15662017464637756,
        "pair_tokens": 295
      }
    ],
    "chunk_c36c0155590c0da356beed7403c524ae": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_c36c0155590c0da356beed7403c524ae",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our method for a suite of question &\nanswering tasks that require sophisticated reason-\ning and domain knowledge and compare it with\nretrieval-based baselines.\n4.1\nExperimental Setup\nWe evaluate the utilization of external knowl-\nedge graphs by MindMap in complex question-\nanswering tasks across three medical Q&A\ndatasets:\nGenMedGPT-5k, CMCQA, and Ex-\nplainCPE. These datasets cover patient-doctor\ndialogues, multi-round clinical dialogues, and\nmultiple-choice questions from the Chinese Na-\ntional Licensed Pharmacist Examination, respec-\ntively. To support KG-enhanced methods, we con-\nstruct two knowledge graphs (EMCKG and CM-\nCKG) containing entities and relationships related\nto medical concepts. The ExplainCPE dataset uti-\nlizes CMCKG with knowledge mismatches to as-\nsess the impact of incorrect retrieval knowledge\non model performance. We compare MindMap’s\nability to integrate implicit and explicit knowledge\nwith various baselines, including vanilla GPT-3.5\nand GPT-4, as well as the tree-of-thought method\n(TOT) (Yao et al., 2023a), which uses a tree struc-\nture for reasoning. Additionally, we consider three\nretrieval-augmented baselines: BM25 retriever,\nText Embedding retriever, and KG retriever, see\ninstruction details in Appendix D. These base-\nlines leverage different methods and sources for\nevidence retrieval, with gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 as the\nbackbone for all retrieval-based methods. Detailed\ndescriptions of these baselines are provided in Ap-\npendix C.\n4.2\nMedical Question Answering\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1536,
        "score": 0.6391732096672058,
        "pair_tokens": 457
      }
    ],
    "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634",
        "text": "The goal of this work is to build a plug-and-play\nprompting approach to elicit the graph-of-thoughts\nreasoning capability in LLMs. We call our method\nMindMap because it enables LLMs to comprehend\ngraphical inputs to build their own mind map that\nsupports evidence-grounded generation. A con-\nceptual demonstration of our framework is in Fig-\nure 2. Specifically, MindMap sparks the graph\nof thoughts of LLMs that (1) consolidates the re-\ntrieved facts from KGs and the implicit knowledge\nfrom LLMs, (2) discovers new patterns in input\nKGs, and (3) reasons over the mind map to yield\nfinal outputs. We conducted experiments on three\ndatasets to illustrate that MindMap outperforms\na series of prompting approaches by a large mar-\ngin. This work underscores how LLM can learn to\nconduct synergistic inference with KG. By integrat-\ning both implicit and explicit knowledge, LLMs\ncan achieve transparent and dependable inference,\nadapting to different levels of correctness in addi-\ntional KG information.\n2\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1004,
        "score": 0.36263054609298706,
        "pair_tokens": 299
      }
    ],
    "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1542,
        "score": 0.23388130962848663,
        "pair_tokens": 433
      }
    ],
    "chunk_38127ddd5689cc678e530ff793d2a6e3": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_38127ddd5689cc678e530ff793d2a6e3",
        "text": "Figure 2: A conceptual demonstration of evidence query sub-graphs, merged reasoning sub-graphs, and mind map.\nThe entity inputs Vq is identified from the input. Lines and circles of the same color indicate that they correspond.\nThe red dashed lines in the MindMap box illustrate the augmentation operation based on the knowledge of LLM.\nknowledge bases, knowledge graphs (KG) are es-\ntablished by the triples of entities and relations, i.e.,\n{head, relation, tail}. They can provide ex-\nplicit knowledge representation and interpretable\nreasoning paths. Besides, KGs are amenable to con-\ntinual modifications to debug the existing knowl-\nedge or add new knowledge.     "chunk_32dac8cfeb94d792bd2f0f86f90c6f12": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_32dac8cfeb94d792bd2f0f86f90c6f12",
        "text": "The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with\nlarge language models (LLMs), particularly in med-\nical contexts, presents several potential challenges.\nOne significant concern is the risk of replicating\nany existing biases or errors in the knowledge\ngraphs. These graphs, often built from pre-existing\ndata sources, might contain outdated or partial in-\nformation, which could inadvertently influence the\nLLM’s outputs. Another issue lies in the integra-\ntion complexity between KGs and LLMs, which\ncould lead to unexpected errors or logical incon-\nsistencies, especially when addressing intricate or\nvague queries. This aspect is critically important\nin the medical field, where precision is paramount.\nMoreover, there’s a possibility that the LLMs might\nbecome excessively dependent on the KGs, which\ncould hinder their performance in scenarios where\nKGs are not accessible or are lacking in infor-\nmation. Additionally, the use of \"mind maps\" to\ntrace the LLMs’ reasoning paths, while innovative,\nraises questions about the models’ interpretability.\nIf these visual representations are complex or ob-\nscure, it may be difficult for users to understand\nhow conclusions were reached, potentially dimin-\nishing trust in these advanced systems. In summary,\nwhile the merger of KGs with LLMs is a promising\ndevelopment, it is crucial to address these poten-\ntial issues to ensure the responsible and efficacious\napplication of this technology.\n\n(b)\nReference\n(c)\nOutput \nMindMap\nGPT-3.5\n(a)\nQuestion\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1498,
        "score": 0.2240554392337799,
        "pair_tokens": 409
      }

    "chunk_5c9e14854565607ec53c355da481c451": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_5c9e14854565607ec53c355da481c451",
        "text": "Enhancing Scalability and Efficiency in Graph LLMs. Recent research endeavors have explored\ntranslating graphs into natural language, such as by flattening nodes and edges into a text sequence,\nenabling their processing by LLMs for graph-based tasks [56, 6]. However, this method faces critical\nscalability issues. Converting a graph with thousands of nodes and edges into a text sequence results\nin an excessive number of tokens, surpassing the input capacity of many LLMs. An alternative of\ntruncating the graph text sequence to fit the LLM’s input token limit leads to loss of information and\nresponse quality. G-Retriever overcomes these issues with its RAG component, which allows for\neffective scaling to larger graphs by selectively retrieving only relevant parts of the graph.\nTailoring the RAG Approach to Graphs. Existing RAG methodologies are primarily designed\nfor simpler data types or knowledge graphs, where information is retrieved in a manner isolated\nfrom the graph structure [7, 1, 36, 16]. Hence, we introduce a new retrieval approach for general\ntextual graphs. Notably, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST)\n2\n\nTable 1: Observation and mitigation of hallucination in graph LLMs.\nUser\nelephants\ngrass\neating\nbushes\nin\nriver\non the side of\nstanding by\nelephant\nWhat kind of animal is in the bushes?\nAnswer the question and list the nodes or edges from the graph that support your answer.\nLLM w/ Graph Prompt Tuning\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1471,
        "score": 0.12179015576839447,
        "pair_tokens": 445
      }
    ],
    "chunk_f9acd01074a4f478a8d9fe8c7e77be91": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_f9acd01074a4f478a8d9fe8c7e77be91",
        "text": "Abstract—Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and GPT4, are making new waves in the field of natural language\nprocessing and artificial intelligence, due to their emergent ability and generalizability. However, LLMs are black-box models, which\noften fall short of capturing and accessing factual knowledge. In contrast, Knowledge Graphs (KGs), Wikipedia and Huapu for example,\nare structured knowledge models that explicitly store rich factual knowledge. KGs can enhance LLMs by providing external knowledge\nfor inference and interpretability. Meanwhile, KGs are difficult to construct and evolve by nature, which challenges the existing methods\nin KGs to generate new facts and represent unseen knowledge. Therefore, it is complementary to unify LLMs and KGs together and\nsimultaneously leverage their advantages. In this article, we present a forward-looking roadmap for the unification of LLMs and KGs.\nOur roadmap consists of three general frameworks, namely, 1) KG-enhanced LLMs, which incorporate KGs during the pre-training and\ninference phases of LLMs, or for the purpose of enhancing understanding of the knowledge learned by LLMs; 2) LLM-augmented KGs,\nthat leverage LLMs for different KG tasks such as embedding, completion, construction, graph-to-text generation, and question\nanswering; and 3) Synergized LLMs + KGs, in which LLMs and KGs play equal roles and work in a mutually beneficial way to enhance\nboth LLMs and KGs for bidirectional reasoning driven by both data and knowledge. We review and summarize existing efforts within\nthese three frameworks in our roadmap and pinpoint their future research directions.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1641,
        "score": 0.029201289638876915,
        "pair_tokens": 451
      }
    ],
    "chunk_67201fef435f6ac14b79550309c5d685": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_67201fef435f6ac14b79550309c5d685",
        "text": "The Need for a Comprehensive GraphQA Benchmark. Question answering (QA) is a fundamen-\ntally important task in natural language processing, serving as a key benchmark for assessing LLMs\nand providing a unified interface for various capabilities. Despite extensive research in QA, a com-\nprehensive benchmark specifically tailored for the graph modality is lacking. In contrast to existing\nbenchmarks that focus on basic graph-based reasoning tasks such as node degree, edge existence, and\nshortest path [6, 44], our benchmark addresses complex and real-world graph applications including\ncommon sense reasoning, scene understanding, and knowledge graph reasoning (refer to Figure 2).\nThis is vital for measuring progress toward a model capable of answering a wide range of questions\nabout graphs from diverse applications.\nNew Architecture for GraphQA. To enable effective and efficient graph QA, even on large graphs,\nwe propose G-Retriever, a new framework combining the strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG\n(Figure 3). Next, we will discuss the motivation, strengths, and details of our model.\n",
        "start_char": 0,

      "quote": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n",

      "quote": "• KG retrieval + GPT-3.5 We compare with exist-\ning KG retrieval methods (Jia et al., 2021; Sun\net al., 2023), which aim to find the shortest KG\npath between every pair of question entities. The\nfinal prompt is then retrieved from KG to guide\nGPT-3.5 model to answer questions. For fair\ncomparisons, we use the same preliminary pro-\ncess as our method to recognize the entities in\nquestion query. The key differences between\nMindMap and these are that they do not think\non multiple evidence KG sub-graphs with multi-\nthought in LLM, and without backtracking evi-\ndence sources.\n• Tree-of-thought (TOT) We compare TOT as a\ntypical Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022b) base-\nline with MindMap. TOT is a method that uses\na tree structure to solve complex problems(Yao\net al., 2023a). By extending one inference path\ninto multiple inference paths, the model can syn-\nthesize the results of multiple inference paths to\nobtain the final conclusion.\nD\nPrompt Engine\n• The instructions of MindMap components.\nTable 9 shows the instruction of Step I: en-\ntity recognition, which aims to identify and\nlabel medical entities in the user query. Table\n10 shows the templates of Step II (Evidence\nGraph Aggregation), which generates natural\nlanguage sentences from the evidence graph\nnodes and edges.\n• The instructions of baseline methods: Table\n11 shows the prompt template of two docu-\nment retrieval methods (BM25 Retrieval and\nEmbedding Retrieval). The input is the ques-\ntion and the most related document context.\n",

      "quote": "In Figure 4(c) (Appendix F), when faced with a\nquestion where GPT-3.5 is accurate but KG Re-\ntriever errs, MindMap achieves an accuracy rate\nof 55%. We attribute the low accuracy of the KG\nRetriever to its inability to retrieve the necessary\nknowledge for problem-solving. MindMap effec-\ntively addresses such instances by leveraging the\nLLM inherent knowledge, identifying pertinent ex-\nternal explicit knowledge, and seamlessly integrat-\ning it into a unified graph structure.\n4.6.2\nHow robust is MindMap to unmatched\nfact queries?\nThe question in Figure 6 (Appendix F) contains\nmisleading symptom facts, such as ‘jaundice in my\neyes’ leading baseline models to retrieve irrelevant\nknowledge linked to ‘eye’. This results in failure\nto identify the correct disease, with recommended\ndrugs and tests unrelated to liver disease. In con-\ntrast, our model MindMap accurately identifies\ncirrhosis’ and recommends the relevant ‘blood test’\nshowcasing its robustness.\n4.6.3\nHow does MindMap aggregate evidence\ngraphs considering entity semantics?\n",

        "text_sha256": "dc7fe58ffd9b85a1fd6dbef21ef8c7fac0976554fcd90520be05dffa58ec229f",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "• KG retrieval + GPT-3.5 We compare with exist-\ning KG retrieval methods (Jia et al., 2021; Sun\net al., 2023), which aim to find the shortest KG\npath between every pair of question entities. The\nfinal prompt is then retrieved from KG to guide\nGPT-3.5 model to answer questions. For fair\ncomparisons, we use the same preliminary pro-\ncess as our method to recognize the entities in\nquestion query. The key differences between\nMindMap and these are that they do not think\non multiple evidence KG sub-graphs with multi-\nthought in LLM, and without backtracking evi-\ndence sources.\n• Tree-of-thought (TOT) We compare TOT as a\ntypical Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022b) base-\nline with MindMap. TOT is a method that uses\na tree structure to solve complex problems(Yao\net al., 2023a). By extending one inference path\ninto multiple inference paths, the model can syn-\nthesize the results of multiple inference paths to\nobtain the final conclusion.\nD\nPrompt Engine\n• The instructions of MindMap components.\nTable 9 shows the instruction of Step I: en-\ntity recognition, which aims to identify and\nlabel medical entities in the user query. Table\n10 shows the templates of Step II (Evidence\nGraph Aggregation), which generates natural\nlanguage sentences from the evidence graph\nnodes and edges.\n• The instructions of baseline methods: Table\n11 shows the prompt template of two docu-\nment retrieval methods (BM25 Retrieval and\nEmbedding Retrieval). The input is the ques-\ntion and the most related document context.\n"

        "text_sha256": "90ca4f68b057c367329013735770680c3cb229ca8407ea6f02fe863718b0e2e4",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n"
      }

        "section": "Method",
        "text": "In Figure 4(c) (Appendix F), when faced with a\nquestion where GPT-3.5 is accurate but KG Re-\ntriever errs, MindMap achieves an accuracy rate\nof 55%. We attribute the low accuracy of the KG\nRetriever to its inability to retrieve the necessary\nknowledge for problem-solving. MindMap effec-\ntively addresses such instances by leveraging the\nLLM inherent knowledge, identifying pertinent ex-\nternal explicit knowledge, and seamlessly integrat-\ning it into a unified graph structure.\n4.6.2\nHow robust is MindMap to unmatched\nfact queries?\nThe question in Figure 6 (Appendix F) contains\nmisleading symptom facts, such as ‘jaundice in my\neyes’ leading baseline models to retrieve irrelevant\nknowledge linked to ‘eye’. This results in failure\nto identify the correct disease, with recommended\ndrugs and tests unrelated to liver disease. In con-\ntrast, our model MindMap accurately identifies\ncirrhosis’ and recommends the relevant ‘blood test’\nshowcasing its robustness.\n4.6.3\nHow does MindMap aggregate evidence\ngraphs considering entity semantics?\n"

        "text": "GPT-3.5\n0.7612\n0.8003\n0.7800\n4.8571\n0.5563\nTree-of-thought(TOT)\n0.7202\n0.7949\n0.7554\n-\n0.5483\nGPT4\n0.7689\n0.7893\n0.7786\n4.1764\n0.5577\nBM25 Retriever\n0.7693\n0.7981\n0.7831\n3.5546\n0.5834\nEmbedding Retriever\n0.7690\n0.8038\n0.7857\n3.1232\n0.5886\nKG Retriever\n0.7717\n0.8030\n0.7868\n3.4159\n0.5871\nploiting the knowledge of LLM itself. However,\nMindMap enables LLM to synergistically infer\nfrom both the retrieved evidence graphs and its\nown knowledge. We attribute this ability to three\naspects: (1) Language Understanding, as LLM can\ncomprehend and extract the knowledge from Gm\nand the query in natural language, (2) Knowledge\nReasoning, as LLM can perform entity disambigua-\ntion and produce the final answer based on the\nmind map constructed from Gm, and (3) Knowl-\nedge Enhancement, as LLM can leverage its im-\nplicit knowledge to expand, connect, and improve\nthe information relevant to the query. This ability\nis especially valuable when the external knowledge\ninput is inaccurate.\n4\n"

        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n"

        "text_sha256": "23a9d6ab71908374430cf7f8100e30632a2b79990a662cb5505545aa9a300795",
        "section": "Method",
        "text": "Figure 4 in Appendix F illustrates MindMap’s per-\nformance on diverse question types.\nFor drug-\nrelated questions (a) and (d), which demand in-\ndepth knowledge, MindMap outperforms other\nmethods.\nDisease-related questions (b) and (f)\nshow comparable results between retrieval methods\nand MindMap, indicating that incorporating exter-\nnal knowledge mitigates errors in language model\noutputs. Notably, for general knowledge questions\n(c), LLMs like GPT-3.5 perform better, while re-\ntrieval methods lag. This suggests that retrieval\nmethods may overlook the knowledge embedded\nin LLMs. Conversely, MindMap performs as well\nas GPT-3.5 in handling general knowledge ques-\ntions, highlighting its effectiveness in synergizing\nLLM and KG knowledge for adaptable inference\nacross datasets with varying KG fact accuracies.\n5\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "301d2001db65c52b87a43c9698e090e5d0df9e1e6213ed8b8ca7533a49e5bfb7",
        "section": "Method",
        "text": "In Figure 7 of Appendix F, nodes like ‘vaginitis’\nand ‘atrophic vaginitis’ are present in different\nevidence sub-graphs but share a semantic iden-\ntity. MindMap allows LLMs to disambiguate and\nmerge these diverse evidence graphs for more ef-\nfective reasoning. The resulting mind maps also\nmap entities back to the input evidence graphs. Ad-\nditionally, Figure 7 illustrates the GPT-4 rater’s\npreference for total factual correctness and disease\ndiagnosis factual correctness across methods. No-\ntably, MindMap is highlighted for providing more\nspecific disease diagnosis results compared to the\nbaseline, which offers vague mentions and lacks\ntreatment options. In terms of disease diagnosis\nfactual correctness, the GPT-4 rater observes that\nMindMap aligns better with the ground truth.\n4.6.4\nHow does MindMap visualize the\ninference process and evidence sources?\nFigure 8 in Appendix F presents a comprehensive\nresponse to a CMCQA question. It includes a sum-\nmary, an inference process, and a mind map. The\nsummary extracts the accurate result from the mind\nmap, while the inference process displays multiple\nreasoning chains from the entities on the evidence\ngraph Gm. The mind map combines all the infer-\nence chains into a reasoning graph, providing an in-\ntuitive understanding of knowledge connections in\neach step and the sources of evidence sub-graphs.\n4.6.5\nHow does MindMap leverage LLM\nknowledge for various tasks?\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "be177440a5c4c624cab1e1c136c414c0e78ce6f931f17d787387a8590bbd2866",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "MindMap still outshines all retrieval-based meth-\nods, including KG Retriever. This suggests previ-\nous retrieval-based approaches might overly rely\non retrieved external knowledge, compromising\nthe language model’s (LLM) ability to grasp intri-\ncate logic and dialogue nuances using its implicit\nknowledge. Conversely, MindMap leverages both\nexternal and implicit knowledge in graph reasoning,\nyielding more accurate answers.\n4.4\nGenerate with Mismatch Knowledge from\nKG\nIn addressing the robustness of MindMap concern-\ning the factual correctness of KG, we leverage\nthe identical KG dataset employed in the second\ndataset - ExplainPE. Consequently, the knowledge\nretrieved may tend to be redundant or devoid of\naccurate information. This aspect is particularly\ncrucial since it mirrors a common scenario in pro-\nduction, where LLM often needs to generate an-\nswers by amalgamating both its implicit knowledge\nand the knowledge retrieved from external sources.\n4.4.1\nEvaluation Metrics\nWe evaluate all methods based on the accuracy of\nthe generated choice and the quality of the expla-\nnations. For assessing explanation quality, we use\nBERTScore and GPT-4 ranking. We specifically\ninstruct the GPT-4 rater to prioritize the correctness\nof the explanation over its helpfulness or integrity.\n4.4.2\nResults\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets. These results\nunderscore the significant reduction in hallucinations with G-Retriever, particularly in the challenging\ntask of accurately citing both nodes and edges in graph-based contexts.\nG\nDemonstrations\nWe demonstrate the interaction capabilities of G-Retriever with creative questions on different\ndatasets: ExplaGraphs, SceneGraphs, and WebQSP. These examples are showcased in Tables 13,\n14, and 15, respectively.         "text_sha256": "ce3d7b113af7b849ddfe175491ce2cdc9295a83de33dbd6849c02e4a4dfc6338",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "The goal of this work is to build a plug-and-play\nprompting approach to elicit the graph-of-thoughts\nreasoning capability in LLMs. We call our method\nMindMap because it enables LLMs to comprehend\ngraphical inputs to build their own mind map that\nsupports evidence-grounded generation. A con-\nceptual demonstration of our framework is in Fig-\nure 2. Specifically, MindMap sparks the graph\nof thoughts of LLMs that (1) consolidates the re-\ntrieved facts from KGs and the implicit knowledge\nfrom LLMs, (2) discovers new patterns in input\nKGs, and (3) reasons over the mind map to yield\nfinal outputs. We conducted experiments on three\ndatasets to illustrate that MindMap outperforms\na series of prompting approaches by a large mar-\ngin. This work underscores how LLM can learn to\nconduct synergistic inference with KG. By integrat-\ning both implicit and explicit knowledge, LLMs\ncan achieve transparent and dependable inference,\nadapting to different levels of correctness in addi-\ntional KG information.\n2\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "a0273f5461005636626a71d4e4d31b99ba6dbf6e6f2e9372ccb6b9a78f459b98",
        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nThis paper introduced knowledge graph (KG)\nprompting that 1) endows LLMs with the capabil-\nity of comprehending KG inputs and 2) facilitates\nLLMs inferring with a combined implicit knowl-\nedge and the retrieved external knowledge. We then\ninvestigate eliciting the mind map, where LLMs\nperform the reasoning and generate the answers\nwith rationales represented in graphs. Through\nextensive experiments on three question & answer-\ning datasets, we demonstrated that our approach,\nMindMap, achieves remarkable empirical gains\nover vanilla LLMs and retrieval-augmented genera-\ntion methods, and is robust to mismatched retrieval\nknowledge. We envision this work opens the door\nto fulfilling reliable and transparent LLM inference\nin production.\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Figure 2: A conceptual demonstration of evidence query sub-graphs, merged reasoning sub-graphs, and mind map.\nThe entity inputs Vq is identified from the input. Lines and circles of the same color indicate that they correspond.\nThe red dashed lines in the MindMap box illustrate the augmentation operation based on the knowledge of LLM.\nknowledge bases, knowledge graphs (KG) are es-\ntablished by the triples of entities and relations, i.e.,\n{head, relation, tail}. They can provide ex-\nplicit knowledge representation and interpretable\nreasoning paths. Besides, KGs are amenable to con-\ntinual modifications to debug the existing knowl-\nedge or add new knowledge. Due to their flexibility,\npreciseness, and interpretability, KGs emerged as a\npromising complement to the drawbacks of LLMs\n(Pan et al., 2023). For instance, KG triples were\nadded to the training of LLMs (Zhang et al., 2019b)\nor KG encoders were entangled with LLM layers\nfor joint inference and optimization on graph and\ntext data (Zhang et al., 2022). By contrast, our work\npivots on the synergistic inference of KGs and fixed\nLLMs, which is applicable to powerful pre-trained\nLLMs, such as commercial LLM-as-service APIs.\nIn general, the prior arts in this venue can be cate-\ngorized into two genres:\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "f09d745f6be393fbeefac283ef11e5fa373bec170414a1eae9ebda9970ce0697",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nLarge language models (LLMs) have achieved\nremarkable performance in natural language\nunderstanding and generation tasks. However,\nthey often suffer from limitations such as diffi-\nculty in incorporating new knowledge, gener-\nating hallucinations, and explaining their rea-\nsoning process. To address these challenges,\nwe propose a novel prompting pipeline, named\nMindMap, that leverages knowledge graphs\n(KGs) to enhance LLMs’ inference and trans-\nparency. Our method enables LLMs to com-\nprehend KG inputs and infer with a combina-\ntion of implicit and external knowledge. More-\nover, our method elicits the mind map of LLMs,\nwhich reveals their reasoning pathways based\non the ontology of knowledge. We evaluate our\nmethod on diverse question & answering tasks,\nespecially in medical domains, and show sig-\nnificant improvements over baselines. We also\nintroduce a new hallucination evaluation bench-\nmark and analyze the effects of different com-\nponents of our method. Our results demonstrate\nthe effectiveness and robustness of our method\nin merging knowledge from LLMs and KGs for\ncombined inference. To reproduce our results\nand extend the framework further, we make our\ncodebase available at https://github.com/wyl-\nwilling/MindMap.\n1\n"
      }
    },
