        "text_sha256": "b6ab2f5a2f84ccea28361c4a730a9200490821231bd0bd5594d92d3b2b0bd502",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with\nlarge language models (LLMs), particularly in med-\nical contexts, presents several potential challenges.\nOne significant concern is the risk of replicating\nany existing biases or errors in the knowledge\ngraphs. These graphs, often built from pre-existing\ndata sources, might contain outdated or partial in-\nformation, which could inadvertently influence the\nLLM’s outputs. Another issue lies in the integra-\ntion complexity between KGs and LLMs, which\ncould lead to unexpected errors or logical incon-\nsistencies, especially when addressing intricate or\nvague queries. This aspect is critically important\nin the medical field, where precision is paramount.\nMoreover, there’s a possibility that the LLMs might\nbecome excessively dependent on the KGs, which\ncould hinder their performance in scenarios where\nKGs are not accessible or are lacking in infor-\nmation. Additionally, the use of \"mind maps\" to\ntrace the LLMs’ reasoning paths, while innovative,\nraises questions about the models’ interpretability.\nIf these visual representations are complex or ob-\nscure, it may be difficult for users to understand\nhow conclusions were reached, potentially dimin-\nishing trust in these advanced systems. In summary,\nwhile the merger of KGs with LLMs is a promising\ndevelopment, it is crucial to address these poten-\ntial issues to ensure the responsible and efficacious\napplication of this technology.\n\n(b)\nReference\n(c)\nOutput \nMindMap\nGPT-3.5\n(a)\nQuestion\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "3714755ac8b668addb92b1cab1fd8d09829a000019a3635a68f283963e91d45d",
        "section": "Method",
        "text": "To evaluate hallucination, we instructed the models to answer graph-related questions, specifically\nidentifying supporting nodes or edges from the graph. We manually reviewed 100 responses from\nboth our method and the baseline (i.e., LLM with graph prompt tuning), verifying the existence\nof the nodes and edges referenced in the model’s output within the actual graph. Table 5 shows\nthat G-Retriever significantly reduces hallucinations by 54% compared to the baseline, as our graph\nretrieval ensures that the data is sourced directly from the actual graph, leading to less hallucination.\nSee Appendix F for details.\n6.5\nAblation Study\nIn this ablation study, we assess the individual impact of key components within our pipeline. As\nshown in Table 6, there are performance drops when any of these components are removed, with the\ngraph encoder and textualized graph showing declines of 22.51% and 19.19%, respectively. This\ndemonstrates their complementary effects in representing the graph in both textual and embedded\nformats. Additionally, the retrieval on graphs is also important to the overall performance. Further\ndetails are available in Appendix B.3. We also present additional studies on our framework: it is\nrobust to the choice of graph encoders (see Appendix B.4) and benefits from the increased scale of\nLLMs (see Appendix B.5).\nAdditionally, we include a detailed comparison with existing retrieval methods (see Appendix D), a\ndiscussion on the complexity (see Appendix E), and demonstrations on how to use G-Retriever to\n‘chat with your graph’ (see Appendix G).\n7\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "e771479ef386d2192338b644237321c2ea9e728e973ce41e7a050cc2be098a5d",
        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "15f54620cc5281b23dbb30933a88888a8a2adf561d08c51720e8f5a8dac1424c",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. While existing works integrate LLMs and\nGNNs in various ways, they mostly focus on conventional graph tasks such as node, edge and graph\n1Our codes and datasets are available at: https://github.com/XiaoxinHe/G-Retriever\narXiv:2402.07630v3  [cs.LG]  27 May 2024\n\nNew Benchmark\nGraphQA\nNew Architecture\nG-Retriever\nTechniques\nRetrieval Augmented Generation\nGraph Prompt Tuning\nGraph Textualization\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "0dc04bc9f3befdf1b26b9fa232c5c8f522ee17ae0f0ad7dc2e1ec5b12e9c46e6",
        "section": "3. LLM reasoning on the mind map: Last, we",
        "text": "To generate a mind map and find final results, we\nprovide LLMs with a prompt that has five compo-\nnents: a system instruction, a question, evidence\ngraphs Gm, a graph-of-thought instruction, and ex-\nemplars. The graph-of-thought instruction uses\nthe Langchain technique to guide LLMs to com-\nprehend and enhance the input, build their own\nmind map for reasoning, and index the knowledge\nsources of the mind map. The prompt template\nis detailed in Figure 3. The final answers consist\nof a summary answer, an inference process, and a\nmind map that shows the graph reasoning pathways.\nThe entities in the mind map are from the evidence\ngraphs Gm and LLM’s own retrieval enhancement,\nas shown in the right red box in Figure 5 in Ap-\npendix D.\n3.3.2\nSynergistic Inference with LLM and KG\nKnowledge\nWe find that previous retrieval-augmented LLMs\ntend to rephrase the retrieved facts without ex-\n\nTable 1: The statistics of the used datasets.\nDataset\nGenMedGPT-5k\nCMCQA\nExplainCPE\nDomain\nEnglish Clinical Q&A\nChinese Long Dialogue\n5-way Choice Question\nMulti-task\nDisease, Drug, Test\nDisease, Drug, Test, Food\nOption, Explanation\nKG dataset\nEMCKG\nCMCKG\nCMCKG\nQuestion\n714\n468\n400\nNode\n1122\n62282\n62282\nTriple\n5802\n506490\n506490\nRelationship\n6\n12\n12\nTable 2: The BERTScore and GPT4 ranking of all meth-\nods for GenMedGPT-5k.\nBERT Score\nGPT4 Ranking\nHallucination\nPrecision\nRecall\nF1 Score\n(Average)\nQuantify\nMindMap\n0.7936\n0.7977\n0.7954\n1.8725\n0.6070\n"

        "text_sha256": "c0453f83b6adf1f5d26a386b0e6c924b5f1ae30b67e4ce7c7739d3f2428d1ea0",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Tackling Hallucination in Graph LLMs. LLMs are prone to hallucination, a phenomenon where the\ngenerated content is factually inaccurate or nonsensical [12]. We validate the presence of this issue in\ngraph settings. In particular, we employ a baseline method that adapts MiniGPT-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31]. Our findings, shown in Table 1, indicate that hallucination, an important problem\nin text-based LLMs, is also prevalent in Graph LLMs. This may be attributed to the baseline’s\ninability to recall the entire graph structure from a single graph embedding, leading to the generation\nof incorrect nodes or edges during the QA task. In contrast, by employing RAG for direct information\nretrieval from the actual graph, our G-Retriever mitigates this issue, as substantiated by Table 1.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "3bd40790bb9dff09d1b1437625139441c9ae55d33b6946da3cafd3c30a15cda2",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "Experiments\nWe evaluate our method for a suite of question &\nanswering tasks that require sophisticated reason-\ning and domain knowledge and compare it with\nretrieval-based baselines.\n4.1\nExperimental Setup\nWe evaluate the utilization of external knowl-\nedge graphs by MindMap in complex question-\nanswering tasks across three medical Q&A\ndatasets:\nGenMedGPT-5k, CMCQA, and Ex-\nplainCPE. These datasets cover patient-doctor\ndialogues, multi-round clinical dialogues, and\nmultiple-choice questions from the Chinese Na-\ntional Licensed Pharmacist Examination, respec-\ntively. To support KG-enhanced methods, we con-\nstruct two knowledge graphs (EMCKG and CM-\nCKG) containing entities and relationships related\nto medical concepts. The ExplainCPE dataset uti-\nlizes CMCKG with knowledge mismatches to as-\nsess the impact of incorrect retrieval knowledge\non model performance. We compare MindMap’s\nability to integrate implicit and explicit knowledge\nwith various baselines, including vanilla GPT-3.5\nand GPT-4, as well as the tree-of-thought method\n(TOT) (Yao et al., 2023a), which uses a tree struc-\nture for reasoning. Additionally, we consider three\nretrieval-augmented baselines: BM25 retriever,\nText Embedding retriever, and KG retriever, see\ninstruction details in Appendix D. These base-\nlines leverage different methods and sources for\nevidence retrieval, with gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 as the\nbackbone for all retrieval-based methods. Detailed\ndescriptions of these baselines are provided in Ap-\npendix C.\n4.2\nMedical Question Answering\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "878dfab9da1f584983c6a8588286f2d607fcbca677d3130da85115644eb0d065",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "The Need for a Comprehensive GraphQA Benchmark. Question answering (QA) is a fundamen-\ntally important task in natural language processing, serving as a key benchmark for assessing LLMs\nand providing a unified interface for various capabilities. Despite extensive research in QA, a com-\nprehensive benchmark specifically tailored for the graph modality is lacking. In contrast to existing\nbenchmarks that focus on basic graph-based reasoning tasks such as node degree, edge existence, and\nshortest path [6, 44], our benchmark addresses complex and real-world graph applications including\ncommon sense reasoning, scene understanding, and knowledge graph reasoning (refer to Figure 2).\nThis is vital for measuring progress toward a model capable of answering a wide range of questions\nabout graphs from diverse applications.\nNew Architecture for GraphQA. To enable effective and efficient graph QA, even on large graphs,\nwe propose G-Retriever, a new framework combining the strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG\n(Figure 3). Next, we will discuss the motivation, strengths, and details of our model.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "b19a2d053faea5a2dddcb08f15db46e39ca91c20626782da7eb4bd762a2963c5",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "[Incorrect response with hallucinated nodes and edges]\nThe animal in the bushes is a deer.\nNodes:\n* Deer (node 1)\n* Bushes (node 2)\nEdges:\n* Deer →Bushes (edge 1)\n* Deer →Grass (edge 2)\n* Bushes →Grass (edge 3)\nG-Retriever (Ours)\n[Correct response with accurate node and edge references]\nBased on the information provided in the graph, the animal in the bushes is an elephant.\nThe nodes that support this answer are:\n* Node 1: The elephant is mentioned in the first line of the graph.\nThe edges that support this answer are:\n* The edge connects the elephant to the bushes, indicating that the elephant is in the bushes.\nTherefore, the answer to the question is: The animal in the bushes is an elephant.\noptimization problem, which takes the neighborhood information into account during retrieval. This\nalso allows the return of a subgraph most relevant to a query, thereby improving explainability.\nThe contributions of this paper are outlined as follows:\n• Pioneering the integration of Graph RAG. We present the first retrieval approach for\ngeneral textual graph tasks, which greatly enhances scalability and efficiency.\n• Enabling ‘Chat with Your Graph’. We develop a flexible question answering framework\nto handle complex and real-world textual graphs through a unified conversational interface.\n• Introducing A Novel GraphQA Benchmark. We introduce a diverse benchmark targeted\nat real-world graph question answering, filling a crucial research gap.\n• Empirical Findings. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of G-Retriever in\nmultiple domains and present the significant finding of hallucination in graph LLMs.\n2\n"

        "text_sha256": "17e686ca305ed342a6e4b876ac96da8f37e68e06319f70c04017865cd2c65d1a",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Enhancing Scalability and Efficiency in Graph LLMs. Recent research endeavors have explored\ntranslating graphs into natural language, such as by flattening nodes and edges into a text sequence,\nenabling their processing by LLMs for graph-based tasks [56, 6]. However, this method faces critical\nscalability issues. Converting a graph with thousands of nodes and edges into a text sequence results\nin an excessive number of tokens, surpassing the input capacity of many LLMs. An alternative of\ntruncating the graph text sequence to fit the LLM’s input token limit leads to loss of information and\nresponse quality. G-Retriever overcomes these issues with its RAG component, which allows for\neffective scaling to larger graphs by selectively retrieving only relevant parts of the graph.\nTailoring the RAG Approach to Graphs. Existing RAG methodologies are primarily designed\nfor simpler data types or knowledge graphs, where information is retrieved in a manner isolated\nfrom the graph structure [7, 1, 36, 16]. Hence, we introduce a new retrieval approach for general\ntextual graphs. Notably, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST)\n2\n\nTable 1: Observation and mitigation of hallucination in graph LLMs.\nUser\nelephants\ngrass\neating\nbushes\nin\nriver\non the side of\nstanding by\nelephant\nWhat kind of animal is in the bushes?\nAnswer the question and list the nodes or edges from the graph that support your answer.\nLLM w/ Graph Prompt Tuning\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "e4509c86bf82b37787fb99000befeacd8d1aad230238fd14513365ed6c189626",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "The results demonstrate that our proposed method exhibits consistent robustness across different graph\nencoders. Notably, all three encoders – GCN, GAT, and GraphTransformer – demonstrate competitive\nand closely aligned performance on the WebQSP dataset, with Hit@1 scores of 70.70, 70.27, and\n70.49, respectively. However, the performance differentiation becomes more pronounced on the\nExplaGraphs dataset, where GraphTransformer exhibits a superior Hit@1 score of 0.8516, followed\nby GAT and GCN with scores of 0.8430 and 0.8394, respectively. This variation in performance\nacross the datasets highlights the importance of encoder selection based on the specific characteristics\nand requirements of the dataset.\nB.5\nThe Choice of LLM\nAs for the choice of LLM, we considered both Llama2-7b and Llama2-13b. Our experiments\ndemonstrate that stronger LLMs enhance the effectiveness of our method, as shown in Table 8,\nindicating that it benefits from the increased scale of the LLMs.\nTable 8: Performance of different LLMs on the WebQSP dataset.\nLLM\nLlama2-7b\nLlama2-13b\nHit@1\n70.49\n75.58\nC\nGraphQA Benchmark\nIn this section, we detail how our GraphQA benchmark differs from the original datasets, including\nthe specific processing steps we employed. For concrete examples that illustrate the differences\nbetween the raw text in the original dataset and in our GraphQA benchmark, please refer to Table 9.\n"

        "text_sha256": "9ff8de731b4b958a056ef7c83d63573d8401a624d9dd02c6bbe1c9c5217ceb8d",
        "section": "unidentified",
        "text": "Abstract—Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and GPT4, are making new waves in the field of natural language\nprocessing and artificial intelligence, due to their emergent ability and generalizability. However, LLMs are black-box models, which\noften fall short of capturing and accessing factual knowledge. In contrast, Knowledge Graphs (KGs), Wikipedia and Huapu for example,\nare structured knowledge models that explicitly store rich factual knowledge. KGs can enhance LLMs by providing external knowledge\nfor inference and interpretability. Meanwhile, KGs are difficult to construct and evolve by nature, which challenges the existing methods\nin KGs to generate new facts and represent unseen knowledge. Therefore, it is complementary to unify LLMs and KGs together and\nsimultaneously leverage their advantages. In this article, we present a forward-looking roadmap for the unification of LLMs and KGs.\nOur roadmap consists of three general frameworks, namely, 1) KG-enhanced LLMs, which incorporate KGs during the pre-training and\ninference phases of LLMs, or for the purpose of enhancing understanding of the knowledge learned by LLMs; 2) LLM-augmented KGs,\nthat leverage LLMs for different KG tasks such as embedding, completion, construction, graph-to-text generation, and question\nanswering; and 3) Synergized LLMs + KGs, in which LLMs and KGs play equal roles and work in a mutually beneficial way to enhance\nboth LLMs and KGs for bidirectional reasoning driven by both data and knowledge. We review and summarize existing efforts within\nthese three frameworks in our roadmap and pinpoint their future research directions.\n"
      }
    },

        "text": "cost(S) = |ES| × Ce,\n(8)\nand Ce denotes a predefined cost per edge, which is adjustable to control the subgraph size.\nThe original PCST algorithm is designed for node prizes only. However, given the significance of\nedge semantics in certain scenarios, we adapt the algorithm to accommodate edge prizes as follows:\nConsider an edge e with a cost Ce and a prize Pe. If Ce > Pe, it can be treated as a reduced edge cost\nof Ce −Pe. However, if Pe > Ce, negative edge costs are not allowed in the original algorithm. Our\nsolution involves replacing edge e with a ‘virtual node’ ve, connected to both endpoints of e. This\nvirtual node is assigned a prize of Pe −Ce, and the cost of the two new edges leading to the virtual\nnode is set to zero. This modification effectively mirrors the original problem, as including edge e\nin the original graph is analogous to including the virtual node in the modified graph. Finally, we\noptimize the PCST problem using a near-linear time approach [9].\n5.4\nAnswer Generation\nGraph Encoder. Let S∗= (V ∗, E∗) represent the retrieved subgraph. We use a graph encoder to\nmodel the structure of this graph, specifically using a standard Graph Attention Network (GAT) [43].\nOur approach for encoding the retrieved subgraph is defined as follows:\nhg = POOL(GNNϕ1(S∗)) ∈Rdg,\n(9)\nHere, POOL denotes the mean pooling operation, and dg is the dimension of the graph encoder.\nProjection Layer.     "chunk_2f4809d54362f998c1c0710e915a721b": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_2f4809d54362f998c1c0710e915a721b",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 676,
        "text": "Abstract\nLarge language models (LLMs) have achieved\nremarkable performance in natural language\nunderstanding and generation tasks. However,\nthey often suffer from limitations such as diffi-\nculty in incorporating new knowledge, gener-\nating hallucinations, and explaining their rea-\nsoning process. To address these challenges,\nwe propose a novel prompting pipeline, named\nMindMap, that leverages knowledge graphs\n(KGs) to enhance LLMs’ inference and trans-\nparency. Our method enables LLMs to com-\nprehend KG inputs and infer with a combina-\ntion of implicit and external knowledge. More-\nover, our method elicits the mind map of LLMs,\nwhich reveals their reasoning pathways ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.26435837149620056,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_2f4809d54362f998c1c0710e915a721b",
        "start_char": 338,
        "end_char": 981,
        "text": " a novel prompting pipeline, named\nMindMap, that leverages knowledge graphs\n(KGs) to enhance LLMs’ inference and trans-\nparency. Our method enables LLMs to com-\nprehend KG inputs and infer with a combina-\ntion of implicit and external knowledge. More-\nover, our method elicits the mind map of LLMs,\nwhich reveals their reasoning pathways based\non the ontology of knowledge. We evaluate our\nmethod on diverse question & answering tasks,\nespecially in medical domains, and show sig-\nnificant improvements over baselines. We also\nintroduce a new hallucination evaluation bench-\nmark and analyze the effects of different com-\nponents of our method",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.1225232183933258,

        "end_char": 1253,

We evaluate our\nmethod on diverse question & answering tasks,\nespecially in medical domains, and show sig-\nnificant improvements over baselines. We also\nintroduce a new hallucination evaluation bench-\nmark and analyze the effects of different com-\nponents of our method. Our results demonstrate\nthe effectiveness and robustness of our method\nin merging knowledge from LLMs and KGs for\ncombined inference.     "chunk_959c988b96d931d1ebc6098683c56d6b": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_959c988b96d931d1ebc6098683c56d6b",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 648,
        "text": "Conclusion\nThis paper introduced knowledge graph (KG)\nprompting that 1) endows LLMs with the capabil-\nity of comprehending KG inputs and 2) facilitates\nLLMs inferring with a combined implicit knowl-\nedge and the retrieved external knowledge. We then\ninvestigate eliciting the mind map, where LLMs\nperform the reasoning and generate the answers\nwith rationales represented in graphs. Through\nextensive experiments on three question & answer-\ning datasets, we demonstrated that our approach,\nMindMap, achieves remarkable empirical gains\nover vanilla LLMs and retrieval-augmented genera-\ntion methods, and is robust to mismatched retrieval\nknowledge. ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.3919876515865326,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_959c988b96d931d1ebc6098683c56d6b",
        "start_char": 324,
        "end_char": 753,
        "text": "enerate the answers\nwith rationales represented in graphs. Through\nextensive experiments on three question & answer-\ning datasets, we demonstrated that our approach,\nMindMap, achieves remarkable empirical gains\nover vanilla LLMs and retrieval-augmented genera-\ntion methods, and is robust to mismatched retrieval\nknowledge. We envision this work opens the door\nto fulfilling reliable and transparent LLM inference\nin production.\n",
        "document_tokens": 105,
        "score": 0.22661244869232178,
        "pair_tokens": 156
      }
    ],

    "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 555,
        "text": "Tackling Hallucination in Graph LLMs. LLMs are prone to hallucination, a phenomenon where the\ngenerated content is factually inaccurate or nonsensical [12]. We validate the presence of this issue in\ngraph settings. In particular, we employ a baseline method that adapts MiniGPT-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31]. Our findings, shown in Table 1, indicate that hallucination, an important problem\nin text-based LLMs, is also prevalent in Graph LLMs. This may ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.001987774157896638,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3",
        "start_char": 277,
        "end_char": 863,
        "text": "-4 [57] to graphs,\nwhere a frozen LLM interacts with a trainable GNN that encodes graph data as a soft prompt, as in\nGraphToken [31]. Our findings, shown in Table 1, indicate that hallucination, an important problem\nin text-based LLMs, is also prevalent in Graph LLMs. This may be attributed to the baseline’s\ninability to recall the entire graph structure from a single graph embedding, leading to the generation\nof incorrect nodes or edges during the QA task. In contrast, by employing RAG for direct information\nretrieval from the actual graph, our G-Retriever mitigates this issue, ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.17217184603214264,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_99b18cdbb0bd9a36674e8b314d553ad3",
        "start_char": 570,
        "end_char": 892,
        "text": "o the baseline’s\ninability to recall the entire graph structure from a single graph embedding, leading to the generation\nof incorrect nodes or edges during the QA task. In contrast, by employing RAG for direct information\nretrieval from the actual graph, our G-Retriever mitigates this issue, as substantiated by Table 1.\n",
        "document_tokens": 81,
        "score": 0.11338309943675995,

These datasets cover patient-doctor\ndialogues, multi-round clinical dialogues, and\nmultiple-choice questions from the Chinese Na-\ntional Licensed Pharmacist Examination, respec-\ntively. To support KG-enhanced methods, we con",

To support KG-enhanced methods, we con-\nstruct two knowledge graphs (EMCKG and CM-\nCKG) containing entities and relationships related\nto medical concepts. The ExplainCPE dataset uti-\nlizes CMCKG with knowledge mismatches to as-\nsess the impact of incorrect retrieval knowledge\non model performance. We compare ",

    "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 632,
        "text": "The goal of this work is to build a plug-and-play\nprompting approach to elicit the graph-of-thoughts\nreasoning capability in LLMs. We call our method\nMindMap because it enables LLMs to comprehend\ngraphical inputs to build their own mind map that\nsupports evidence-grounded generation. A con-\nceptual demonstration of our framework is in Fig-\nure 2. Specifically, MindMap sparks the graph\nof thoughts of LLMs that (1) consolidates the re-\ntrieved facts from KGs and the implicit knowledge\nfrom LLMs, (2) discovers new patterns in input\nKGs, and (3) reasons over the mind map to yield\nfinal outputs. We conducted experiments on three\n",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.3353508412837982,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634",
        "start_char": 316,
        "end_char": 976,
        "text": " our framework is in Fig-\nure 2. Specifically, MindMap sparks the graph\nof thoughts of LLMs that (1) consolidates the re-\ntrieved facts from KGs and the implicit knowledge\nfrom LLMs, (2) discovers new patterns in input\nKGs, and (3) reasons over the mind map to yield\nfinal outputs. We conducted experiments on three\ndatasets to illustrate that MindMap outperforms\na series of prompting approaches by a large mar-\ngin. This work underscores how LLM can learn to\nconduct synergistic inference with KG. By integrat-\ning both implicit and explicit knowledge, LLMs\ncan achieve transparent and dependable inference,\nadapting to different levels of correctness in add",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.448516845703125,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_12db03641fcfe27c25e6c6b5b44ba634",
        "start_char": 646,
        "end_char": 1004,
        "text": "lustrate that MindMap outperforms\na series of prompting approaches by a large mar-\ngin. This work underscores how LLM can learn to\nconduct synergistic inference with KG. By integrat-\ning both implicit and explicit knowledge, LLMs\ncan achieve transparent and dependable inference,\nadapting to different levels of correctness in addi-\ntional KG information.\n2\n",
        "document_tokens": 84,

    "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 645,
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.004905405919998884,
        "pair_tokens": 211

        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 721,
        "text": "Abstract—Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and GPT4, are making new waves in the field of natural language\nprocessing and artificial intelligence, due to their emergent ability and generalizability. However, LLMs are black-box models, which\noften fall short of capturing and accessing factual knowledge. In contrast, Knowledge Graphs (KGs), Wikipedia and Huapu for example,\nare structured knowledge models that explicitly store rich factual knowledge. KGs can enhance LLMs by providing external knowledge\nfor inference and interpretability. Meanwhile, KGs are difficult to construct and evolve by nature, which challenges the existing methods\nin KGs to generate new facts and represent unseen knowledge. There",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.01923425868153572,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_f9acd01074a4f478a8d9fe8c7e77be91",
        "start_char": 360,
        "end_char": 1047,
        "text": "ia and Huapu for example,\nare structured knowledge models that explicitly store rich factual knowledge. KGs can enhance LLMs by providing external knowledge\nfor inference and interpretability. Meanwhile, KGs are difficult to construct and evolve by nature, which challenges the existing methods\nin KGs to generate new facts and represent unseen knowledge. Therefore, it is complementary to unify LLMs and KGs together and\nsimultaneously leverage their advantages. In this article, we present a forward-looking roadmap for the unification of LLMs and KGs.\nOur roadmap consists of three general frameworks, namely, 1) KG-enhanced LLMs, which incorporate KGs during the pre-training and\ninf",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.02157406695187092,

In this article, we present a forward-looking roadmap for the unification of LLMs and KGs.\nOur roadmap consists of three general frameworks, namely, 1) KG-enhanced LLMs, which incorporate KGs during the pre-training and\ninference phases of LLMs, or for the purpose of enhancing understanding of the knowledge learned by LLMs; 2) LLM-augmented KGs,\nthat leverage LLMs for different KG tasks such as embedding, completion, construction, graph-to-text generation, and question\nanswering",

        "chunk_id": "chunk_67201fef435f6ac14b79550309c5d685",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 680,
        "text": "The Need for a Comprehensive GraphQA Benchmark. Question answering (QA) is a fundamen-\ntally important task in natural language processing, serving as a key benchmark for assessing LLMs\nand providing a unified interface for various capabilities. Despite extensive research in QA, a com-\nprehensive benchmark specifically tailored for the graph modality is lacking. In contrast to existing\nbenchmarks that focus on basic graph-based reasoning tasks such as node degree, edge existence, and\nshortest path [6, 44], our benchmark addresses complex and real-world graph applications including\ncommon sense reasoning, scene understanding, and knowledge graph reasoning (refer to Figure ",
        "document_tokens": 160,
        "score": 0.002560870721936226,
        "pair_tokens": 211
      },
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_67201fef435f6ac14b79550309c5d685",
        "start_char": 340,
        "end_char": 996,
        "text": "aph modality is lacking.       "text_sha256": "766351f6fd8de8bacfaba8094b95b7a79d6f5c409bc3ed7a6cf51c19fbbb4a02",
      "section": "Introduction",
      "text": "Node Specificity. We introduce node specificity as a neurobiologically plausible way to further\nimprove retrieval. It is well known that global signals for word importance, like inverse document\nfrequency (IDF), can improve information retrieval. However, in order for our brain to leverage IDF\nfor retrieval, the number of total “passages” encoded would need to be aggregated with all node\nactivations before memory retrieval is complete. While simple for normal computers, this process\nwould require activating connections between an aggregator neuron and all nodes in the hippocampal\nindex every time retrieval occurs, likely introducing prohibitive computational overhead. Given\nthese constraints, we propose node specificity as an alternative IDF signal which requires only local\nsignals and is thus more neurobiologically plausible. We define the node specificity of node i as\nsi = |Pi|−1, where Pi is the set of passages in P from which node i was extracted, information that\nis already available at each node. Node specificity is used in retrieval by multiplying each query node\nprobability #»n with si before PPR; this allows us to modulate each of their neighborhood’s probability\nas well as their own. We illustrate node specificity in Figure 2 through relative symbol size: the\nStanford logo grows larger than the Alzheimer’s symbol since it appears in fewer documents.\n3\nExperimental Setup\n3.1\nDatasets\n"
    },

      "text_sha256": "e79defa25ad077beb683a3cd64c26e51086287a51eceddab31c89b7f9ee7723a",
      "section": "Related Work",
      "text": "This step aims to construct a subgraph that encompasses as many relevant nodes and edges as possible,\nwhile keeping the graph size manageable. This approach offers two key benefits: Firstly, it helps\nto filter out nodes and edges that are not pertinent to the query. This is crucial because irrelevant\ninformation can overshadow the useful data, potentially diverting the focus of the subsequent LLM\nfrom the information of interest. Secondly, it enhances efficiency; by keeping the graph size\nmanageable, it becomes feasible to translate the graph into natural language and then input it into the\nLLM for processing. The Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree algorithm [2] serves as our primary method\nfor identifying such optimally sized and relevant subgraphs. See Step 3 in Figure 3.\nPrize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST). The PCST problem aims to find a connected subgraph that\nmaximizes the total prize values of its nodes while minimizing the total costs of its edges. Our\napproach assigns higher prize values to nodes and edges more relevant to the query, as measured by\ncosine similarity. Specifically, the top k nodes/edges are assigned descending prize values from k\ndown to 1, with the rest assigned zero. The node prize assignment is as follows:\nprize(n) =\n\u001ak −i,\nif n ∈Vk and n is the top i node,\n0,\notherwise.\n(6)\nEdge prizes are assigned similarly. The objective is to identify a subgraph, S∗= (V ∗, E∗), that\noptimizes the total prize of nodes and edges, minus the costs associated with the size of the subgraph:\nS∗=\nargmax\nS⊆G,\nS is connected\nX\nn∈VS\nprize(n) +\nX\ne∈ES\nprize(e) −cost(S),\n(7)\nwhere\n"

In\ncontrast, in both the FACTKG and MetaQA 3-hop\nscenarios, the performance of the 4-shot learning\nscenario was similar to that of the baselines which\ndid not utilize graph evidence. Thus, the findings highlight the importance\nof formulating in-context examples according to\nthe complexity of the task.\n4.4.2\nTop-K Relation Retrieval\nTable 11 shows the performance according to the\nvalue of k in FACTKG. As a result, performance\ndid not significantly vary depending on the value of\nk. Table 12 illustrates the average number of triples\nretrieved for both supported and refuted claims, de-\npending on k. Despite the increase in the number\nof triples as the value of k grows, it does not im-\npact the accuracy. This suggests that the additional\ntriples are not significantly influential.\nIn MetaQA, the performance and the average\nnumber of retrieved triples are also depicted in\nTable 13 and Table 14, respectively. Unlike the\nFACTKG experiment, as the value of k rises in\nMetaQA, it appears that more significant triples are\nretrieved, leading to improved performance.\n5\n"

      "quote": "PPR Alternatives. As shown in Table 5 (rows 5-6), to examine how much of our results are due to\nthe strength of PPR, we replace the PPR output with the query node probability #»n multiplied by node\nspecificity values (row 5) and a version of this that also distributes a small amount of probability to the\ndirect neighbors of each query node (row 6). First, we find that PPR is a much more effective method\nfor including associations for retrieval on all three datasets compared to both simple baselines.       "quote": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. In\ncontrast, synonymy edges have the largest effect on 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that noisy entity\nstandardization is useful when most relevant concepts are named entities, and improvements to\nsynonymy detection could lead to stronger performance in other datasets.\n5.2\nHippoRAG’s Advantage: Single-Step Multi-Hop Retrieval\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "90ca4f68b057c367329013735770680c3cb229ca8407ea6f02fe863718b0e2e4",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n"
      }

        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "7c357b448e5680712a09e43acea7708d22e67cc997b09b517737f7b0694e07e6",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "IRCoT + HippoRAG (Contriever)\n43.9\n56.6\n75.3\n93.4\n65.8\n82.3\n61.7\n77.4\nIRCoT + HippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n45.3\n57.6\n75.8\n93.9\n67.0\n83.0\n62.7\n78.2\n3.4\nImplementation Details\nBy default, we use GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 [55] with temperature of 0 as our LLM L and Contriever\n[35] or ColBERTv2 [70] as our retriever M. We use 100 examples from MuSiQue’s training data\nto tune HippoRAG’s two hyperparameters: the synonymy threshold τ at 0.8 and the PPR damping\nfactor at 0.5, which determines the probability that PPR will restart a random walk from the query\nnodes instead of continuing to explore the graph. Generally, we find that HippoRAG’s performance\nis rather robust to its hyperparameters. More implementation details can be found in Appendix H.\n4\n"

        "text_sha256": "5afd9348719b7383794053ee8b411be509786259a96b53a3b8f539a11cede540",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Graph-Augmented Reading Comprehension. Earlier works in this category are mainly supervised\nmethods which mix signal from a hyperlink or co-occurrence graph with a language model through a\ngraph neural network (GNN) [20, 67, 65]. More recent works use LLMs and introduce knowledge\ngraph triples directly into the LLM prompt [57, 43, 47]. Although these works share HippoRAG’s\nuse of graphs for multi-hop QA, their generation-based improvements are fully complementary to\nHippoRAG’s, which are solely based on improved retrieval.\nGraph-Augmented Retrieval. In this second category, previous work trains a re-ranking module\nwhich can traverse a graph made using Wikipedia hyperlinks [16, 100, 54, 14, 4, 44]. HippoRAG,\nin contrast, builds a KG from scratch using LLMs and performs multi-hop retrieval without any\nsupervision, making it much more adaptable.\n6.3\nLLMs & KGs\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "35871b0592520ab8f62019ccd53994928ee8acdc397db26626d99faeaa882c8f",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "Results\nWe present our retrieval and QA experimental results below. Given that our method indirectly affects\nQA performance, we report QA results on our best-performing retrieval backbone ColBERTv2 [70].\nHowever, we report retrieval results for several strong single-step and multi-step retrieval techniques.\nSingle-Step Retrieval Results. As seen in Table 2, HippoRAG outperforms all other methods,\nincluding recent LLM-augmented baselines such as Propositionizer and RAPTOR, on our main\ndatasets, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, while achieving competitive performance on HotpotQA.\nWe notice an impressive improvement of 11 and 20% for R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand around 3% on MuSiQue. This difference can be partially explained by 2WikiMultiHopQA’s\nentity-centric design, which is particularly well-suited for HippoRAG. Our lower performance on\nHotpotQA is mainly due to its lower knowledge integration requirements, as explained in Appendix\nB, as well as a due to a concept-context tradeoff which we alleviate with an ensembling technique\ndescribed in Appendix F.2.\nMulti-Step Retrieval Results. For multi-step or iterative retrieval, our experiments in Table 3\ndemonstrate that IRCoT [78] and HippoRAG are complementary. Using HippoRAG as the re-\ntriever for IRCoT continues to bring R@5 improvements of around 4% for MuSiQue, 18% for\n2WikiMultiHopQA and an additional 1% on HotpotQA.\n6\n\nTable 4: QA performance. HippoRAG’s QA improvements correlate with its retrieval improvements\non single-step (rows 1-3) and multi-step retrieval (rows 4-5).\nMuSiQue\n2Wiki\nHotpotQA\nAverage\nRetriever\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\n"
      }

        "text": "Method\nExplaGraphs\nSceneGraphs\nWebQSP\nInference-only\nZero-shot\n0.5650\n0.3974\n41.06\nZero-CoT [18]\n0.5704\n0.5260\n51.30\nCoT-BAG [44]\n0.5794\n0.5680\n39.60\nKAPING [1]\n0.6227\n0.4375\n52.64\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt tuning\n0.5763 ± 0.0243\n0.6341 ± 0.0024\n48.34 ± 0.64\nGraphToken [31]\n0.8508 ± 0.0551\n0.4903 ± 0.0105\n57.05 ± 0.74\nG-Retriever\n0.8516 ± 0.0092\n0.8131 ± 0.0162\n70.49 ± 1.21\n∆Prompt tuning\n↑47.77%\n↑28.23%\n↑45.81%\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n0.8538 ± 0.0353\n0.7862 ± 0.0031\n66.03 ± 0.47\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n0.8705 ± 0.0329\n0.8683 ± 0.0072\n73.79 ± 0.70\n∆LoRA\n↑1.95%\n↑11.74%\n↑10.44%\nTable 3 demonstrates the effectiveness of our method across three datasets in various configurations.\nIn the inference-only setting, G-Retriever surpasses all baselines. For frozen LLM with prompt tuning, G-Retriever\noutperforms traditional prompt tuning and GraphToken [31], a graph prompt tuning-based method,\nwith average performance increases of 40.6% and 30.8% respectively.         "text": "None\n12.5\n24.1\n31.0\n39.6\n30.4\n42.8\n24.6\n35.5\nColBERTv2\n15.5\n26.4\n33.4\n43.3\n43.4\n57.7\n30.8\n42.5\nHippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n19.2\n29.8\n46.6\n59.5\n41.8\n55.0\n35.9\n48.1\nIRCoT (ColBERTv2)\n19.1\n30.5\n35.4\n45.1\n45.5\n58.4\n33.3\n44.7\nIRCoT + HippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n21.9\n33.3\n47.7\n62.7\n45.7\n59.2\n38.4\n51.7\nQuestion Answering Results. We report QA results for HippoRAG, the strongest retrieval baselines,\nColBERTv2 and IRCoT, as well as IRCoT using HippoRAG as a retriever in Table 4. As expected,\nimproved retrieval performance in both single and multi-step settings leads to strong overall im-\nprovements of up to 3%, 17% and 1% F1 scores on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA\nrespectively using the same QA reader. Notably, single-step HippoRAG is on par or outperforms\nIRCoT while being 10-30 times cheaper and 6-13 times faster during online retrieval (Appendix G).\n5\nDiscussions\n5.1\nWhat Makes HippoRAG Work?\n"

        "text_sha256": "af3a6d4226d6b3c87366e20e5b65424897f765f4155e48849aad79e39c2506cc",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "HippoRAG\nContriever\n41.0\n52.1\n71.5\n89.5\n59.0\n76.2\n57.2\n72.6\nColBERTv2\n40.9\n51.9\n70.7\n89.1\n60.5\n77.7\n57.4\n72.9\nHippoRAG w/\nUncertainty Ensemble\nContriever\n42.3\n54.5\n71.3\n87.2\n60.6\n79.1\n58.1\n73.6\nColBERTv2\n42.5\n54.8\n71.9\n89.0\n62.5\n80.0\n59.0\n74.6\nTo get a better trade-off between concepts and context, we introduce an ensembling setting where\nHippoRAG scores are ensembled with dense retrievers when our parahippocampal region shows\nuncertainty regarding the link between query and KG entities. This process represents instances\nwhen no hippocampal index was fully activated by the upstream parahippocampal signal and thus\nthe neocortex must be relied on more strongly. We only use uncertainty ensembling if one of the\nquery-KG entity scores cosine_similarity(M(ci), M(ej)) is lower than a threshold θ, for example,\nif there was no Stanford node in the KG and the closest node in the KG is something that has a cosine\nsimilarity lower than θ such as Stanford Medical Center. The final passage score for uncertainty\n26\n\nensembling is the average of the HippoRAG scores and standard passage retrieval using model M,\nboth of which are first normalized into the 0 to 1 over all passages.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "c40ce0f9ae46cb4e647633a2056fc8610097438333f98b5bdf50d1814191c07d",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Nevertheless, several limitations can be addressed in future work to enable HippoRAG to achieve\nthis goal better. First, we note that all components of HippoRAG are currently used off-the-shelf\nwithout any extra training. There is therefore much room to improve our method’s practical viability\nby performing specific component fine-tuning. This is evident in the error analysis discussed in\nAppendix F, which shows most errors made by our system are due to NER and OpenIE and thus\ncould benefit from direct fine-tuning. Given that the rest of the errors are graph search errors, also in\nAppendix F, we note that several avenues for improvements over simple PPR exist, such as allowing\nrelations to guide graph traversal directly. Additionally, as shown in Appendix F.4, more work must\nbe done to improve the consistency of OpenIE in longer compared to shorter documents. Finally,\nand perhaps most importantly, HippoRAG’s scalability still calls for further validation. Although we\nshow that Llama-3.1 could obtain similar performance to closed-source models and thus reduce costs\nconsiderably, we are yet to empirically prove the efficiency and efficacy of our synthetic hippocampal\nindex as its size grows way beyond current benchmarks.\n"
      }

        "section": "References",
        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets. These results\nunderscore the significant reduction in hallucinations with G-Retriever, particularly in the challenging\ntask of accurately citing both nodes and edges in graph-based contexts.\nG\nDemonstrations\nWe demonstrate the interaction capabilities of G-Retriever with creative questions on different\ndatasets: ExplaGraphs, SceneGraphs, and WebQSP.         "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n"

        "text_sha256": "ffadad8a24b98afff5373c3d1a13f932f8b1ebfa0fc1da41a2a7f203f2283e40",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "62d2d6bc92494bd2583e0391cd268b756f954000661bdb5a9432e49168a291d3",
        "section": "Limitations",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "93f2bbcd4f2e73d22123a0b360c4293fdaea9ddbdb4e4a14f998b2eb37755844",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "One of HippoRAG’s main advantages against iterative retrieval methods is the dramatic online\nretrieval efficiency gains brought on by its single-step multi-hop retrieval ability in terms of both\ncost and time. Specifically, as seen in Table 17, retrieval costs for IRCoT are 10 to 30 times higher\nthan HippoRAG since it only requires extracting relevant named entities from the query instead of\nprocessing all of the retrieved documents. In systems with extremely high usage, a cost difference of\nan order of magnitude such as this one could be extremely important. The difference with IRCoT in\nterms of latency is also substantial, although more challenging to measure exactly. Also as seen in\nTable 17, HippoRAG can be 6 to 13 times faster than IRCoT, depending on the number of retrieval\nrounds that need to be executed (2-4 in our experiments).6\nTable 17: Average cost and efficiency measurements for online retrieval using GPT-3.5 Turbo on\n1,000 queries.\nColBERTv2\nIRCoT\nHippoRAG\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n1-3\n0.1\nTime (minutes)\n1\n20-40\n3\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "b19a2d053faea5a2dddcb08f15db46e39ca91c20626782da7eb4bd762a2963c5",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "text": "[Incorrect response with hallucinated nodes and edges]\nThe animal in the bushes is a deer.\nNodes:\n* Deer (node 1)\n* Bushes (node 2)\nEdges:\n* Deer →Bushes (edge 1)\n* Deer →Grass (edge 2)\n* Bushes →Grass (edge 3)\nG-Retriever (Ours)\n[Correct response with accurate node and edge references]\nBased on the information provided in the graph, the animal in the bushes is an elephant.\nThe nodes that support this answer are:\n* Node 1: The elephant is mentioned in the first line of the graph.\nThe edges that support this answer are:\n* The edge connects the elephant to the bushes, indicating that the elephant is in the bushes.\nTherefore, the answer to the question is: The animal in the bushes is an elephant.\noptimization problem, which takes the neighborhood information into account during retrieval. We present the first retrieval approach for\ngeneral textual graph tasks, which greatly enhances scalability and efficiency.\n• Enabling ‘Chat with Your Graph’. We develop a flexible question answering framework\nto handle complex and real-world textual graphs through a unified conversational interface.\n• Introducing A Novel GraphQA Benchmark. We introduce a diverse benchmark targeted\nat real-world graph question answering, filling a crucial research gap.\n• Empirical Findings.         "text_sha256": "6fbaf67674d4e4f6e2cdb830663f2349a150fb69b239a972d0ba553f2ae14289",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "The choice of similarity function is also important. In this work, we use cosine similarity, a widely\nadopted metric for measuring vector similarity in models that process vision and language. For\ninstance, CLIP also employs cosine similarity to assess the similarity between text and image\nfeatures. Although it might not be the optimal choice, we believe that cosine similarity is a general,\nrepresentative, and valid choice for facilitating fast retrieval tasks.\nD.4\nThe Quality of Retrieval\nWe quantify the quality of our retrieval method as follows: We examine the retrieval subgraph, and if\nthe label is contained within it, we consider it a successful retrieval. We calculate the retrieval success\nrate of our method and the retrieval method proposed in KAPING [1] on the WebQSP dataset.\nTable 11: The quality of retrieval methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nMethod\nRetrieval Accuracy\nKAPING [1] (top-k triple retrieval)\n60.81\nG-Retriever\n70.49\nAs shown in Table 11, these results validate the effectiveness of our retrieval method. In contrast to\nthe triple-based retrieval in KAPING, which relies on the similarity between triples and the query,\nour PCST-based subgraph retrieval is more accurate as it takes the graph structure into account. By\ndesign, it retrieves connected subgraphs, capturing not just nodes or edges with high relevance scores,\nbut also those that act as \"bridges\" connecting other highly relevant nodes and edges.\n18\n\nE\nDiscussion on the Complexity\nE.1\nThe integration of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG\n"

        "section": "References",
        "text": "Most existing GraphRAG methods are designed specifically for knowledge graphs and focus on node,\nedge, or triples-level retrieval [1, 36, 16, 38]. Our method is different in two main ways: 1) It focuses\non more general textual graphs, not just knowledge graphs. 2) It enables the return of a subgraph most\nclosely related to a query, rather than a list of top-k triples. The triples in other methods are chosen in\nisolation from the graph, failing to capture neighborhood information effectively. In contrast, our\nmethod takes the context into account during retrieval.\nD.2\nThe Impact of K for Retrieval\nWe identify the most relevant nodes and edges and use a k-nearest neighbors retrieval approach (see\nEquation 6). Small k values may omit crucial knowledge or information relevant to the query, while\nlarge k values could introduce excessive information, distracting the model from the essential details.\nTo evaluate the impact of the number of k, we have conducted additional experiments by varying the\nchoice of k to 3, 5, 10, and 20.\nTable 10: The impact of k on the webqsp dataset.\nk\n3\n5\n10\n20\nHit@1\n0.6977\n0.7063\n0.7248\n0.7039\nAs shown in Table 10, the Hit@1 metric initially rises for small k values, peaks at a certain point, and\nthen declines for large k values. Determining the optimal k value can be achieved through techniques\nlike cross-validation using a validation set.\nD.3\nThe Choice of Similarity Function\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "e3645042e8fa1db19322302d9398f691f06ddf5d1d132e559caa7e5dbad8ccae",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "• LLM Rerankers: Claude3 and GPT-4 rerankers [11, 62]. These models improve the precision of\ntop-k ada-002 results by reranking them using large language models. We employ GPT-4-turbo\n(gpt-4-1106-preview) and Claude3 (claude-3-opus), setting k = 20 for synthesized\nqueries and k = 10 for human-generated queries. Given a query, the LLMs assign a satisfaction\nscore from 0 to 1 to each candidate entity based on textual and relational information. Due to high\ncomputational costs, we evaluate these rerankers on a random 10% sample of test queries.\nThe performance of these models are measured using standard retrieval metrics below.\n• Hit@k assesses whether the correct item is among the top-k results from the model. We used\nk = 1 and k = 5 for evaluation. At k = 1, it evaluates the accuracy of the top recommendation; at\nk = 5, it examines the model’s precision in a wider recommendation set.\n• Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant items in the top-k results. For synthesized queries,\nk = 20 is used, as the answer length of all of the queries in our benchmarks are equal or smaller\nthen 20. This metric offers insight into the model’s ability to identify all relevant items, particularly\nin scenarios where missing any could be critical.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "d6b58a666b2849bb189238a9d940ca09ddb474ff811b55a632b50a665f227eee",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "This capacity for single-step multi-hop retrieval yields strong performance improvements of around\n3 and 20 points over current RAG methods [10, 35, 53, 70, 71] on two popular multi-hop QA\nbenchmarks, MuSiQue [77] and 2WikiMultiHopQA [33]. Additionally, HippoRAG’s online retrieval\nprocess is 10 to 30 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster than current iterative retrieval methods\nlike IRCoT [78], while still achieving comparable performance. Furthermore, our approach can be\ncombined with IRCoT to provide complementary gains of up to 4% and 20% on the same datasets\nand even obtain improvements on HotpotQA, a less challenging multi-hop QA dataset. Finally, we\n2\n\nprovide a case study illustrating the limitations of current methods as well as our method’s potential\non the previously discussed path-finding multi-hop QA setting.\n2\nHippoRAG\nIn this section, we first give a brief overview of the hippocampal memory indexing theory, followed\nby how HippoRAG’s indexing and retrieval design was inspired by this theory, and finally offer a\nmore detailed account of our methodology.\n2.1\nThe Hippocampal Memory Indexing Theory\nThe hippocampal memory indexing theory [75] is a well-established theory that provides a functional\ndescription of the components and circuitry involved in human long-term memory. In this theory,\nTeyler and Discenna [75] propose that human long-term memory is composed of three components\nthat work together to accomplish two main objectives: pattern separation, which ensures that the\nrepresentations of distinct perceptual experiences are unique, and pattern completion, which enables\nthe retrieval of complete memories from partial stimuli [19, 76].\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "15f54620cc5281b23dbb30933a88888a8a2adf561d08c51720e8f5a8dac1424c",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. While existing works integrate LLMs and\nGNNs in various ways, they mostly focus on conventional graph tasks such as node, edge and graph\n1Our codes and datasets are available at: https://github.com/XiaoxinHe/G-Retriever\narXiv:2402.07630v3  [cs.LG]  27 May 2024\n\nNew Benchmark\nGraphQA\nNew Architecture\nG-Retriever\nTechniques\nRetrieval Augmented Generation\nGraph Prompt Tuning\nGraph Textualization\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "ffc9f975f2b7353123b586effa1bd8d3b9c4f9b7f2fbb883fbaf6af993ed8df7",
        "section": "Supplementary",
        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. However, on MuSiQue, KNN-MDR achieves the\nworst trade-off between Precision and SF-EM compared\nwith KNN-ST and TF-IDF. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality. Note that\nalthough here KNN-ST leads to a better KG than KNN-\nMDR, it does not mean the KNN baseline in Table 1 should\nperform better than MDR because the baseline name only\nrefers to the retrieval method while the name in this figure\nrefers to the KG construction method.\n"

        "section": "1. Ultrasonic characterization of",
        "text": "Finally, regardless of the higher computational costs of the rerankers, their performance remains\nsuboptimal. For instance, the Hit@1 scores for the GPT-4 reranker are only about 18% on STARK-\nPRIMEand 41% on STARK-MAG, indicating that the top-ranked answers are frequently incorrect.\nSimilarly, the Recall@20 metrics are below 60% across all datasets, with the GPT-4 reranker\nachieving Recall@20 scores of 55% on STARK-AMAZON, 49% on STARK-MAG, and 34% on\nSTARK-PRIME. This suggests that the ranking results miss a significant portion of relevant answers.\nThe MRR scores are also relatively low, especially for STARK-PRIME, where the GPT-4 reranker\nattains an MRR of only around 27%.\nThe insufficient performances may be attributed to the complexity and diversity of queries in SKBs,\nwhere nuanced understanding and detailed contextual information are crucial. These findings highlight\nsignificant room for improvement in the ranking process.\nResults on human-generated dataset. Table 7 presents the testing results on the human-generated\ndatasets. For example, the rerankers consistently outperform others, showing their reasoning and\ncontext understanding ability. Compared to the synthesized datasets, the performance on human-\ngenerated queries is generally higher for most models, but the overall trends remain consistent. This\nindicates that synthesized datasets may be more challenging, highlighting the complexity of the tasks\non our synthesized queries.\n"

        "text": "C\nDATASET\nThe statistics of the datasets used in this paper are shown in Table 9.     "chunk_833d3ae6337718121b5253c6b1048934": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_833d3ae6337718121b5253c6b1048934",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 650,
        "text": "Most existing GraphRAG methods are designed specifically for knowledge graphs and focus on node,\nedge, or triples-level retrieval [1, 36, 16, 38]. Our method is different in two main ways: 1) It focuses\non more general textual graphs, not just knowledge graphs. 2) It enables the return of a subgraph most\nclosely related to a query, rather than a list of top-k triples. The triples in other methods are chosen in\nisolation from the graph, failing to capture neighborhood information effectively. In contrast, our\nmethod takes the context into account during retrieval.\nD.2\nThe Impact of K for Retrieval\nWe identify the most relevant nodes and edges ",

        "text": "a query, rather than a list of top-k triples. The triples in other methods are chosen in\nisolation from the graph, failing to capture neighborhood information effectively.     "chunk_f800cd4e8fa59900491c3efa5f890329": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_f800cd4e8fa59900491c3efa5f890329",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 571,
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n",
        "document_tokens": 136,
        "score": 0.17342814803123474,
        "pair_tokens": 208
      }
    ],

    "chunk_19d8ae70b909311cb894aeddbb600ad8": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_19d8ae70b909311cb894aeddbb600ad8",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 710,
        "text": "One of HippoRAG’s main advantages against iterative retrieval methods is the dramatic online\nretrieval efficiency gains brought on by its single-step multi-hop retrieval ability in terms of both\ncost and time. Specifically, as seen in Table 17, retrieval costs for IRCoT are 10 to 30 times higher\nthan HippoRAG since it only requires extracting relevant named entities from the query instead of\nprocessing all of the retrieved documents.         "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real",

    "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 684,
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data.         "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, resp",

      "quote": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n",
