        "text_sha256": "35871b0592520ab8f62019ccd53994928ee8acdc397db26626d99faeaa882c8f",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "Results\nWe present our retrieval and QA experimental results below. Given that our method indirectly affects\nQA performance, we report QA results on our best-performing retrieval backbone ColBERTv2 [70].\nHowever, we report retrieval results for several strong single-step and multi-step retrieval techniques.\nSingle-Step Retrieval Results. As seen in Table 2, HippoRAG outperforms all other methods,\nincluding recent LLM-augmented baselines such as Propositionizer and RAPTOR, on our main\ndatasets, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, while achieving competitive performance on HotpotQA.\nWe notice an impressive improvement of 11 and 20% for R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand around 3% on MuSiQue. This difference can be partially explained by 2WikiMultiHopQA’s\nentity-centric design, which is particularly well-suited for HippoRAG. Our lower performance on\nHotpotQA is mainly due to its lower knowledge integration requirements, as explained in Appendix\nB, as well as a due to a concept-context tradeoff which we alleviate with an ensembling technique\ndescribed in Appendix F.2.\nMulti-Step Retrieval Results. For multi-step or iterative retrieval, our experiments in Table 3\ndemonstrate that IRCoT [78] and HippoRAG are complementary. Using HippoRAG as the re-\ntriever for IRCoT continues to bring R@5 improvements of around 4% for MuSiQue, 18% for\n2WikiMultiHopQA and an additional 1% on HotpotQA.\n6\n\nTable 4: QA performance. HippoRAG’s QA improvements correlate with its retrieval improvements\non single-step (rows 1-3) and multi-step retrieval (rows 4-5).\nMuSiQue\n2Wiki\nHotpotQA\nAverage\nRetriever\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "2550d49bf589c10eaf3da6906e6fddd6ee4871f919e56b9a6e8330772ff390fe",
        "section": "Results",
        "text": "PPR Alternatives. As shown in Table 5 (rows 5-6), to examine how much of our results are due to\nthe strength of PPR, we replace the PPR output with the query node probability #»n multiplied by node\nspecificity values (row 5) and a version of this that also distributes a small amount of probability to the\ndirect neighbors of each query node (row 6). First, we find that PPR is a much more effective method\nfor including associations for retrieval on all three datasets compared to both simple baselines. It is\ninteresting to note that adding the neighborhood of Rq nodes without PPR leads to worse performance\nthan only using the query nodes themselves.\nAblations. As seen in Table 5 (rows 7-8), node specificity obtains considerable improvements on\nMuSiQue and HotpotQA and yields almost no change in 2WikiMultiHopQA. This is likely because\n2WikiMultiHopQA relies on named entities with little differences in terms of term weighting. In\ncontrast, synonymy edges have the largest effect on 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that noisy entity\nstandardization is useful when most relevant concepts are named entities, and improvements to\nsynonymy detection could lead to stronger performance in other datasets.\n5.2\nHippoRAG’s Advantage: Single-Step Multi-Hop Retrieval\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "8fbdca23d54c9ee8f535699e55a0f1e762eed7dc58accd90bfbe033b7c288db8",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "IRCoT + HippoRAG (Contriever)\n43.9\n56.6\n75.3\n93.4\n65.8\n82.3\n61.7\n77.4\nIRCoT + HippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n45.3\n57.6\n75.8\n93.9\n67.0\n83.0\n62.7\n78.2\n3.4\nImplementation Details\nBy default, we use GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 [55] with temperature of 0 as our LLM L and Contriever\n[35] or ColBERTv2 [70] as our retriever M. We use 100 examples from MuSiQue’s training data\nto tune HippoRAG’s two hyperparameters: the synonymy threshold τ at 0.8 and the PPR damping\nfactor at 0.5, which determines the probability that PPR will restart a random walk from the query\nnodes instead of continuing to explore the graph. Generally, we find that HippoRAG’s performance\nis rather robust to its hyperparameters. More implementation details can be found in Appendix H.\n4\n"

        "text_sha256": "90ca4f68b057c367329013735770680c3cb229ca8407ea6f02fe863718b0e2e4",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets. Our experiments had a training batch size of 16 and an evaluation batch size of 32,\nyielding the following results.\nTable 12: Performance and Efficiency of Various Methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nSettting\nMethod\nHit@1\nTime\nInference-only\nQuestion only\n61.16\n31 min\nTextual graph and question\n41.06\n40 min\nFrozen LLM w/ PT\nPrompt Tuning\n48.34\n18.7 min/epoch\nG-Retriever\n70.49\n6.2 min/epoch\nTuned LLM\nLoRA\n66.03\n19 min/epoch\nG-Retriever w/ LoRA\n73.79\n6.9 min/epoch\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "af3a6d4226d6b3c87366e20e5b65424897f765f4155e48849aad79e39c2506cc",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "HippoRAG\nContriever\n41.0\n52.1\n71.5\n89.5\n59.0\n76.2\n57.2\n72.6\nColBERTv2\n40.9\n51.9\n70.7\n89.1\n60.5\n77.7\n57.4\n72.9\nHippoRAG w/\nUncertainty Ensemble\nContriever\n42.3\n54.5\n71.3\n87.2\n60.6\n79.1\n58.1\n73.6\nColBERTv2\n42.5\n54.8\n71.9\n89.0\n62.5\n80.0\n59.0\n74.6\nTo get a better trade-off between concepts and context, we introduce an ensembling setting where\nHippoRAG scores are ensembled with dense retrievers when our parahippocampal region shows\nuncertainty regarding the link between query and KG entities. This process represents instances\nwhen no hippocampal index was fully activated by the upstream parahippocampal signal and thus\nthe neocortex must be relied on more strongly. We only use uncertainty ensembling if one of the\nquery-KG entity scores cosine_similarity(M(ci), M(ej)) is lower than a threshold θ, for example,\nif there was no Stanford node in the KG and the closest node in the KG is something that has a cosine\nsimilarity lower than θ such as Stanford Medical Center. The final passage score for uncertainty\n26\n\nensembling is the average of the HippoRAG scores and standard passage retrieval using model M,\nboth of which are first normalized into the 0 to 1 over all passages.\n"
      }

        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "The findings on MetaQA are presented in Table 2.\nThe performance of KG-GPT is impressive, scoring\n96.3%, 94.4%, and 94.0% on 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-\nhop tasks respectively. This demonstrates its strong\nability to generalize from a limited number of ex-\namples, a critical trait when handling real-world\napplications with varying degrees of complexity.\nStage\nFactKG\nMetaQA\nMetaQA\nMetaQA\n1-hop\n2-hop\n3-hop\nSentence\n39\n3\n63\n100\nSegmentation\nGraph Retrieval\n17\n4\n3\n0\nInference\n44\n93\n34\n0\nTable 3: Number of errors from 100 incorrect samples\nacross each dataset.\nInterestingly, the performance of KG-GPT\nclosely matches that of a fully-supervised model.\nParticularly, it surpasses KV-Mem by margins of\n0.1%, 11.7%, and 45.1% across three distinct tasks\nrespectively, signifying its superior performance.\nWhile the overall performance of KG-GPT is simi-\nlar to that of GraftNet, a noteworthy difference is\npronounced in the 3-hop task, wherein KG-GPT\noutperforms GraftNet by 16.3%. The qualitative\nresults including the graphs retrieved by KG-GPT\nare in Appendix E.2.\n4.3\nError Analysis\n"

        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "[Incorrect response with hallucinated nodes and edges]\nThe animal in the bushes is a deer.\nNodes:\n* Deer (node 1)\n* Bushes (node 2)\nEdges:\n* Deer →Bushes (edge 1)\n* Deer →Grass (edge 2)\n* Bushes →Grass (edge 3)\nG-Retriever (Ours)\n[Correct response with accurate node and edge references]\nBased on the information provided in the graph, the animal in the bushes is an elephant.\nThe nodes that support this answer are:\n* Node 1: The elephant is mentioned in the first line of the graph.\nThe edges that support this answer are:\n* The edge connects the elephant to the bushes, indicating that the elephant is in the bushes.\nTherefore, the answer to the question is: The animal in the bushes is an elephant.\noptimization problem, which takes the neighborhood information into account during retrieval. This\nalso allows the return of a subgraph most relevant to a query, thereby improving explainability.\nThe contributions of this paper are outlined as follows:\n• Pioneering the integration of Graph RAG. We present the first retrieval approach for\ngeneral textual graph tasks, which greatly enhances scalability and efficiency.\n• Enabling ‘Chat with Your Graph’. We develop a flexible question answering framework\nto handle complex and real-world textual graphs through a unified conversational interface.\n• Introducing A Novel GraphQA Benchmark. We introduce a diverse benchmark targeted\nat real-world graph question answering, filling a crucial research gap.\n• Empirical Findings. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of G-Retriever in\nmultiple domains and present the significant finding of hallucination in graph LLMs.\n2\n"

        "section": "Conclusion",
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "ffadad8a24b98afff5373c3d1a13f932f8b1ebfa0fc1da41a2a7f203f2283e40",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n"
      }
    },

        "section": "References",
        "text": "One of HippoRAG’s main advantages against iterative retrieval methods is the dramatic online\nretrieval efficiency gains brought on by its single-step multi-hop retrieval ability in terms of both\ncost and time. Specifically, as seen in Table 17, retrieval costs for IRCoT are 10 to 30 times higher\nthan HippoRAG since it only requires extracting relevant named entities from the query instead of\nprocessing all of the retrieved documents. In systems with extremely high usage, a cost difference of\nan order of magnitude such as this one could be extremely important. The difference with IRCoT in\nterms of latency is also substantial, although more challenging to measure exactly. Also as seen in\nTable 17, HippoRAG can be 6 to 13 times faster than IRCoT, depending on the number of retrieval\nrounds that need to be executed (2-4 in our experiments).6\nTable 17: Average cost and efficiency measurements for online retrieval using GPT-3.5 Turbo on\n1,000 queries.\nColBERTv2\nIRCoT\nHippoRAG\nAPI Cost ($)\n0\n1-3\n0.1\nTime (minutes)\n1\n20-40\n3\n"

        "text_sha256": "93f2bbcd4f2e73d22123a0b360c4293fdaea9ddbdb4e4a14f998b2eb37755844",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n"
      }

        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets. These results\nunderscore the significant reduction in hallucinations with G-Retriever, particularly in the challenging\ntask of accurately citing both nodes and edges in graph-based contexts.\nG\nDemonstrations\nWe demonstrate the interaction capabilities of G-Retriever with creative questions on different\ndatasets: ExplaGraphs, SceneGraphs, and WebQSP. These examples are showcased in Tables 13,\n14, and 15, respectively.         "text_sha256": "5afd9348719b7383794053ee8b411be509786259a96b53a3b8f539a11cede540",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Graph-Augmented Reading Comprehension. Earlier works in this category are mainly supervised\nmethods which mix signal from a hyperlink or co-occurrence graph with a language model through a\ngraph neural network (GNN) [20, 67, 65]. More recent works use LLMs and introduce knowledge\ngraph triples directly into the LLM prompt [57, 43, 47]. Although these works share HippoRAG’s\nuse of graphs for multi-hop QA, their generation-based improvements are fully complementary to\nHippoRAG’s, which are solely based on improved retrieval.\nGraph-Augmented Retrieval. In this second category, previous work trains a re-ranking module\nwhich can traverse a graph made using Wikipedia hyperlinks [16, 100, 54, 14, 4, 44]. HippoRAG,\nin contrast, builds a KG from scratch using LLMs and performs multi-hop retrieval without any\nsupervision, making it much more adaptable.\n6.3\nLLMs & KGs\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "b19a2d053faea5a2dddcb08f15db46e39ca91c20626782da7eb4bd762a2963c5",
        "section": "Abstract",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "c40ce0f9ae46cb4e647633a2056fc8610097438333f98b5bdf50d1814191c07d",
        "section": "Related Work",
        "text": "Nevertheless, several limitations can be addressed in future work to enable HippoRAG to achieve\nthis goal better. First, we note that all components of HippoRAG are currently used off-the-shelf\nwithout any extra training. There is therefore much room to improve our method’s practical viability\nby performing specific component fine-tuning. This is evident in the error analysis discussed in\nAppendix F, which shows most errors made by our system are due to NER and OpenIE and thus\ncould benefit from direct fine-tuning. Given that the rest of the errors are graph search errors, also in\nAppendix F, we note that several avenues for improvements over simple PPR exist, such as allowing\nrelations to guide graph traversal directly. Additionally, as shown in Appendix F.4, more work must\nbe done to improve the consistency of OpenIE in longer compared to shorter documents. Finally,\nand perhaps most importantly, HippoRAG’s scalability still calls for further validation. Although we\nshow that Llama-3.1 could obtain similar performance to closed-source models and thus reduce costs\nconsiderably, we are yet to empirically prove the efficiency and efficacy of our synthetic hippocampal\nindex as its size grows way beyond current benchmarks.\n"
      }

        "section": "References",
        "text": "The choice of similarity function is also important. In this work, we use cosine similarity, a widely\nadopted metric for measuring vector similarity in models that process vision and language. For\ninstance, CLIP also employs cosine similarity to assess the similarity between text and image\nfeatures. Although it might not be the optimal choice, we believe that cosine similarity is a general,\nrepresentative, and valid choice for facilitating fast retrieval tasks.\nD.4\nThe Quality of Retrieval\nWe quantify the quality of our retrieval method as follows: We examine the retrieval subgraph, and if\nthe label is contained within it, we consider it a successful retrieval. We calculate the retrieval success\nrate of our method and the retrieval method proposed in KAPING [1] on the WebQSP dataset.\nTable 11: The quality of retrieval methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nMethod\nRetrieval Accuracy\nKAPING [1] (top-k triple retrieval)\n60.81\nG-Retriever\n70.49\nAs shown in Table 11, these results validate the effectiveness of our retrieval method. In contrast to\nthe triple-based retrieval in KAPING, which relies on the similarity between triples and the query,\nour PCST-based subgraph retrieval is more accurate as it takes the graph structure into account.         "text_sha256": "62d2d6bc92494bd2583e0391cd268b756f954000661bdb5a9432e49168a291d3",
        "section": "Limitations",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n"
      }
    },

        "text_sha256": "69abe6a4474d2cefde097e9e74403b7c69b9b41456f72f0ac86fde38db6bf54d",
        "section": "References",
        "text": "Most existing GraphRAG methods are designed specifically for knowledge graphs and focus on node,\nedge, or triples-level retrieval [1, 36, 16, 38]. Our method is different in two main ways: 1) It focuses\non more general textual graphs, not just knowledge graphs. 2) It enables the return of a subgraph most\nclosely related to a query, rather than a list of top-k triples. The triples in other methods are chosen in\nisolation from the graph, failing to capture neighborhood information effectively. In contrast, our\nmethod takes the context into account during retrieval.\nD.2\nThe Impact of K for Retrieval\nWe identify the most relevant nodes and edges and use a k-nearest neighbors retrieval approach (see\nEquation 6). Small k values may omit crucial knowledge or information relevant to the query, while\nlarge k values could introduce excessive information, distracting the model from the essential details.\nTo evaluate the impact of the number of k, we have conducted additional experiments by varying the\nchoice of k to 3, 5, 10, and 20.\nTable 10: The impact of k on the webqsp dataset.\nk\n3\n5\n10\n20\nHit@1\n0.6977\n0.7063\n0.7248\n0.7039\nAs shown in Table 10, the Hit@1 metric initially rises for small k values, peaks at a certain point, and\nthen declines for large k values. Determining the optimal k value can be achieved through techniques\nlike cross-validation using a validation set.\nD.3\nThe Choice of Similarity Function\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "e3645042e8fa1db19322302d9398f691f06ddf5d1d132e559caa7e5dbad8ccae",
        "section": "Experiments",
        "text": "• LLM Rerankers: Claude3 and GPT-4 rerankers [11, 62]. These models improve the precision of\ntop-k ada-002 results by reranking them using large language models. We employ GPT-4-turbo\n(gpt-4-1106-preview) and Claude3 (claude-3-opus), setting k = 20 for synthesized\nqueries and k = 10 for human-generated queries. Given a query, the LLMs assign a satisfaction\nscore from 0 to 1 to each candidate entity based on textual and relational information. Due to high\ncomputational costs, we evaluate these rerankers on a random 10% sample of test queries.\nThe performance of these models are measured using standard retrieval metrics below.\n• Hit@k assesses whether the correct item is among the top-k results from the model. We used\nk = 1 and k = 5 for evaluation. At k = 1, it evaluates the accuracy of the top recommendation; at\nk = 5, it examines the model’s precision in a wider recommendation set.\n• Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant items in the top-k results. For synthesized queries,\nk = 20 is used, as the answer length of all of the queries in our benchmarks are equal or smaller\nthen 20. This metric offers insight into the model’s ability to identify all relevant items, particularly\nin scenarios where missing any could be critical.\n"
      }

        "text_sha256": "15f54620cc5281b23dbb30933a88888a8a2adf561d08c51720e8f5a8dac1424c",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. While existing works integrate LLMs and\nGNNs in various ways, they mostly focus on conventional graph tasks such as node, edge and graph\n1Our codes and datasets are available at: https://github.com/XiaoxinHe/G-Retriever\narXiv:2402.07630v3  [cs.LG]  27 May 2024\n\nNew Benchmark\nGraphQA\nNew Architecture\nG-Retriever\nTechniques\nRetrieval Augmented Generation\nGraph Prompt Tuning\nGraph Textualization\n"
      }

Implementing our graph-based\nretrieval significantly decreases the number of tokens required to describe the graphs in text, reduces\nthe number of nodes in graphs, and speeds up the training process. Specifically, for the SceneGraphs\ndataset, tokens decreased by 83%, nodes by 74%, and training time by 29%. For the WebQSP dataset,\ntokens decreased by 99%, nodes by 99%, and training time by 67%.         "text_sha256": "d6b58a666b2849bb189238a9d940ca09ddb474ff811b55a632b50a665f227eee",
        "section": "Introduction",
        "text": "This capacity for single-step multi-hop retrieval yields strong performance improvements of around\n3 and 20 points over current RAG methods [10, 35, 53, 70, 71] on two popular multi-hop QA\nbenchmarks, MuSiQue [77] and 2WikiMultiHopQA [33]. Additionally, HippoRAG’s online retrieval\nprocess is 10 to 30 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster than current iterative retrieval methods\nlike IRCoT [78], while still achieving comparable performance. Furthermore, our approach can be\ncombined with IRCoT to provide complementary gains of up to 4% and 20% on the same datasets\nand even obtain improvements on HotpotQA, a less challenging multi-hop QA dataset. Finally, we\n2\n\nprovide a case study illustrating the limitations of current methods as well as our method’s potential\non the previously discussed path-finding multi-hop QA setting.\n2\nHippoRAG\nIn this section, we first give a brief overview of the hippocampal memory indexing theory, followed\nby how HippoRAG’s indexing and retrieval design was inspired by this theory, and finally offer a\nmore detailed account of our methodology.\n2.1\nThe Hippocampal Memory Indexing Theory\nThe hippocampal memory indexing theory [75] is a well-established theory that provides a functional\ndescription of the components and circuitry involved in human long-term memory. In this theory,\nTeyler and Discenna [75] propose that human long-term memory is composed of three components\nthat work together to accomplish two main objectives: pattern separation, which ensures that the\nrepresentations of distinct perceptual experiences are unique, and pattern completion, which enables\nthe retrieval of complete memories from partial stimuli [19, 76].\n"
      }
    },

        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. However, on MuSiQue, KNN-MDR achieves the\nworst trade-off between Precision and SF-EM compared\nwith KNN-ST and TF-IDF. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality. Note that\nalthough here KNN-ST leads to a better KG than KNN-\nMDR, it does not mean the KNN baseline in Table 1 should\nperform better than MDR because the baseline name only\nrefers to the retrieval method while the name in this figure\nrefers to the KG construction method.\n"

        "text_sha256": "f774520d941e0bceaf357ecf8f60c10ec9a7db021fe3bc96c9bc627faeb3ca4c",
        "section": "1. Ultrasonic characterization of",
        "text": "Finally, regardless of the higher computational costs of the rerankers, their performance remains\nsuboptimal. For instance, the Hit@1 scores for the GPT-4 reranker are only about 18% on STARK-\nPRIMEand 41% on STARK-MAG, indicating that the top-ranked answers are frequently incorrect.\nSimilarly, the Recall@20 metrics are below 60% across all datasets, with the GPT-4 reranker\nachieving Recall@20 scores of 55% on STARK-AMAZON, 49% on STARK-MAG, and 34% on\nSTARK-PRIME. This suggests that the ranking results miss a significant portion of relevant answers.\nThe MRR scores are also relatively low, especially for STARK-PRIME, where the GPT-4 reranker\nattains an MRR of only around 27%.\nThe insufficient performances may be attributed to the complexity and diversity of queries in SKBs,\nwhere nuanced understanding and detailed contextual information are crucial. These findings highlight\nsignificant room for improvement in the ranking process.\nResults on human-generated dataset. Table 7 presents the testing results on the human-generated\ndatasets. For example, the rerankers consistently outperform others, showing their reasoning and\ncontext understanding ability. Compared to the synthesized datasets, the performance on human-\ngenerated queries is generally higher for most models, but the overall trends remain consistent. This\nindicates that synthesized datasets may be more challenging, highlighting the complexity of the tasks\non our synthesized queries.\n"

    "chunk_b1e16d1c0cce0b7a5286e2e0f30b9821": [

        "chunk_id": "chunk_b1e16d1c0cce0b7a5286e2e0f30b9821",
        "text": "Results\nWe present our retrieval and QA experimental results below. Given that our method indirectly affects\nQA performance, we report QA results on our best-performing retrieval backbone ColBERTv2 [70].\nHowever, we report retrieval results for several strong single-step and multi-step retrieval techniques.\nSingle-Step Retrieval Results. As seen in Table 2, HippoRAG outperforms all other methods,\nincluding recent LLM-augmented baselines such as Propositionizer and RAPTOR, on our main\ndatasets, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, while achieving competitive performance on HotpotQA.\nWe notice an impressive improvement of 11 and 20% for R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand around 3% on MuSiQue. This difference can be partially explained by 2WikiMultiHopQA’s\nentity-centric design, which is particularly well-suited for HippoRAG. Our lower performance on\nHotpotQA is mainly due to its lower knowledge integration requirements, as explained in Appendix\nB, as well as a due to a concept-context tradeoff which we alleviate with an ensembling technique\ndescribed in Appendix F.2.\nMulti-Step Retrieval Results. For multi-step or iterative retrieval, our experiments in Table 3\ndemonstrate that IRCoT [78] and HippoRAG are complementary. Using HippoRAG as the re-\ntriever for IRCoT continues to bring R@5 improvements of around 4% for MuSiQue, 18% for\n2WikiMultiHopQA and an additional 1% on HotpotQA.\n6\n\nTable 4: QA performance. HippoRAG’s QA improvements correlate with its retrieval improvements\non single-step (rows 1-3) and multi-step retrieval (rows 4-5).\nMuSiQue\n2Wiki\nHotpotQA\nAverage\nRetriever\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\n",

As expected,\nimproved retrieval performance in both single and multi-step settings leads to strong overall im-\nprovements of up to 3%, 17% and 1% F1 scores on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA\nrespectively using the same QA reader. Notably, single-step HippoRAG is on par or outperforms\nIRCoT while being 10-30 times cheaper and 6-13 times faster during online retrieval (Appendix G).\n5\nDiscussions\n5.1\nWhat Makes HippoRAG Work?\n",

    "chunk_833d3ae6337718121b5253c6b1048934": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_833d3ae6337718121b5253c6b1048934",
        "text": "Most existing GraphRAG methods are designed specifically for knowledge graphs and focus on node,\nedge, or triples-level retrieval [1, 36, 16, 38]. Our method is different in two main ways: 1) It focuses\non more general textual graphs, not just knowledge graphs. 2) It enables the return of a subgraph most\nclosely related to a query, rather than a list of top-k triples. The triples in other methods are chosen in\nisolation from the graph, failing to capture neighborhood information effectively. In contrast, our\nmethod takes the context into account during retrieval.\nD.2\nThe Impact of K for Retrieval\nWe identify the most relevant nodes and edges and use a k-nearest neighbors retrieval approach (see\nEquation 6). Small k values may omit crucial knowledge or information relevant to the query, while\nlarge k values could introduce excessive information, distracting the model from the essential details.\nTo evaluate the impact of the number of k, we have conducted additional experiments by varying the\nchoice of k to 3, 5, 10, and 20.\nTable 10: The impact of k on the webqsp dataset.\nk\n3\n5\n10\n20\nHit@1\n0.6977\n0.7063\n0.7248\n0.7039\nAs shown in Table 10, the Hit@1 metric initially rises for small k values, peaks at a certain point, and\nthen declines for large k values. Determining the optimal k value can be achieved through techniques\nlike cross-validation using a validation set.\nD.3\nThe Choice of Similarity Function\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1424,
        "score": 0.0699218362569809,
        "pair_tokens": 429
      }
    ],
    "chunk_f800cd4e8fa59900491c3efa5f890329": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_f800cd4e8fa59900491c3efa5f890329",
        "text": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 571,
        "score": 0.17342814803123474,
        "pair_tokens": 208
      }
    ],
    "chunk_67a081d945c23e9c2de3a746cbacb122": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_67a081d945c23e9c2de3a746cbacb122",
        "text": "HippoRAG\nContriever\n41.0\n52.1\n71.5\n89.5\n59.0\n76.2\n57.2\n72.6\nColBERTv2\n40.9\n51.9\n70.7\n89.1\n60.5\n77.7\n57.4\n72.9\nHippoRAG w/\nUncertainty Ensemble\nContriever\n42.3\n54.5\n71.3\n87.2\n60.6\n79.1\n58.1\n73.6\nColBERTv2\n42.5\n54.8\n71.9\n89.0\n62.5\n80.0\n59.0\n74.6\nTo get a better trade-off between concepts and context, we introduce an ensembling setting where\nHippoRAG scores are ensembled with dense retrievers when our parahippocampal region shows\nuncertainty regarding the link between query and KG entities. This process represents instances\nwhen no hippocampal index was fully activated by the upstream parahippocampal signal and thus\nthe neocortex must be relied on more strongly. We only use uncertainty ensembling if one of the\nquery-KG entity scores cosine_similarity(M(ci), M(ej)) is lower than a threshold θ, for example,\nif there was no Stanford node in the KG and the closest node in the KG is something that has a cosine\nsimilarity lower than θ such as Stanford Medical Center. The final passage score for uncertainty\n26\n\nensembling is the average of the HippoRAG scores and standard passage retrieval using model M,\nboth of which are first normalized into the 0 to 1 over all passages.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1182,
        "score": 0.2041831612586975,
        "pair_tokens": 416
      }
    ],

    "chunk_e1075e95da37350e255f0b8602384c99": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_e1075e95da37350e255f0b8602384c99",
        "text": "The choice of similarity function is also important. In this work, we use cosine similarity, a widely\nadopted metric for measuring vector similarity in models that process vision and language. For\ninstance, CLIP also employs cosine similarity to assess the similarity between text and image\nfeatures. Although it might not be the optimal choice, we believe that cosine similarity is a general,\nrepresentative, and valid choice for facilitating fast retrieval tasks.\nD.4\nThe Quality of Retrieval\nWe quantify the quality of our retrieval method as follows: We examine the retrieval subgraph, and if\nthe label is contained within it, we consider it a successful retrieval. We calculate the retrieval success\nrate of our method and the retrieval method proposed in KAPING [1] on the WebQSP dataset.\nTable 11: The quality of retrieval methods on the WebQSP dataset.\nMethod\nRetrieval Accuracy\nKAPING [1] (top-k triple retrieval)\n60.81\nG-Retriever\n70.49\nAs shown in Table 11, these results validate the effectiveness of our retrieval method. In contrast to\nthe triple-based retrieval in KAPING, which relies on the similarity between triples and the query,\nour PCST-based subgraph retrieval is more accurate as it takes the graph structure into account. By\ndesign, it retrieves connected subgraphs, capturing not just nodes or edges with high relevance scores,\nbut also those that act as \"bridges\" connecting other highly relevant nodes and edges.\n18\n\nE\nDiscussion on the Complexity\nE.1\nThe integration of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1523,
        "score": 0.104843370616436,
        "pair_tokens": 454
      }
    ],
    "chunk_000fb51c29790f99fdf023d7b338666c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_000fb51c29790f99fdf023d7b338666c",
        "text": "Results. The results, as depicted in Table 5, illustrate the comparative effectiveness of the G-Retriever\nover the baseline LLM+Graph Prompt Tuning method in reducing hallucinations. The LLM+Graph\nPrompt Tuning approach demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy in referencing graph elements,\n19\n\nwith only 31% of nodes and 12% of edges being valid, and the entire set of nodes and edges being\nvalid only 8% of the time. In contrast, G-Retriever showed substantial improvements: 77% validity\nin nodes, 76% in edges, and 62% in the overall validity of referenced node-edge sets. These results\nunderscore the significant reduction in hallucinations with G-Retriever, particularly in the challenging\ntask of accurately citing both nodes and edges in graph-based contexts.\nG\nDemonstrations\nWe demonstrate the interaction capabilities of G-Retriever with creative questions on different\ndatasets: ExplaGraphs, SceneGraphs, and WebQSP. These examples are showcased in Tables 13,\n14, and 15, respectively. Additionally, the examples are visualized in Figure 1.\n20\n\nTable 13: Example of creative chat on ExplaGraphs.\nGraph\nnode_id,node_attr\n0,human\n1,cosmetic surgery\n2,women\n3,change appearance\n4,addiction\n5,searching for perfection\n6,stop\n7,positive\nsrc,edge_attr,dst\n0,receives action,1\n2,part of,0\n1,used for,3\n3,capable of,4\n4,created by,5\n4,not capable of,6\n4,is not a,7\nUser\nWrite a 500-word argument essay based on the information provided in the explanation graph.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1469,
        "score": 0.1474323868751526,
        "pair_tokens": 487
      }
    ],

        "text": "IRCoT + HippoRAG (Contriever)\n43.9\n56.6\n75.3\n93.4\n65.8\n82.3\n61.7\n77.4\nIRCoT + HippoRAG (ColBERTv2)\n45.3\n57.6\n75.8\n93.9\n67.0\n83.0\n62.7\n78.2\n3.4\nImplementation Details\nBy default, we use GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 [55] with temperature of 0 as our LLM L and Contriever\n[35] or ColBERTv2 [70] as our retriever M. We use 100 examples from MuSiQue’s training data\nto tune HippoRAG’s two hyperparameters: the synonymy threshold τ at 0.8 and the PPR damping\nfactor at 0.5, which determines the probability that PPR will restart a random walk from the query\nnodes instead of continuing to explore the graph. Generally, we find that HippoRAG’s performance\nis rather robust to its hyperparameters. More implementation details can be found in Appendix H.\n4\n",

    "chunk_2da94a87e97c2e0f30e8eec5659e202d": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_2da94a87e97c2e0f30e8eec5659e202d",
        "text": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n",

        "chunk_id": "chunk_5165b9cf6ecfd6eecbf447ff18649999",
        "text": "Nevertheless, several limitations can be addressed in future work to enable HippoRAG to achieve\nthis goal better. First, we note that all components of HippoRAG are currently used off-the-shelf\nwithout any extra training. There is therefore much room to improve our method’s practical viability\nby performing specific component fine-tuning. This is evident in the error analysis discussed in\nAppendix F, which shows most errors made by our system are due to NER and OpenIE and thus\ncould benefit from direct fine-tuning. Given that the rest of the errors are graph search errors, also in\nAppendix F, we note that several avenues for improvements over simple PPR exist, such as allowing\nrelations to guide graph traversal directly. Additionally, as shown in Appendix F.4, more work must\nbe done to improve the consistency of OpenIE in longer compared to shorter documents. Finally,\nand perhaps most importantly, HippoRAG’s scalability still calls for further validation. Although we\nshow that Llama-3.1 could obtain similar performance to closed-source models and thus reduce costs\nconsiderably, we are yet to empirically prove the efficiency and efficacy of our synthetic hippocampal\nindex as its size grows way beyond current benchmarks.\n",

        "chunk_id": "chunk_b8f804ce7bc81bbbf659aff60ac33d60",
        "text": "G-Retriever is framework integrate the strengths of GNNs, LLMs and GraphRAG. The LLM+X\nframework, which involves enriching LLMs with multi-modal capabilities by integrating an LLM\nwith an encoder from another modality, is a widely adopted approach. Notable examples include\nLlava, MiniGPT-4, and Flamingo, among others. They are not complex in terms of understanding\nor implementation. Regarding the integration of GraphRAG, it does not require training and can\nbe implemented during the preprocessing stage or on the fly. This approach does not significantly\nincrease time complexity or computational complexity. On the contrary, it can substantially reduce\nthe size of the graph (e.g., eliminating 99% of nodes in the WebQSP dataset), which in turn speeds\nup the overall running time (e.g., reducing it from 18.7 min/epoch to 6.2 min/epoch on the WebQSP\ndataset).\nE.2\nComputational Resources\nUtilizing two A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of memory, we conducted tests on Llama2-7b and\nWebQSP datasets.         "text": "Introduction\nGraphs and Large Language Models (LLMs). The advent of LLMs has significantly shaped the\nartificial intelligence landscape. As these models are applied to increasingly diverse tasks, their ability\nto process complex structured data will be increasingly vital. In particular, in our interconnected\nworld, a significant portion of real-world data inherently possesses a graph structure, such as the\nWeb, e-commerce, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and many others. Moreover, many\nof these involve graphs with textual attributes (i.e., textual graphs), making them well-suited for\nLLM-centric methods. This has spurred interest in combining graph-based technologies, particularly\ngraph neural networks (GNNs), with LLMs to enhance their reasoning on graphs [44, 15, 24].\nThe Present Work: Enabling ‘Chat With Your Graph’. Due to high\ncomputational costs, we evaluate these rerankers on a random 10% sample of test queries.\nThe performance of these models are measured using standard retrieval metrics below.\n• Hit@k assesses whether the correct item is among the top-k results from the model. At k = 1, it evaluates the accuracy of the top recommendation; at\nk = 5, it examines the model’s precision in a wider recommendation set.\n• Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant items in the top-k results. For synthesized queries,\nk = 20 is used, as the answer length of all of the queries in our benchmarks are equal or smaller\nthen 20.         "text": "This capacity for single-step multi-hop retrieval yields strong performance improvements of around\n3 and 20 points over current RAG methods [10, 35, 53, 70, 71] on two popular multi-hop QA\nbenchmarks, MuSiQue [77] and 2WikiMultiHopQA [33]. Additionally, HippoRAG’s online retrieval\nprocess is 10 to 30 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster than current iterative retrieval methods\nlike IRCoT [78], while still achieving comparable performance. Finally, we\n2\n\nprovide a case study illustrating the limitations of current methods as well as our method’s potential\non the previously discussed path-finding multi-hop QA setting.\n2\nHippoRAG\nIn this section, we first give a brief overview of the hippocampal memory indexing theory, followed\nby how HippoRAG’s indexing and retrieval design was inspired by this theory, and finally offer a\nmore detailed account of our methodology.\n2.1\nThe Hippocampal Memory Indexing Theory\nThe hippocampal memory indexing theory [75] is a well-established theory that provides a functional\ndescription of the components and circuitry involved in human long-term memory. In this theory,\nTeyler and Discenna [75] propose that human long-term memory is composed of three components\nthat work together to accomplish two main objectives: pattern separation, which ensures that the\nrepresentations of distinct perceptual experiences are unique, and pattern completion, which enables\nthe retrieval of complete memories from partial stimuli [19, 76].\n",

In\ncontrast, synonymy edges have the largest effect on 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that noisy entity\nstandardization is useful when most relevant concepts are named entities, and improvements to\nsynonymy detection could lead to stronger performance in other datasets.\n5.2\nHippoRAG’s Advantage: Single-Step Multi-Hop Retrieval\n",

    "chunk_a4963bc9a949cc8fa87d1c46b7c95760": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_a4963bc9a949cc8fa87d1c46b7c95760",
        "text": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1477,
        "score": 0.15215818583965302,
        "pair_tokens": 497
      }
    ],
    "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_3a7f7a1f47b2586d9d9877afb9110567",
        "text": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1542,
        "score": 0.14033624529838562,
        "pair_tokens": 454
      }
    ],
    "chunk_d9eb528a051dc54a057f53f0af7fe0e6": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_d9eb528a051dc54a057f53f0af7fe0e6",
        "text": "Require logically ordered\nsupporting facts to pre-train the model\nKnowledge\nBase\nEntity\nRelationship\nSpecific\nHuman\nYes\n/\nPowerful in encoding\nfactual information\nRelation Extraction is non-trivial\nDomain Specific\n8.6\nAdditional Results and Discussions\nQuality of KG on MuSiQue\nSimilar to the setting used\nfor Figure 5, we change the hyperparameters to construct\nKGs for each question in MuSiQue with varying levels\nof sparsity and measure how much percentage of the sup-\nporting facts are covered by neighbors of the seeding pas-\nsages that are initially retrieved by TF-IDF. The general\ntrend is similar to the one in Figure 5, i.e., as the graph\nbecomes denser, the precision decreases while the SF-EM\nincreases. However, on MuSiQue, KNN-MDR achieves the\nworst trade-off between Precision and SF-EM compared\nwith KNN-ST and TF-IDF. This is because our KNN-MDR\nis pre-trained on HotpotQA and due to the distribution shift\nfrom HotpotQA to MuSiQue, it is expected for the graph\nconstructed with KNN-MDR to have less quality. Note that\nalthough here KNN-ST leads to a better KG than KNN-\nMDR, it does not mean the KNN baseline in Table 1 should\nperform better than MDR because the baseline name only\nrefers to the retrieval method while the name in this figure\nrefers to the KG construction method.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 1299,
        "score": 0.012920473702251911,
        "pair_tokens": 411
      }

    "chunk_513a6dee6b9d2e8bac593f0a139f9ba4": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_513a6dee6b9d2e8bac593f0a139f9ba4",
        "text": "Graph-Augmented Reading Comprehension. Earlier works in this category are mainly supervised\nmethods which mix signal from a hyperlink or co-occurrence graph with a language model through a\ngraph neural network (GNN) [20, 67, 65]. More recent works use LLMs and introduce knowledge\ngraph triples directly into the LLM prompt [57, 43, 47]. Although these works share HippoRAG’s\nuse of graphs for multi-hop QA, their generation-based improvements are fully complementary to\nHippoRAG’s, which are solely based on improved retrieval.\nGraph-Augmented Retrieval. In this second category, previous work trains a re-ranking module\nwhich can traverse a graph made using Wikipedia hyperlinks [16, 100, 54, 14, 4, 44]. HippoRAG,\nin contrast, builds a KG from scratch using LLMs and performs multi-hop retrieval without any\nsupervision, making it much more adaptable.\n6.3\nLLMs & KGs\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 870,
        "score": 0.14426936209201813,
        "pair_tokens": 313
      }
    ],
    "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_c8372b1b00fdee8ddcf8b17d0c6a629c",
        "text": "Limitations\nOur study has two key limitations. Firstly, KG-GPT\nis highly dependent on in-context learning, and its\nperformance varies significantly with the number\nof examples provided. The framework struggles\nparticularly with complex tasks when there are in-\nsufficient or low-quality examples. Secondly, de-\nspite its impressive performance in fact-verification\nand question-answering tasks, KG-GPT still lags\nbehind fully supervised KG-specific models. The\ngap in performance highlights the challenges faced\nby KG-GPT in a few-shot learning scenario due to\nlimited data. Future research should focus on op-\ntimizing language models leveraging KGs to over-\ncome these limitations.\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 684,
        "score": 0.09434341639280319,
        "pair_tokens": 226
      }
    ],
    "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_61e96cb10e247f7d002b4163920cc737",
        "text": "Abstract\nWhile large language models (LLMs) have\nmade considerable advancements in under-\nstanding and generating unstructured text, their\napplication in structured data remains underex-\nplored. Particularly, using LLMs for complex\nreasoning tasks on knowledge graphs (KGs)\nremains largely untouched. To address this,\nwe propose KG-GPT, a multi-purpose frame-\nwork leveraging LLMs for tasks employing\nKGs. KG-GPT comprises three steps: Sentence\nSegmentation, Graph Retrieval, and Inference,\neach aimed at partitioning sentences, retriev-\ning relevant graph components, and deriving\nlogical conclusions, respectively. We evalu-\nate KG-GPT using KG-based fact verification\nand KGQA benchmarks, with the model show-\ning competitive and robust performance, even\noutperforming several fully-supervised models.\nOur work, therefore, marks a significant step\nin unifying structured and unstructured data\nprocessing within the realm of LLMs.1\n1\n",
        "start_char": 0,
        "end_char": 936,
        "score": 0.16626887023448944,
        "pair_tokens": 314
      }
    ],
    "chunk_a8be21889a1afd7a234a4d0521059da8": [
      {
        "chunk_id": "chunk_a8be21889a1afd7a234a4d0521059da8",
        "text": "Finally, regardless of the higher computational costs of the rerankers, their performance remains\nsuboptimal. For instance, the Hit@1 scores for the GPT-4 reranker are only about 18% on STARK-\nPRIMEand 41% on STARK-MAG, indicating that the top-ranked answers are frequently incorrect.\nSimilarly, the Recall@20 metrics are below 60% across all datasets, with the GPT-4 reranker\nachieving Recall@20 scores of 55% on STARK-AMAZON, 49% on STARK-MAG, and 34% on\nSTARK-PRIME. This suggests that the ranking results miss a significant portion of relevant answers.\nThe MRR scores are also relatively low, especially for STARK-PRIME, where the GPT-4 reranker\nattains an MRR of only around 27%.\nThe insufficient performances may be attributed to the complexity and diversity of queries in SKBs,\nwhere nuanced understanding and detailed contextual information are crucial. These findings highlight\nsignificant room for improvement in the ranking process.\nResults on human-generated dataset. Table 7 presents the testing results on the human-generated\ndatasets. For example, the rerankers consistently outperform others, showing their reasoning and\ncontext understanding ability. Compared to the synthesized datasets, the performance on human-\ngenerated queries is generally higher for most models, but the overall trends remain consistent. This\nindicates that synthesized datasets may be more challenging, highlighting the complexity of the tasks\non our synthesized queries.\n",

This\nalso allows the return of a subgraph most relevant to a query, thereby improving explainability.\nThe contributions of this paper are outlined as follows:\n• Pioneering the integration of Graph RAG. We present the first retrieval approach for\ngeneral textual graph tasks, which greatly enhances scalability and efficiency.\n• Enabling ‘Chat with Your Graph’.
